Executable evidence in-repo: test/GelatoVRFCoordinator.t.sol:68-93 and the full-gameplay test at 221-244 both request and fulfil with no `vm.roll` and no `vm.warp` between them, and pass (verified by running `forge test --match-path test/GelatoVRFCoordinator.t.sol`, 8/8 pass). This directly contradicts the core's stated invariant at FWA.sol:230-232: 'Floor on requestConfirmations. It is the security axiom — no VRF word can exist before this many blocks'. FWA sends `requestConfirmations = 3` and the coordinator silently discards it. Grinding variant: `_nextRound()` (215-221) picks `round(block.timestamp) + 1` on chain 999, whose beacon publishes between `block.timestamp+1` and `block.timestamp+3` seconds. If the block's timestamp is behind real time by that margin, the beacon is already public when the acquisition executes. An attacker deploys a wrapper W, calls `FWA.acquire` (which returns `requestId`, FWA.sol:1250-1257), reads `coordinator.requests(requestId).targetRound`, recomputes `keccak256(abi.encode(knownRandomness, address(coordinator), 999, requestId)) % pool.totalWeight()` with `knownRandomness` passed in as calldata, and `revert`s the entire transaction unless the resulting slot is the desired listing. Cost per attempt is gas on a reverted transaction; the loop is repeated until a favourable block, giving a free re-roll on the draw with no operator collusion.
findings.impact: The core's explicit anti-reorg / anti-prediction axiom is unenforced at the boundary that is supposed to enforce it. Under any sustained timestamp lag, ordinary users can select their own outcome by revert-grinding, taking high-backing listings at the pool's flat fee — the same depositor-value drain as the operator attack but available to anyone. Even absent lag, the safety margin on 999 is one drand period (~3 s) of wall-clock, with zero block-height enforcement, versus Chainlink's 3-block commitment that FWA was written against.
findings.minimalFix: In `fulfillRandomness`, add both gates: `if (block.number < uint256(request.requestedAtBlock) + request.requestConfirmations) revert TooEarly();` and `if (block.timestamp < DRAND_GENESIS_TIME + (round - 1) * DRAND_PERIOD_SECONDS) revert RoundNotAvailable();` (the second mirrors DrandRelayCoordinator.sol:163). Additionally widen `_nextRound()` on 999 from `+1` to an offset that covers `requestConfirmations` blocks plus a clock-skew margin (e.g. `+3`, ~9 s), and document that the offset must exceed the chain's worst-case timestamp lag.
findings.regressionTest: `testFulfillmentRejectedBeforeConfirmationsAndBeforeRound`: request, then (a) fulfil in the same block and expect `TooEarly`; (b) `vm.roll(+3)` but keep `block.timestamp` before `roundTimestamp(targetRound)` and expect `RoundNotAvailable`; (c) roll and warp past both and assert success. Plus `testTargetRoundIsAlwaysStrictlyFutureByMargin`: fuzz `block.timestamp`, assert `roundTimestamp(_nextRound()) >= block.timestamp + MARGIN`.

refutationNotes.reason: SURVIVES on facts, high is overstated; correct severity is medium. Every factual claim verified: Request.requestedAtBlock (line 34) and requestConfirmations (line 36) are written at 123/125 and read nowhere in logic; fulfillRandomness (140-168) has no block.number and no block.timestamp gate, while the testnet sibling DOES gate at DrandRelayCoordinator.sol:163 (`if (block.timestamp < roundTimestamp(round)) revert RoundNotAvailable()`); _nextRound() at 215-221 uses `block.chainid == 1 ? 4 : 1`, so 999 targets currentRound+1, which by the round arithmetic publishes only 1-3 seconds after block.timestamp; and the FWA.sol:230-232 comment ('It is the security axiom — no VRF word can exist before this many blocks') is verbatim as quoted. I re-ran test/GelatoVRFCoordinator.t.sol: 8/8 pass with request and fulfilment in the same block, no vm.roll and no vm.warp, so the absence of any confirmation gate is executably demonstrated. The downgrade is about exploitability, not accuracy: the user-side revert-grinding attack requires block.timestamp to lag wall-clock by >=3 s in a sustained way, which is asserted but nowhere evidenced for HyperEVM and is not something the repo can show; absent that lag the target round is genuinely unpublished at acquire time. The remaining, unconditional content is that the boundary meant to enforce the core's stated axiom does not enforce it and is strictly weaker than the 998 rehearsal contract — a gate that fails open, which is exactly medium under the rubric. It is also substantially subsumed by finding 1: an operator that can pick any word does not need the timing lever.

THE CODE OBSERVATION IS TRUE; THE EXPLOIT IS NOT ESTABLISHED, SO 'high' IS MATERIALLY OVERSTATED. Confirmed: `requestedAtBlock` (34, written 123) and `requestConfirmations` (36, written 125) are read nowhere; `fulfillRandomness` (140-168) checks only operator, status and payload hash; DrandRelayCoordinator.sol:163 does gate on `block.timestamp < roundTimestamp(round)` and the Gelato one does not. I ran `forge test --match-path test/GelatoVRFCoordinator.t.sol` — 8/8 pass with request and fulfilment in the same block, as claimed. But the central assertion, that FWA's anti-prediction axiom is unenforced, is wrong in substance: it IS enforced, at request time rather than fulfil time, by `_nextRound()` (215-221), which pins a drand round whose beacon publishes strictly after `block.timestamp` (by 1-3 s on chain 999). A word for that round does not exist when the request is made. Second, an 'early' fulfilment is reachable only by the OPERATOR, who by finding #1 can already supply any word — so the missing round gate grants no capability that does not already exist. Third, the only independent claim, revert-grinding by an ordinary user, requires the attacker to precommit `knownRandomness` in calldata for a round that publishes strictly after the mined block's timestamp; that is possible only if `block.timestamp` is BEHIND the wall-clock moment the attacker built the transaction. Under normal operation the block timestamp is at or after submission time, so the target round is unpublished and the grind cannot start. The finding offers no evidence that HyperEVM produces past-dated timestamps — it is an assumed chain anomaly, and the mandate's evidence bar is not met. What survives is hardening: the worst-case margin is one second of integer timestamp, which is thin for a security property, and widening the `_nextRound()` offset on 999 plus adding the two gates is cheap and correct.

findings.title: Nest can permanently brick the FWA market, the buyback engine and the purchaser token-claim path; FWATokenNest has no HYPE rescue
findings.preconditions: Nest market launched and wired (token.pool/plugin/adapter/rewardsPool set). The Nest factory administrator (an external third party) changes any of the FWA pool's fee, communityFee, tickSpacing, plugin address, or pluginConfig. The hyperevm-fork-test proves this authority exists and is exercised: NestDeployment.t.sol:99-105 impersonates factory.owner() to call pool.setFee/setCommunityFee/setTickSpacing, and testNestCurrentDefaultsRequireAdminConfigurationForFWA asserts Nest's platform defaults are fee=500 and communityFee=1000 while the live wHYPE/USDC pool runs communityFee=1000 and tickSpacing=5.
findings.scenario: 1) Launch completes with pool.fee=10000, communityFee=0, tickSpacing=60, pluginConfig=7 — the FWA pool is the only Nest pool earning Nest zero community fee. 2) Nest later restores their platform default with a single pool.setCommunityFee(1000) (or setPlugin to their standard dynamic-fee plugin, or setTickSpacing back to their per-pool value). 3) FWATokenNest._afterTokenTransfer (line 411-414) runs _assertLivePoolConfiguration on EVERY transfer where `from` or `to` is the pool, and line 434-436 compares against the `constant` POOL_FEE=10_000 / POOL_TICK_SPACING=60 / REQUIRED_COMMUNITY_FEE=0 / REQUIRED_PLUGIN_CONFIG=7 and the one-shot `plugin` storage slot. Every such transfer now reverts InvalidPoolConfiguration. 4) Consequences, all permanent: retail holders can no longer sell (to == marketPool reverts); buyback() reverts at the adapter swap, so the HYPE accumulated in the token from FWA.payoutFees() can never leave — FWATokenNest has receive() at line 439 and no rescue function of any kind; FWARewardsHyperEVM.claimAccruedTokens reverts because the adapter's swap delivers FWA from the pool to the rewards module, so every purchaser's tokenBuyAllowance HYPE is frozen and only escapable by putting the whole core into withdrawOnly (FWARewardsHyperEVM.sol:460-470); acceptBidAsTokens reverts. 5) There is no admin path back: POOL_FEE/POOL_TICK_SPACING/REQUIRED_COMMUNITY_FEE/REQUIRED_PLUGIN_CONFIG are `constant`, and `plugin` can only be set once (setMarketInfrastructure reverts MarketAlreadyConfigured at line 179-181). Only Nest restoring the exact prior parameters unblocks it.
findings.impact: A third party holds a permanent, unilateral kill switch over the $FWA market and over the reward-delivery path, with a standing economic incentive to pull it (the FWA pool is configured to pay Nest zero community fee). Result: holders cannot exit, all protocol HYPE routed to the token is permanently locked (no rescue exists), and purchaser HYPE allowances are frozen. The existing test testPoolConfigDriftStopsEverySwap/testRemovingPluginCannotBypassTokenCircuitBreaker treats this as a feature and never checks that recovery is possible.
findings.minimalFix: Two independent changes. (a) Add an owner-updatable expected-config struct (expectedFee / expectedTickSpacing / expectedCommunityFee / expectedPluginConfig / plugin) behind a timelock or a Safe, replacing the four `constant`s in _assertLivePoolConfiguration, so an intentional Nest parameter change can be re-attested instead of bricking the token. (b) Add an owner-only `rescueHype(address to)` to FWATokenNest so the buyback reserve is never permanently trapped when the swap path is unavailable; the reference FWAToken can afford to omit it because its v4 pool parameters are fixed by the immutable PoolKey and cannot be changed by anyone, which is not true of an Algebra pool owned by Nest.
findings.regressionTest: test/FWANestIntegration.t.sol: after a full launch and a successful buyback, prank the pool admin to setCommunityFee(1000); assert token.buyback() reverts, assert a holder's transfer(pool, x) reverts, assert rewards.claimAccruedTokens reverts, then assert the owner can re-attest the new config (or rescue the HYPE) and that both paths recover. Add the symmetric case for setPlugin and setTickSpacing.
findings.evidence: FWATokenNest.sol:431-437 `_assertLivePoolConfiguration`: `if (poolContract.plugin() != plugin || config != REQUIRED_PLUGIN_CONFIG || poolContract.fee() != POOL_FEE || poolContract.tickSpacing() != POOL_TICK_SPACING || communityFee != REQUIRED_COMMUNITY_FEE) revert InvalidPoolConfiguration();` reached from line 411-414 for any transfer touching the pool. hyperevm-fork-test/NestDeployment.t.sol:44-45 asserts `factory.defaultFee()==500` and `factory.defaultCommunityFee()==1000`.

refutationNotes.reason: MECHANISM CONFIRMED, IMPACT MATERIALLY OVERSTATED. Verified: FWATokenNest.sol:412-414 routes every pool-touching transfer into _assertLivePoolConfiguration (431-437) against four `constant`s (29-32) and a one-shot `plugin` (179-181); hyperevm-fork-test/NestDeployment.t.sol:64-105 proves factory.owner() can call setPlugin/setFee/setCommunityFee/setTickSpacing on a live Nest pool. So a Nest parameter change does halt swaps, buyback() and claimAccruedTokens. Four load-bearing sub-claims are wrong. (1) 'the reward-delivery path' is NOT bricked: claimDepositorTokens (473-492), withdrawTokens (495-502) and claimEpochTokens (505-525) transfer FWA straight from the module to the user, never touching the pool, and _afterTokenTransfer:415 returns early for the module's distributor flag. Only the HYPE->FWA swap path is blocked, and it has a deliberate ETH escape hatch (460-470). (2) 'no rescue' is exact reference parity, not a port gap: FWA_ETHEREUM_REFERENCE/FWAToken/sources/src/FWAToken.sol:456 is `receive() external payable {}` with no rescue function of any kind. (3) 'all protocol HYPE routed to the token is permanently locked' — the token has no funding source at all in this release: protocolFeeToTokenBps is 0 by design (FWA.sol:493-496 '`0` = off (default) — flip on for Phase 2') and no script sets it, which the same auditor's finding 6 establishes; FWA_ETHEREUM_REFERENCE/FWAToken/state-snapshot.json shows balanceWei 0 and lastBuybackBlock 0 upstream. The trapped amount at launch is zero and, even under Phase 2, is bounded by BUYBACK_INCREMENT drained per block. (4) The proposed fix (a) — an owner-updatable expected-config struct — WEAKENS the property it targets: it would let a compromised owner re-attest a Nest plugin that drops the exact-input rule and the pre-open buy gate, plus a communityFee that skims 10% of every trade. testPoolConfigDriftStopsEverySwap / testRemovingPluginCannotBypassTokenCircuitBreaker / testLaunchRejectsNestCommunityFeeCapture all pass; the breaker fails CLOSED, which is the safe direction, and FWA_PARITY_MANIFEST.md already books 'Dérive fee/communityFee/plugin, refus administrateur Nest' as the identified risk with 'accord Nest requis' as the mitigation. Residual real content: the port added a trap condition that cannot exist behind an immutable v4 PoolKey while inheriting the reference's no-rescue design — an owner-only rescueHype is worthwhile defence in depth. medium (third-party-dependent DoS, recoverable by Nest restoring parameters), not high.

Mechanism verified (FWATokenNest.sol:407-437 asserts live pool config on every pool-touching transfer; the four expected values are `constant` and `plugin` is one-shot at :179-181), but three load-bearing claims fail.

(1) NOT PERMANENT. Every drifted parameter is restorable by the same Nest role that changed it (pool.setPlugin/setPluginConfig/setFee/setCommunityFee/setTickSpacing). The finding concedes this in its own scenario step 5 and then calls the result 'permanent' four times. A halt reversible by the counterparty is not a permanent brick.

(2) DISCLOSED, TWICE, AS ACCEPTED RESIDUAL TRUST. NEST_ADMIN_HANDOFF.md:79-81 states verbatim that the token and plugin block FWA flows if plugin, flags, fee, community fee or tick spacing drift, that Nest roles retain native Algebra pool authority, and that the requested agreement therefore covers configuration stability or an explicit governance/timelock. FWA_PARITY_MANIFEST.md:153 lists 'plugin administrable par Nest' as the divergence, 'Dérive fee/communityFee/plugin, refus administrateur Nest' as the risk, and 'accord Nest requis pour pool, plugin, fee 1 % et communityFee 0' as the decision. This is the disclosed-limit case.

(3) NOT A NEW KILL SWITCH. Nest already holds pool.setPlugin; installing any reverting plugin halts every swap regardless of FWATokenNest's assert. The assert does not grant Nest a capability it lacked; it converts a silent fee-capture (communityFee 1000 = 10% of LP fees) into a visible fail-closed stop. That is the deliberate trade-off the two cited tests encode.

(4) 'No HYPE rescue' is EXACT PARITY with the verified reference: FWA_ETHEREUM_REFERENCE/FWAToken/sources/src/FWAToken.sol:456 is `receive() external payable {}` with no rescue function anywhere in the file. The proposed fix (add owner rescueHype) would introduce a new owner drain power over the buyback reserve — directly contradicting this same auditor's finding 13 about aggregate admin blast radius.

What legitimately survives is narrow and low: there is no re-attestation path, so a LEGITIMATE Nest parameter migration forces a full FWATokenNest + FWARewardsHyperEVM redeploy. Worth recording as low/info operational rigidity, not high.

findings.title: Irreversible $FWA launch price comes from an unvalidated env var; the shipped mainnet template is 8 orders of magnitude off the Ethereum reference and the two irreversible pricing scripts lack the tokenomics gate
findings.preconditions: Operator runs the Nest phase sequence on chain 999 with NEST_MAINNET_DEPLOYMENT_CONFIRMED=true and an unedited (or fat-fingered) FWA_INITIAL_SQRT_PRICE_X96.
findings.scenario: `.env.mainnet.example:61` ships FWA_INITIAL_SQRT_PRICE_X96=79228162514264337593543950336, which is exactly 2**96, i.e. a starting price of 1.0 — 1 FWA = 1 wHYPE, a 1,000,000,000 HYPE fully-diluted valuation. The verified Ethereum deployment launched at 40,000,000 FWA per ETH (derived from the reference state snapshot: FWA_ETHEREUM_REFERENCE/FWAToken/state-snapshot.json buybackSqrtPriceLimitX96 = 477782542051216404772491119593238, and FWAToken.launch sets that to sqrtPriceX96*9535/10000, so launch sqrtPriceX96 = 501082896750095862372827603139211 → price 4.0e7 → ~25 ETH FDV). Every other secret-bearing field in the template is a zero placeholder; this one is a live-looking number that will silently be consumed. InitializeNestMarket.s.sol:35-38 only rejects values above uint160; FWATokenNest.initializeMarket (line 261) only bounds it to the open interval (MIN_SQRT_RATIO, MAX_SQRT_RATIO). Consuming it is terminal: marketInitialized is one-shot (line 255), launched is one-shot (line 295), the 500M LP is minted to FWANestLiquidityLocker which has no decrease/transfer function by design, and FWANestPlugin.beforeModifyPosition (line 92) rejects every liquidityDelta > 0 outside the token's own `launching()` window, so liquidity can never be re-seeded at a corrected price. Recovery requires a whole new FWATokenNest — which also forces a new FWARewardsHyperEVM, because `token` and `swapAdapter` are immutable and `setFWA` is one-shot. Compounding this: DeployNestToken.s.sol:49 and DeployNestModules.s.sol:56 both require FWA_TOKENOMICS_CONFIRMED=true, but InitializeNestMarket and LaunchNestMarket — the only two transactions that actually fix the price and the liquidity range — do not.
findings.impact: A single unedited or mistyped env value permanently mis-prices the canonical wHYPE/FWA pool and permanently locks 500M FWA (50% of supply) into an unusable position, bricking the entire token + rewards stack with no on-chain recovery. The off-chain gate that the surrounding phases carry is missing precisely on the irreversible steps.
findings.minimalFix: (1) Remove the concrete value from .env.mainnet.example (use an empty placeholder like every other field). (2) Require FWA_TOKENOMICS_CONFIRMED in InitializeNestMarket.s.sol and LaunchNestMarket.s.sol, matching DeployNestToken/DeployNestModules. (3) Add explicit sanity bounds in the scripts: require the derived FDV in HYPE to fall inside an operator-supplied [min,max] band read from env, and echo the human-readable price/FDV before broadcasting. (4) Consider requiring an on-chain `expectedFdvHype` argument to initializeMarket so the price is asserted, not assumed.
findings.regressionTest: Add a script-level test that runs InitializeNestMarket with FWA_TOKENOMICS_CONFIRMED unset and asserts it reverts, and a FWANestIntegration test asserting that after finalizeLaunch no further liquidity can be added (plugin NotLaunching) and that initializeMarket/finalizeLaunch each revert on a second call — documenting the irreversibility the gate is protecting.
findings.evidence: `.env.mainnet.example:61` FWA_INITIAL_SQRT_PRICE_X96=79228162514264337593543950336 (== 2**96, price 1.0). InitializeNestMarket.s.sol:35-38 `if (rawSqrtPrice > type(uint160).max) revert InvalidPrice();` is the only validation. FWATokenNest.sol:261 `if (sqrtPriceX96 <= MIN_SQRT_RATIO || sqrtPriceX96 >= MAX_SQRT_RATIO) revert InvalidRange();`.

refutationNotes.reason: GATE ASYMMETRY CONFIRMED, TRIGGER AND IMPACT OVERSTATED. Verified: .env.mainnet.example:61 is 2**96 (price 1.0); InitializeNestMarket.s.sol:35-38 validates only `> type(uint160).max`; FWATokenNest.sol:261 only bounds the open interval; marketInitialized (255) and launched (295) are one-shot; FWANestPlugin.sol:92 rejects every positive liquidityDelta outside `launching()`; DeployNestToken.s.sol:49 and DeployNestModules.s.sol:56 require FWA_TOKENOMICS_CONFIRMED while InitializeNestMarket and LaunchNestMarket do not. That asymmetry on the two irreversible pricing transactions is a genuine defect. But: (1) 'an unedited template will silently be consumed' is FALSE — the same file ships NEST_MAINNET_DEPLOYMENT_CONFIRMED=false (line 13) and InitializeNestMarket.s.sol:27-29 reverts MainnetNotConfirmed on chain 999 unless it is true, so an unedited template cannot reach initializeMarket at all; the residual scenario requires an operator who deliberately flips the mainnet gate but leaves the price. (2) '8 orders of magnitude off the reference' is not like-for-like — the reference 4e7 is FWA per ETH, the HyperEVM pool is denominated in wHYPE, so no parity delta can be derived from it; only the direction (a 1:1 launch is absurd) stands. (3) 'this one is a live-looking number while every other field is a zero placeholder' is FALSE — lines 55-58 and 62 ship live NEST_FACTORY/ROUTER/POSITION_MANAGER/WHYPE and FWA_LP_RANGE_WIDTH_TICKS=3600 by design, and 2**96 is the canonical 'price = 1.0' placeholder the project's own fork test uses (NestDeployment.t.sol `initializeMarket(uint160(1 << 96))`). (4) 'bricking the entire token + rewards stack' is wrong: a mispriced pool is still a functioning pool, and depositor emissions, tokenCredit and epoch claims are plain ERC-20 transfers unaffected by pool price; what degrades is the economics of the protocol buy paths, and buybacks are unfunded at launch anyway. This is exactly the rubric's medium: 'a gate that fails open under a plausible operational error'.

SURVIVES. Every mechanical fact checks out. .env.mainnet.example:61 ships FWA_INITIAL_SQRT_PRICE_X96=79228162514264337593543950336 = 2**96 exactly (ratio 1.0). InitializeNestMarket.s.sol:35-38 validates only `> type(uint160).max`; FWATokenNest.sol:261 bounds only (MIN_SQRT_RATIO, MAX_SQRT_RATIO). Irreversibility confirmed end to end: marketInitialized one-shot (:255), launched one-shot (:295), FWANestPlugin.sol:92 rejects every liquidityDelta > 0 outside `launching()`, and I confirmed FWANestLiquidityLocker exposes only bind/setFeeRecipient/collectFees/onERC721Received — no decrease, no transfer, so the 500M position can never be unwound or re-seeded. Recovery genuinely requires a new token AND a new rewards module (`token`/`swapAdapter` immutable, setFWA one-shot). The gate asymmetry is real: DeployNestToken.s.sol:49 and DeployNestModules.s.sol:56 require FWA_TOKENOMICS_CONFIRMED; InitializeNestMarket.s.sol:27 and LaunchNestMarket.s.sol:38 require only NEST_MAINNET_DEPLOYMENT_CONFIRMED.

Severity corrected high -> medium. At the moment InitializeNestMarket/LaunchNestMarket run, external buys are still closed and no third party holds $FWA, so no user funds or NFTs are at risk; the loss is a protocol-internal redeploy of the token+rewards stack. That is not 'direct loss of user funds' nor 'a launch step that irreversibly opens the product early' — it is precisely 'a gate that fails open under a plausible operational error' = medium.

Two framings should be dropped from the write-up: (a) the '8 orders of magnitude off the Ethereum reference' comparison is rhetoric, not a parity requirement — the reference's 4e7 FWA/ETH (25 ETH FDV, correctly derived from state-snapshot.json buybackSqrtPriceLimitX96 / 0.9535) is a business choice for a different asset; (b) MAINNET_RELEASE_RUNBOOK_2026-07-26.md:28 already lists 'Marché | prix initial, largeur de range...' among the values to freeze before any broadcast, so it is not undocumented — it is merely unenforced. Recommendation (2) (add FWA_TOKENOMICS_CONFIRMED) is cosmetic: a second boolean flipped by the same operator adds nothing. The valuable half of the fix is (1) empty the template value and (3)/(4) assert a derived FDV band.

findings.title: Mainnet activation irreversibly starts the 15-day emission without attesting that emissions are configured or that the 300M FWA budget is funded
findings.preconditions: Core bound to rewards via BindNestRewards; owner runs ActivateHyperEVMMainnet.
findings.scenario: `fwa.setBool(ACQUISITIONS_ENABLED, true)` (line 80) causes FWA.setConfig to call `r.startEmission()`, which sets `emissionStart = block.timestamp` and is idempotent-forever (FWARewardsHyperEVM.sol:368-373). From that instant `setEmission` reverts EmissionAlreadyStarted (line 589), so depositorRatePerSec and purchaserDailyPot are frozen for the life of the module, and `_advanceToken` burns the fixed 15-day wall-clock window regardless of activity or of any later pause. The activation script's InvalidWiring block (lines 65-76) checks addresses and Splitter bps but never reads `rewards.depositorRatePerSec()`, `rewards.purchaserDailyPot()`, `rewards.emissionStart()`, or `IERC20(token).balanceOf(rewards)`. VerifyNestModules.s.sol:54-78 — the designated pre-activation attestation — is equally silent on all four. Concrete failure: DeployNestModules is interrupted after `rewards.setFWA` but before the 300M transfer at line 96 (or a partial re-run, or an earlier rescueTokens which zeroes both rates at FWARewardsHyperEVM.sol:628-629). Activation still succeeds, emissionStart is set, and depositorRatePerSec is now permanently 0 — depositors accrue nothing for the entire program and there is no way to raise it. In the mirror case (rates set, module unfunded) claims revert on transfer and the first claimants drain whatever is there, first-come-first-served.
findings.impact: The single most irreversible economic transaction of the launch is executed without any check that the 300M FWA reward program it commits to is configured and funded. Failure modes range from a silently zeroed 150M depositor stream to an insolvent claim queue, with the only remedy being withdrawOnly + rescueTokens + a full redeploy of the rewards module.
findings.minimalFix: Add to ActivateHyperEVMMainnet's InvalidWiring block: `rewards.emissionStart() != 0 || rewards.depositorRatePerSec() == 0 || rewards.purchaserDailyPot() == 0 || IERC20(rewards.token()).balanceOf(address(rewards)) < DEPOSITOR_EMISSION + PURCHASER_EMISSION`, and mirror the same four assertions in VerifyNestModules so the attestation script covers them too. Ideally also make FWARewardsHyperEVM.startEmission revert when depositorRatePerSec == 0 && purchaserDailyPot == 0, so the on-chain invariant does not depend on a script.
findings.regressionTest: Fork/unit test: deploy the full Nest stack, call rewards.setFWA but skip the 300M funding transfer, then assert ActivateHyperEVMMainnet's wiring predicate reverts InvalidWiring; and a second test asserting that once startEmission has run, setEmission reverts EmissionAlreadyStarted and depositorRatePerSec can never be changed.
findings.evidence: FWARewardsHyperEVM.sol:588-589 `function setEmission(...) external onlyOwner { if (emissionStart != 0) revert EmissionAlreadyStarted(); ...}`; ActivateHyperEVMMainnet.s.sol:65-76 contains no rewards emission or balance term; VerifyNestModules.s.sol:54-78 likewise.

refutationNotes.reason: THE CLAIMED REACHABLE STATE IS NOT REACHABLE BY ANY ROUTE THE FINDING GIVES. The attestation gap is real (ActivateHyperEVMMainnet.s.sol:65-76 and VerifyNestModules.s.sol:55-78 contain no emission-rate or balance term; setBool(ACQUISITIONS_ENABLED,true) does call startEmission via FWA.sol:2298-2301; setEmission is locked after by 588-589). But all three stated triggers fail. (a) 'DeployNestModules interrupted after rewards.setFWA but before the 300M transfer at line 96 => depositorRatePerSec permanently 0' is internally inconsistent: the script order is setFWA (93) -> setEmission (94) -> transfer (96), so any interruption between 94 and 96 leaves the rates SET. The zero-rate outcome needs a failure in the single-transaction window between 93 and 94, where setEmission is an onlyOwner call on a freshly deployed contract with emissionStart == 0 that cannot revert. (b) 'a partial re-run' cannot produce it: a re-run deploys a fresh adapter and rewards, then calls token.setAdapter, which reverts AdapterAlreadySet (FWATokenNest.sol:206) before any emission state is touched. (c) 'an earlier rescueTokens which zeroes both rates' cannot precede activation: rescueTokens requires IFWARewardsCore(fwa).canRescueRewards(), i.e. withdrawOnly && unsettledAcquisitionCount == 0 (FWA.sol:2361-2363); the core deploys with acquisitions disabled and withdrawOnly false, and once emissionStart is set startEmission is a no-op anyway. The script also carries an in-band guarantee the finding omits: line 96 does the 300M transfer and line 97 asserts token.balanceOf(deployer) == LEGACY_ALLOCATION, a hard on-chain check that it landed — so the 'rates set, module unfunded' mirror case needs the same one-transaction-window failure. The recommendation (assert emissionStart/rates/balance in the activation and verification scripts) is sound defence in depth, but with no adversarial path and no plausible operational path this is low, not high.

SURVIVES ONLY AS HARDENING. The abstract gap is real and verified: FWA.sol:2301 makes setBool(ACQUISITIONS_ENABLED,true) call r.startEmission(); startEmission (FWARewardsHyperEVM.sol:368-373) is write-once; setEmission (:588-589) reverts EmissionAlreadyStarted forever after; and neither ActivateHyperEVMMainnet.s.sol:65-76 nor VerifyNestModules.s.sol:54-78 reads emissionStart, depositorRatePerSec, purchaserDailyPot or the module's FWA balance, despite VerifyNestModules checking ~35 other invariants. Adding those four terms is cheap and correct.

But all three concrete instantiations offered fail on inspection, which is why high is badly overstated:

(a) 'DeployNestModules is interrupted after rewards.setFWA but before the 300M transfer at line 96 ... depositorRatePerSec is now permanently 0' — WRONG ORDERING. setEmission(DEPOSITOR_EMISSION, PURCHASER_EMISSION) is line 94, BEFORE the transfer at line 96. An interruption in the stated window leaves the rates correctly SET. The headline scenario does not reproduce.

(b) 'or an earlier rescueTokens which zeroes both rates' — UNREACHABLE PRE-ACTIVATION. rescueTokens (:623-633) requires IFWARewardsCore(fwa).canRescueRewards(), i.e. withdrawOnly && no unsettled acquisitions on a core the module is ALREADY bound to. Since setFWA is one-shot, a module whose rates were zeroed that way can never be re-bound to the fresh core being activated. This path cannot feed an activation.

(c) the mirror 'rates set, module unfunded -> first claimants drain whatever is there, first-come-first-served' — with zero funding there is nothing to drain; SafeTransferLib.safeTransfer simply reverts for everyone. And that state also implies the legacy transfer and the three transferOwnership calls never ran, which is loud.

What remains reachable is a compound operator error: partial broadcast (the runbook mandates --slow, so forge aborts visibly), followed by a hand-repair that re-runs the wiring but omits setEmission and the funding transfer (a plain DeployNestModules re-run cannot silently patch it — token.setAdapter reverts AdapterAlreadySet), followed by both Verify scripts passing. Consequence even then is a silently zeroed depositor stream, not fund loss: the 300M is recoverable via rescueTokens. Not 'fund lock-up', not 'permanent DoS of settlement/withdrawals', not 'irreversibly opens the product early'. Low.

findings.title: Nest pool administrator can permanently brick the FWA market and trap the HYPE buyback reserve, with no on-chain recovery path
findings.lines: 431-437 (_assertLivePoolConfiguration); 178-202 (setMarketInfrastructure, one-shot); 204-219 (setAdapter, one-shot); 369-405 (buyback, the only HYPE outlet); 439 (receive)
findings.preconditions: Mainnet launch complete. Nest holds the Algebra POOLS_ADMINISTRATOR authority over the FWA/wHYPE pool. Verified live on chain 999 by read-only eth_call from 0x…dEaD against pool 0xBE512f5881b85c48D9C17BC5bb2bE047d156D696: setPlugin(address), setPluginConfig(uint8), setCommunityFee(uint16) and setTickSpacing(int24) all revert notAllowed() (0x932984d2), i.e. they are administrator-gated, not public. Nest already re-tunes live pools: the repo's own fork test asserts the production wHYPE/USDC pool runs tickSpacing == 5 while the factory default is 60 (hyperevm-fork-test/NestDeployment.t.sol:56-58), and factory.defaultCommunityFee() == 1000.
findings.scenario: After launch Nest calls pool.setTickSpacing(5) — or setCommunityFee(1000), or setFee(500), or setPlugin(anything) — as routine per-pool maintenance. From that block on, every FWA transfer where from == pool or to == pool enters _assertLivePoolConfiguration (FWATokenNest.sol:411-414) and reverts InvalidPoolConfiguration. Concretely: (a) every buy and every sell of $FWA reverts, permanently; (b) FWANestLiquidityLocker.collectFees() reverts whenever an FWA-side fee is owed, so accrued LP fees are stuck; (c) FWATokenNest.buyback() reverts, and because the token has no HYPE withdrawal function at all — receive() is the only inlet, buyback() the only outlet — the accumulated buyback reserve is frozen. That reserve is real protocol revenue: FWA.payoutFees() sends accrued * protocolFeeToTokenBps / BPS to the token address on every payout (FWA_ETHEREUM_REFERENCE/FWA/sources/src/FWA.sol:1999). Recovery is impossible on-chain: pool/plugin/liquidityLocker are one-shot (MarketAlreadyConfigured, line 179-181) and adapter is one-shot (AdapterAlreadySet, line 206), so the owner cannot re-point the token at a replacement pool, plugin or adapter, and the 500M FWA seeded into the locked LP is unrecoverable by construction.
findings.impact: Permanent, third-party-triggered destruction of the $FWA market plus permanent lock-up of the HYPE buyback reserve (real user-derived funds) and of the 500M-FWA locked LP position. This is a risk the Ethereum reference does not carry: there the Uniswap v4 pool key and hook are immutable and no third party can alter pool parameters, so buyback() cannot be externally disabled. The failure is triggerable by ordinary operational maintenance, not only by malice, and NEST_ADMIN_HANDOFF.md:77-81 currently only *requests* configuration stability rather than securing it.
findings.minimalFix: Three-part, all inside FWA's own contracts. (1) Split the live attestation: keep the hard revert only for the two parameters that actually enforce the gate — pool.plugin() == plugin and pluginConfig == REQUIRED_PLUGIN_CONFIG — and demote fee/tickSpacing/communityFee to owner-updatable expected values via an event-emitting setExpectedPoolEconomics(uint16,int24,uint16), so an economic re-tune by Nest cannot brick transfers. (2) Add a permissionless FWANestPlugin.restorePluginConfig() that calls POOL.setPluginConfig(REQUIRED_PLUGIN_CONFIG); Algebra permits the plugin itself to set its own config (`if (msg.sender != plugin) _checkIfAdministrator()`), making pluginConfig drift self-healing. (3) Guarantee the HYPE reserve is never trapped: either make `adapter` replaceable behind a timelock, or add an owner sweepHype(address) that only unlocks after buyback() has been unusable for a defined period.
findings.regressionTest: Fork test on chain 999: launch the market, then vm.prank(factory.owner()) and call pool.setTickSpacing(5). Assert (a) a user sell reverts InvalidPoolConfiguration, (b) locker.collectFees() reverts, (c) token.buyback() reverts with a non-zero token HYPE balance. Then assert that after the proposed fix the gate still blocks unauthorised buys while the HYPE reserve remains recoverable.
findings.evidence: cast call <pool> "setPlugin(address)" --from 0x…dEaD → revert 0x932984d2 == notAllowed(); same for setCommunityFee/setTickSpacing/setPluginConfig. cast call <factory> "createPool(address,address)" --from 0x…dEaD → AccessControl missing-role revert. hyperevm-fork-test/NestDeployment.t.sol:58 asserts a live Nest pool already deviates from the factory default tick spacing.

refutationNotes.reason: SURVIVES at high. Every mechanical claim reconstructs. FWATokenNest.sol:412-414 calls _assertLivePoolConfiguration on ANY transfer where from==pool or to==pool, and :431-437 reverts on drift in plugin, pluginConfig, fee, tickSpacing OR communityFee. I additionally verified something the finding did not state, which strengthens it: the assertion at :412-414 runs BEFORE the isDistributor escape (:415) and before the owner escape (:417-418), so the owner cannot even whitelist the pool via setDistributor(pool,true) to route around it — the revert is unconditional for every pool-touching transfer. I confirmed by grep that FWATokenNest has exactly one HYPE outlet: receive() at :439 is the only inlet, and buyback() (:369-405, via SafeTransferLib at :403 and the adapter call at :383) is the only spend; there is no owner sweep, and buyAmount can never be 0 for a non-zero balance, so no partial drain path exists either. FWA.payoutFees (FWA_ETHEREUM_REFERENCE/FWA/sources/src/FWA.sol:1993-1999) does forceSafeTransferETH(token, tokenPortion) permissionlessly and forever, so the trapped balance is real, user-derived revenue and keeps growing. setMarketInfrastructure (:179-181), setAdapter (:206) and setRewardsPool (:222) are all genuinely one-shot, so there is no re-pointing. Two corrections that do not change the verdict: (a) the impact overstates by counting the 500M-FWA locked LP as a loss caused by the brick — that principal is irrecoverable by deliberate design (FWANestLiquidityLocker has no decrease/transfer function), not by this defect; (b) a partial mitigation exists that the finding misses — the FWA owner can set protocolFeeToTokenBps to 0 (FWA.sol:2284) to stop FUTURE accrual into the trap, though the already-accumulated balance stays stuck. The likelihood evidence is a little stretched: NestDeployment.t.sol:56-58 proves Nest sets per-pool tickSpacing (live wHYPE/USDC pool at 5 vs factory default 60), not that Nest re-tunes pools that already carry third-party LPs. But the authority is real and NEST_ADMIN_HANDOFF.md:81 concedes it in prose while only requesting stability. Note for the fix reviewer: proposal (1) must keep the plugin and pluginConfig legs as hard reverts — test/FWANestIntegration.t.sol:218-238 shows that leg is the last line of defence when the plugin is removed — and demoting communityFee to an owner-set expected value would let Nest siphon LP fees; the durable fix is the recovery path in proposal (3).

SURVIVES IN REDUCED FORM; severity overstated. Mechanically confirmed: FWATokenNest.sol:431-437 gates every pool-touching transfer on plugin/pluginConfig/fee/tickSpacing/communityFee, three of which are purely economic and Nest-mutable (INestAlgebra.sol:29-33); pool/plugin/locker are one-shot (178-181) and adapter is one-shot (206); receive() (439) is the only HYPE inlet and buyback() (369-405) the only outlet, with no owner sweep anywhere in the 440-line file; and the trapped HYPE is real revenue (FWA.sol:1999 forceSafeTransferETH(token, tokenPortion)). BUT the 'brick' half is neither new nor a defect: it is an intentional, documented, tested circuit breaker. NEST_ADMIN_HANDOFF.md:79-81 states it explicitly ('Le token et le plugin bloquent les flux FWA si plugin, flags, fee, community fee ou tick spacing derivent... Les roles Nest conservent neanmoins l'autorite native du pool Algebra') and asks Nest for stability or a documented timelock; test/FWANestIntegration.t.sol:197 (testPoolConfigDriftStopsEverySwap) and :218 assert exactly this fail-closed behaviour. Three impact claims are wrong or inflated: (a) the 500M-FWA LP is unrecoverable BY DESIGN (FWANestLiquidityLocker has no decrease/transfer function on purpose) - citing it as damage from this bug is double-counting; (b) 'permanent DoS of settlement/withdrawals' is false - FWA core custody, acquisitions, depositor earnings and acceptDepositorBid all still work; only the optional token-denominated path acceptBidAsTokens (FWA.sol:1779-1786, itself behind acceptBidAsTokensEnabled) and claimAccruedTokens break; (c) the trigger is the legitimate pool administrator FWA deliberately chose to deploy under, not an arbitrary third party. The genuinely novel and valid kernel - not covered by the disclosure - is the absence of ANY escape hatch for the token's HYPE reserve (and, unmentioned by the finding, for tokenBuyAllowance ETH in FWARewardsHyperEVM, whose only exit withdrawTokenBuyAllowanceAsETH requires the owner to put the core into withdraw-only mode). That is a real fund-lock-up gap worth fixing, but it is protocol fee revenue accruing over time, contingent on a trusted partner's action, with core user funds unaffected: medium, not high. Fix parts (1) and (3) are sound; fix part (2) is speculative (it asserts Algebra permits `msg.sender == plugin` to call setPluginConfig, which is not verifiable from anything in this repo - the vendored INestAlgebra.sol is a minimal interface with no implementation).

findings.title: `features.writesEnabled` is a UI-only flag: 11 of 15 wallet write paths execute while the manifest declares the app read-only
findings.lines: 1301-1393 (settle/claims), 1256-1259 (the one client-side feature gate that does exist); C:/Users/eliot/Documents/FWA FORK/frontend/src/protocol/provider.tsx:240; C:/Users/eliot/Documents/FWA FORK/frontend/src/components/positions/PositionsScreen.tsx:179
findings.preconditions: dataMode = testnet|mainnet, manifest loads with status "ready" (all addresses valid, chainId matches), and `features.writesEnabled: false`. This is exactly the state produced by `WriteMainnetManifest.ps1` per MAINNET_RELEASE_RUNBOOK_2026-07-26.md §5.2 and held through the whole §6 canary ("Le frontend reste read-only pendant cette phase").
findings.scenario:
1. Ops publishes `hyperevm-mainnet-999.json` with `{"writesEnabled": false, "acquisitionsEnabled": false}` and deploys the frontend (runbook §5.2/§5.3).
2. `ViemProtocolRoot` sees `manifestState.status === "ready"`, so it constructs a live `ViemProtocolClient` (provider.tsx:188-191) and only the *context value* `writesEnabled` becomes false.
3. `ViemProtocolClient` never reads `manifest.features.writesEnabled` anywhere — grep confirms the only feature check in the client is `acquisitionsEnabled` in `acquire()` (line 1257).
4. Only four UI sites consult the flag: DepositFlow (early return), SwapPanel, PurchaseSidebar, and one `disabled=` on the PositionsScreen Withdraw button. Every other call site goes straight through `useProtocolAction.run` → client → `wallet.writeContract`.
5. Concretely, with the canary listing from runbook §6.3 allocated, a user opens /positions or /acquisitions/<id> and presses Settle: `settle({kind:"keep"})` → `keepNFT(listingId)` is signed and mined. Same for `relistNFT` (payable), `acceptDepositorBid`, `acceptBidAsTokens`, `depositorReclaimNFT`, `depositorReclaimBacking`, `finalizeUnsettled` (permissionless after 7d), `recoverStuckNFT`, `withdrawEarnings`, `withdrawAcquisitionRefund`, `claimListingFees`, `claimDepositorTokens`, `claimEpochTokens`.
findings.impact: The documented read-only gate fails open for every settlement, finalization and HYPE/FWA claim. §5.2's assertion "Il ne peut donc pas ouvrir le produit accidentellement" is only true for deposits, acquisitions and swaps. Settlements are irreversible on-chain, so a settle executed during a phase the runbook declares read-only cannot be undone. There is no theft and no unauthorised power (the contract still authorises), but a launch gate that is enforced in four hand-written `if`s and not at the client layer will drift the moment a new screen is added.
findings.minimalFix: Enforce the flag once, at the boundary: in `ViemProtocolClient.executeWrite` (line 363) add `if (!this.manifest.features.writesEnabled) throw new ProtocolError("WRITES_DISABLED", "The deployment manifest has writes disabled.")` before `createTransaction`. Then decide the intended semantics explicitly — if runbook §8 line 178 ("préserver les sorties de listings, refunds, settlements et recovery") is the real requirement, split the flag into `writesEnabled` (entry: list/approve/acquire/swap) and `exitsEnabled` (settle/claim/withdraw/recover) rather than leaving the distinction implicit in which components remembered to check.
findings.regressionTest: Vitest against `ViemProtocolClient`: build the client with the existing test manifest (`ViemProtocolClient.test.ts:17-22` already has `writesEnabled: false`), stub `getAccount` to return a connected in-chain account and a wallet client whose `writeContract` records calls, then assert that every method in the write surface — settle (all 7 kinds), recoverStuckNFT, withdrawEarnings, withdrawAcquisitionRefund, claimListingFees, claimCrown, claimRewards, approveNFT, listNFT, withdrawListing — rejects and that `writeContract` was never invoked. Table-drive it so a newly added write method fails the test by default.

refutationNotes.reason: The mechanical observation is true (ViemProtocolClient never reads manifest.features.writesEnabled; grep confirms the only source-tree consumers are provider.tsx:44/169/240, DepositFlow.tsx:40/155, SwapPanel.tsx:43/281, EnvBanner.tsx:14/28, PositionsScreen.tsx:38/179, PurchaseSidebar.tsx:151/183), but the impact claim is contradicted by the code and by the very runbook it cites. (1) The stated harm -- 'a launch step that irreversibly opens the product early' -- cannot occur. Every entry-side write is blocked when the flag is false: listNFT and approveNFT are reachable ONLY from DepositFlow (verified by grep for all UI callers), which early-returns at DepositFlow.tsx:155; acquire is reachable only from PurchaseBox, blocked BOTH by the blocker ladder (PurchaseSidebar.tsx:178-183) and independently at the client boundary (ViemProtocolClient.ts:1257) -- and scripts/WriteMainnetManifest.ps1:68-69 and scripts/PromoteMainnetManifest.ps1:31-32 flip writesEnabled and acquisitionsEnabled together, so the two are never independently false; swap is reachable only from SwapPanel and the viem client throws unconditionally anyway (ViemProtocolClient.ts:1182-1188). (2) The writes that do stay live -- settle, finalizeUnsettled, recoverStuckNFT, withdrawEarnings, withdrawAcquisitionRefund, claimListingFees, claimRewards -- are exactly what MAINNET_RELEASE_RUNBOOK_2026-07-26.md sec.8 line 178 REQUIRES to stay open ('preserver les sorties de listings, refunds, settlements et recovery'). So this is the documented intent, not a gate failing open; the finding cites that same line in its own fix section, which makes it self-refuting. (3) During the sec.6 canary the only party holding an allocated listing is ops performing the canary settlement that step 5 mandates; the public cannot acquire through the frontend. (4) Category 'contract-bug' is wrong -- no contract is involved. Residual worth recording at info only: the entry/exit split is implicit in which components remembered to check, so a future screen could drift.

Facts confirmed: grep over frontend/src shows `writesEnabled` is read in exactly 5 places (provider.tsx:240, EnvBanner.tsx:28, PurchaseSidebar.tsx:183, DepositFlow.tsx:155, SwapPanel.tsx:281, PositionsScreen.tsx:179) and never inside ViemProtocolClient.ts; the only client-layer feature gate is `acquisitionsEnabled` at line 1257. But severity and category are wrong. (a) Category `contract-bug` is unsupportable — no contract is involved. (b) The claimed consequence 'the documented read-only gate fails open' does not hold in the runbook state it cites: in that state `acquisitionsEnabled:false` is ALSO set, and that flag IS enforced at the client boundary (ViemProtocolClient.ts:1256-1259); deposits are hard-blocked before any UI renders (DepositFlow.tsx:155 returns an EmptyState); swaps throw unconditionally (ViemProtocolClient.ts:1182-1188). So only exits (settle/finalize/reclaim/claim/recover) remain reachable, and only for an address that already holds an allocated listing or a credit balance — on a fresh chain-999 deployment that is exclusively the ops canary wallet, and MAINNET_RELEASE_RUNBOOK §6 step 5 explicitly requires ops to verify settlement from that wallet. (c) §8 line 178 ('préserver les sorties de listings, refunds, settlements et recovery') means the code's actual entry-gated/exit-open split matches documented intent; the real observation is only that the split is implicit and uncentralised, and that §5.2's 'ne peut pas ouvrir le produit accidentellement' is a claim about the script's `acquisitionsEnabled:false`, which the client does honour. (d) A working hard stop exists: §8's other option, removing the manifest, makes `loadManifest` return non-ready so `client` stays null (provider.tsx:188-192) and every write is impossible. Correct rating: low (hardening / undefined flag semantics). Note also that this finding and the next one are contradictory halves of one issue — one says too little is gated, the other says the one gated thing should not be.

findings.title: Emergency read-only manifest disables the depositor exit (`withdrawListing`) — the one write the runbook requires to stay open
findings.preconditions: An incident triggers MAINNET_RELEASE_RUNBOOK_2026-07-26.md §8: ops promotes a read-only manifest (`writesEnabled: false`) while keeping the core contract live.
findings.scenario: Runbook §8 line 177-178 prescribes "retirer le manifest public/promouvoir une version read-only" AND "préserver les sorties de listings, refunds, settlements et recovery". The code does the exact opposite of the second clause for listings: `disabled={!writesEnabled || inFlightLock}` on the Withdraw button (line 179) is the ONLY `writesEnabled` check in PositionsScreen. A depositor holding an active listing during the incident opens /positions, sees the Withdraw button greyed out with no explanation (the `title` only mentions the in-flight lock), and has no UI path to reclaim their ERC-721 plus HYPE backing — while the neighbouring Claim fees, Reclaim backing, Reclaim NFT, Finalize and Withdraw-earnings buttons all remain live.
findings.impact: UI-level lock-out of the depositor exit precisely in the scenario the runbook designed the read-only manifest for. The on-chain `withdrawListing` is still callable directly, so this is not an on-chain fund lock — but the users most likely to be affected (retail depositors during an incident) will not construct a raw calldata call. It also reads as inconsistent: exits that go through `settle` work, the exit that goes through `withdrawListing` does not.
findings.minimalFix: Remove `!writesEnabled` from line 179 and instead classify the write in the client per the split proposed in the previous finding (`withdrawListing` belongs to the exit class that stays open). If the button must stay disabled, the `title`/blocker text must say why ("read-only manifest") rather than showing a bare disabled control.
findings.regressionTest: React Testing Library test rendering `<PositionsScreen>` under a mocked `useProtocol()` returning `{writesEnabled: false, manifestState: {status:"ready", ...}}` with one active deposited listing: assert `withdraw-<id>` is enabled and that clicking it calls `client.withdrawListing`. Pair it with a snapshot test asserting the read-only banner text names the feature flag, not a missing manifest.

refutationNotes.reason: SURVIVES on the facts: PositionsScreen.tsx:179 `disabled={!writesEnabled || inFlightLock}` is the only writesEnabled gate in the file, it sits on withdrawListing, and it is the inverse of runbook sec.8 line 178 which requires listing exits to be preserved under a read-only manifest. Withdraw is the sole exit closed while Claim fees (171), Reclaim backing (272), Reclaim NFT (285), Finalize (296), Withdraw earnings (365), refunds (372) and Retry stuck delivery (421) all stay live -- verified line by line. Severity is overstated at medium: this gate fails CLOSED, not open (the rubric's medium is for a gate that fails OPEN), there is no on-chain lock (FWA.withdrawListing remains callable), the user is not left with zero explanation because EnvBanner.tsx:35 renders a global 'READ-ONLY -- writes disabled' bar, and the state is fully recoverable by ops republishing the manifest -- which costs nothing operationally since, per verdict 1, writesEnabled gates nothing else that matters during an incident. Low.

Verified: `disabled={!writesEnabled || inFlightLock}` at PositionsScreen.tsx:179 is the only `writesEnabled` gate on that screen, and grep confirms PositionsScreen.tsx:186 is the ONLY UI call site of `client.withdrawListing` in the whole tree. The `title` prop (lines 180-184) is `undefined` unless `inFlightLock`, so with a read-only manifest the user gets a bare greyed button with no explanation, while Claim fees (171), Reclaim backing (274), Reclaim NFT (285), Finalize (296), Withdraw earnings (365) and Retry stuck delivery (421) stay live. MAINNET_RELEASE_RUNBOOK §8 line 178 does prescribe preserving 'les sorties de listings'. So the inconsistency is real. Severity medium is overstated: there is no fund or NFT lock (FWA.sol `withdrawListing` stays callable, and the gate is a single client-side boolean an operator restores with a one-line JSON edit), no theft, and no accounting error. This is 'misleading UI with no fund impact' plus a missing blocker explanation → low.

findings.title: Indexer outage disables acquisitions entirely: a display-only field is fetched inside `getPoolSnapshot`, and its fallback throws above 1,000 listings
findings.preconditions: Mainnet with `NEXT_PUBLIC_INDEXER_URL` configured, the Goldsky subgraph unreachable or returning an error, and `nextListingId > 1001` (i.e. more than ~1,000 listings ever created).
findings.scenario:
1. `getPoolSnapshot` fans out 11 on-chain reads that fully cover the acquisition path (`quoteAcquisitionPrice`, `activeListingCount`, `weightedBackingTotal`, `totalWeight`, `pendingAcquisitionCount`, crown state).
2. It then queries the indexer for two purely cosmetic fields, `stagedListingCount` and `totalBacking` (line 431-435), used only in PoolStatCards and one PoolScreen caption.
3. Goldsky 5xx → `indexerQuery` throws → the `catch` at line 436 calls `getAllListingsDirect()`.
4. `getAllListingsDirect` (line 526-528) throws `ProtocolError("INDEXER_DOWN", "The direct testnet reader reached its 1,000-listing safety bound.")` as soon as `nextListingId > 1001n`. The throw is *inside* the catch, so it propagates out of `getPoolSnapshot`.
5. `usePoolSnapshot` has no `isError` handling anywhere (PoolScreen.tsx:50 destructures `data` only), so `snapshot` stays `undefined`. `PurchaseBox`'s blocker ladder returns `{label: "Loading pool…"}` (PurchaseSidebar.tsx:177) forever, with a 6 s `refetchInterval` re-failing silently.
6. Result: nobody can acquire, and the UI shows an eternal spinner with no error and no banner explaining why.
findings.impact: Contradicts the stated trust boundary in frontend/INTEGRATION_NEEDS.md ("Le subgraph est une infrastructure de découverte non fiable : aucun droit ni quote n'en dépend") — a quote-gating snapshot does depend on it. Secondary effect on pools of ≤1,000 listings: the fallback enumerates every listing at 3 RPC reads each, every 6 s, per open tab (~2,700 reads / 6 s at 900 listings) against Hyperliquid's IP-rate-limited public RPC, which will get users throttled and turn a subgraph blip into an app-wide outage.
findings.minimalFix: Move the two cosmetic fields out of the critical path: make them a separate optional query (`usePoolExtras`) whose failure degrades those two stat cards to "—", and have `getPoolSnapshot` return `stagedListingCount: undefined` / `totalBacking: undefined` when unavailable instead of enumerating. Never call `getAllListingsDirect()` from `getPoolSnapshot`. Additionally surface `usePoolSnapshot().isError` in `EnvBanner` and in the `PurchaseBox` blocker so the failure is visible rather than an infinite "Loading pool…".
findings.regressionTest: Vitest: construct `ViemProtocolClient` with an indexer URL, stub `fetch` to reject, stub `pub.readContract` so `nextListingId` returns `5000n` and the 11 snapshot reads return valid values, then assert `getPoolSnapshot()` resolves (does not throw), that `acquisitionsEnabled` is computed from the on-chain `activeListingCount`/`total`, and that `totalBacking`/`stagedListingCount` are reported as unavailable.

refutationNotes.reason: SURVIVES on the code path: ViemProtocolClient.ts:429-442 fetches stagedListingCount/totalBacking from the subgraph inside getPoolSnapshot, the catch at 436 calls getAllListingsDirect, and 526-529 throws INDEXER_DOWN once nextListingId > 1001n -- inside the catch, so it propagates. usePoolSnapshot (state/queries.ts:14-22) exposes no isError anywhere, and PurchaseSidebar.tsx:177 returns 'Loading pool...' whenever snapshot is undefined. Both cited fields are display-only (only PoolScreen.tsx:350 and PoolStatCards.tsx:34/134/212). But three claims are materially overstated, so medium is too high. (a) 'a quote-gating snapshot depends on it' is wrong about the quote: quoteAcquisition (649-674) is chain-only, is a separate react-query key, and ITS failure IS surfaced (PurchaseSidebar.tsx:252-259). No right, price or guard depends on the subgraph -- only the CTA's blocker does, which is the trust boundary holding, imperfectly, rather than breaking. (b) The RPC-amplification figure is off by ~40x: RPC_TRANSPORT_OPTIONS (lines 55-59) coalesces at batchSize 40, so 900 listings is ~68 HTTP requests per refresh, not 2,700 -- the code comment at 52-54 says this is precisely why batching exists. (c) TanStack Query retains the last successful data across a failed background refetch, so a warm session degrades to stale numbers; only a cold load produces the permanent spinner. Add that the >1,000 bound only bites above 1,000 lifetime listings and that the direct reader is documented (132-137) as the no-indexer fallback. Genuine availability defect worth the proposed fix (split the cosmetic fields out, surface isError); low.

Core mechanism confirmed line by line: ViemProtocolClient.ts:429-442 fetches `protocolState { stagedListingCount totalBacking }` from the indexer inside `getPoolSnapshot`; the catch at 436 calls `getAllListingsDirect()`, which throws `ProtocolError('INDEXER_DOWN', …)` at line 527-529 when `nextListingId > 1001n` — inside the catch, so it propagates out of `getPoolSnapshot`. `usePoolSnapshot` (state/queries.ts:14-22) is destructured for `data` only at PoolScreen.tsx:50, and PurchaseSidebar.tsx:177 returns the 'Loading pool…' blocker whenever `!snapshot`, so the acquisition CTA is stuck with no error surface. Grep confirms `totalBacking`/`stagedListingCount` are consumed only in PoolStatCards.tsx:34,134,212 and PoolScreen.tsx:350 — genuinely cosmetic, gating nothing. This does contradict INTEGRATION_NEEDS.md line 33 ('aucun droit ni quote n'en dépend'). Severity medium is overstated: the failure is transient and self-healing (6 s refetch), affects only the acquisition surface (PositionsScreen tolerates `snapshot === undefined` via `?? 0n` / `?? 0` at lines 46 and 144, so exits keep working), and carries no fund impact → low. The secondary amplification figure is also materially overstated: the transport batches (RPC_TRANSPORT_OPTIONS `batch: {batchSize: 40}`, lines 55-59, with an explicit comment about Hyperliquid's IP rate limit), so 900 listings is ~70 HTTP requests per cycle, not 2,700.

findings.title: The acquisitions kill switch is never read back on-chain, and no write is simulated before the wallet prompt
findings.lines: 466-467 (open/closed derivation) and 1256-1298 (acquire submits with no simulateContract); contract evidence: C:/Users/eliot/Documents/FWA FORK/vendor/fwa-reference-union/src/FWA.sol:281 and :1357
findings.preconditions: Mainnet live, manifest promoted with `acquisitionsEnabled: true`, then ops executes the §8 emergency stop "fermer ACQUISITIONS_ENABLED" on-chain.
findings.scenario: `FWA.sol:281` declares `bool internal acquisitionsEnabled;` — internal, no public getter — so the frontend cannot read it. It therefore derives the UI state from the static manifest: `acquisitionsEnabled: this.manifest.features.acquisitionsEnabled && total > 0n && Number(activeCount) > 0` (line 466). After the owner sets the on-chain flag false, the JSON file served from `/deployments/hyperevm-mainnet-999.json` still says true, so the Acquire CTA stays green. A user picks quantity 3, presses Confirm; `acquire()` re-reads the quote and `weightedBackingTotal` (correctly) but then calls `wallet.writeContract` directly — viem's `writeContract` on a JSON-RPC account does no simulation — so the transaction is signed, broadcast and reverts with `AcquisitionsNotEnabled` (FWA.sol:1357). The escrowed `value` is returned; the gas is not. The frontend even has a decoder for this revert (`normalizeWriteError`, line 325) which is only reachable *after* the money has been spent on gas.
findings.impact: The emergency stop does not propagate to the UI until someone edits the manifest JSON and redeploys the frontend, during which every purchase attempt burns gas and the product appears open while it is closed. The same absence of pre-flight simulation means every other write (settle, finalize, reclaim, claim) can be signed in a state that will certainly revert.
findings.minimalFix: Add a `this.pub.simulateContract({ account, address: this.core, abi, functionName, args, value, gasPrice })` immediately before `wallet.writeContract` in `acquire()` (and ideally in `executeWrite` generically), and map a revert to a pre-signature `ProtocolError`. Feed the result back into `getPoolSnapshot`: probe `acquire` with a zero-value staticcall and treat an `AcquisitionsNotEnabled` revert as closed, so the UI reflects the on-chain switch instead of a JSON file.
findings.regressionTest: Vitest: stub `pub.simulateContract` to reject with an error whose message contains `AcquisitionsNotEnabled`, and assert `acquire()` rejects with code `ACQUISITIONS_DISABLED` *and* that the wallet's `writeContract` was never called. Add a second case asserting the pool snapshot reports `acquisitionsEnabled: false` when the probe reverts even though the manifest says true.

refutationNotes.reason: Facts check out -- FWA.sol:281 is `bool internal acquisitionsEnabled` with no getter (grep confirms the only touchpoint is setBool at 2295-2299), ViemProtocolClient.ts:466-467 derives UI state from the manifest, and no simulateContract precedes wallet.writeContract -- but the defect framing does not survive. (1) The consequence is bounded to gas, and only if the user overrides their wallet: viem's writeContract on a JSON-RPC account emits eth_sendTransaction with no `gas` field (acquire passes gasPrice only, 1282/1296), so the wallet runs its own eth_estimateGas, hits AcquisitionsNotEnabled and warns/blocks before signing. The 'signed, broadcast and reverts' path is the exception, not the norm. (2) _validateAcquisition (FWA.sol:1356-1358) reverts the whole call, so the escrowed value never moves -- no fund impact, which the finding concedes. (3) acquire() is not an unguarded write: it hard-blocks on the manifest flag at 1257 and re-reads quoteAcquisitionPrice and weightedBackingTotal on-chain at 1261-1271 before submitting. listNFT (1209-1229) and approveNFT (1192) likewise pre-flight ownership/approval/whitelist on-chain, so 'no pre-flight simulation for every other write' overstates the gap. (4) The manifest/on-chain divergence window is a documented operational step, not an unguarded gate: runbook sec.8 lists closing ACQUISITIONS_ENABLED and promoting a read-only manifest as items in the same emergency checklist. (5) The unreadability is a property of the frozen Ethereum core that is intended to ship byte-unchanged, so it is not a HyperEVM port divergence. Reclassify as low hardening ('probe acquire with a staticcall and add a generic simulateContract'), not a medium external-config defect.

Confirmed against the contract: `bool internal acquisitionsEnabled;` at vendor/fwa-reference-union/src/FWA.sol:281 with no public getter, reverting at :1357 via `_validateAcquisition`, and `quoteAcquisitionPrice()` (:1232-1236) does not consult it — so the frontend genuinely cannot read the switch and derives UI state from the static manifest at ViemProtocolClient.ts:466-467. `acquire()` (1256-1298) calls `wallet.writeContract` with no `simulateContract`. `loadManifest` runs once per mount (provider.tsx:183-197) and PromoteMainnetManifest.ps1 defaults `-ManifestPath frontend/public/deployments/hyperevm-mainnet-999.json`, so propagation needs a redeploy plus a tab reload. All accurate. Severity medium is overstated: the on-chain gate holds, no unauthorised action occurs, `value` never leaves the wallet (the tx reverts, so nothing is 'returned' — it is simply never transferred), and the loss is gas on HyperEVM. Mitigations the finding omits: injected wallets run `eth_estimateGas` before the prompt and warn on a certain revert; and §8 prescribes promoting the read-only manifest in the same emergency step, bounding the window to minutes. Same class applies to `withdrawOnly` (FWA.sol:286) and `whitelistEnabled` (:292), also internal — worth folding into one finding. Correct rating: low.

findings.title: Metadata proxy is an unauthenticated, unthrottled outbound-fetch amplifier; allowlist ignores the port and has no self-origin guard
findings.preconditions: Production deployment; the route is public, requires no auth and no referer, and runs server-side with production network access. `NFT_METADATA_ALLOWED_HOSTS` populated per runbook §5.4.
findings.scenario:
(a) Amplification: `GET /api/nft-metadata?uri=ipfs://Qm<random-32-chars>` produces a cache miss every time (`s-maxage` is keyed on the unique URI), and each miss issues one server-side `fetch` to the IPFS gateway held open for up to `FETCH_TIMEOUT_MS = 5_000`. There is no rate limit, no per-IP throttle and no concurrency cap. A few hundred requests per second with unique CIDs pin the Node process's outbound sockets and event loop for 5 s each; on a serverless host it is a direct cost/quota attack.
(b) Port: `allowedHTTPSURL` compares `url.hostname` only. I verified with a Node probe that `https://metadata.example:8443/a.json` passes the allowlist unchanged. A hostile NFT in an allowlisted collection can therefore steer the server at any TCP port of a reviewed host (co-hosted admin panels, internal services on the same name).
(c) Recursion: if the operator allowlists the app's own hostname — plausible when collection metadata is self-hosted on the same domain — then `?uri=https://app.example/api/nft-metadata?uri=https://app.example/api/nft-metadata?...` recurses. `AbortSignal.timeout` aborts the *parent's* socket but does not cancel the already-dispatched child request, so one inbound request spawns an unbounded server-side chain.
(d) No resolved-IP guard exists at all: the hostname allowlist is the sole SSRF control. `redirect: "error"` correctly kills redirect-based rebinding, so the residual is DNS rebinding on a reviewed host plus operator misconfiguration of `NFT_IPFS_GATEWAY_BASE_URL` to an internal gateway.
findings.impact: Frontend availability and hosting cost; no fund or NFT impact and no confirmed reach into internal infrastructure. But this is the only server-side surface in the product with production network access, and it is reachable by anyone with the URL — it should not be the least-defended route.
findings.minimalFix: (1) Require `url.port === ""` in `allowedHTTPSURL` (line 44). (2) Reject any host that resolves to a private/loopback/link-local/CGNAT range: resolve with `dns.lookup({all:true})` and check before fetching, or pin the socket via a custom `lookup`. (3) Refuse the request's own origin host outright. (4) Add a bounded in-process concurrency semaphore (e.g. 8 in-flight outbound fetches) plus a per-IP token bucket, and return 429 instead of queuing. (5) Consider an LRU negative cache so repeated bogus CIDs stop reaching the gateway.
findings.regressionTest: Extend `frontend/e2e/metadata.spec.ts` (it currently covers only the data: happy path and one 127.0.0.1 rejection): add cases for (i) an allowlisted host with an explicit non-443 port → 422, (ii) a `uri` pointing at the app's own `/api/nft-metadata` → 422, (iii) 50 concurrent unique `ipfs://` URIs → at least one 429 and total outbound fetch count bounded, (iv) an upstream 302 → 422 (locks in `redirect:"error"`), (v) a 1 MB body with a lying `content-length` → 422 (locks in the streaming cap).

refutationNotes.reason: SURVIVES in part. Verified in route.ts: allowedHTTPSURL (41-49) compares url.hostname only, so an explicit non-443 port on a reviewed host passes; there is no rate limit, per-IP throttle or concurrency cap; there is no resolved-IP/private-range guard; redirect:'error' (122) is correctly present. But sub-claim (c) is materially wrong and drags the severity down: the self-recursion is BOUNDED, not unbounded. Each nesting level must percent-encode the whole previous URL (roughly doubling its length) and line 106 rejects any uri over MAX_URI_LENGTH = 4_096, capping the chain at ~6-7 hops; it additionally requires the operator to allowlist the app's own hostname, which runbook sec.5.4 does not instruct. Sub-claim (a) is 1:1 outbound-per-inbound with a 5 s AbortSignal that also bounds body streaming, and the 422 failure path is CDN-cacheable (line 147) -- that is a generic public-endpoint flood, not an amplifier. With no fund impact, no confirmed reach into internal infrastructure and the collection-host allowlist already in place (a disclosed known limit), this is defence-in-depth: low, not medium. The port check and a private-range guard are worth adding.

Sub-claims (a), (b) and (d) confirmed. (b) verified executably: `new URL('https://metadata.example:8443/a.json').hostname === 'metadata.example'`, and route.ts:44 tests only `url.hostname`, so any port on an allowlisted host passes. (a) route.ts:104-149 has no auth, no per-IP throttle and no concurrency cap; each unique `uri` is a cache miss holding a 5 s `AbortSignal.timeout` fetch. (d) the hostname allowlist plus `redirect:'error'` (line 122) is the only SSRF control; no resolved-IP check exists. Sub-claim (c) is REFUTED as written: the self-recursion is not 'unbounded'. Each request spawns exactly one child, and `MAX_URI_LENGTH = 4_096` (line 3) hard-bounds nesting — percent-encoding roughly doubles-to-triples the URI per level, capping the chain at ~5-7 hops, a small constant amplification. It also presupposes the operator allowlists the app's own hostname, which is speculative. Severity: the finding's own impact section concedes 'no fund or NFT impact and no confirmed reach into internal infrastructure' — under the stated ladder that is defence in depth → low, not medium. The response surface is further limited to `safeName` (≤120 chars, control chars stripped, route.ts:87-91) and `safeImageURL` (route.ts:93-102, SVG correctly excluded), so it is a weak port-scan oracle rather than an exfiltration channel.

findings.title: Receipt-polling timeouts and RPC blips are reported to the user as `reverted`; the defined `timeout` phase is never set
findings.preconditions: Any live write. Triggered by viem's `waitForTransactionReceipt` default `timeout: 180_000` ms (confirmed in node_modules/viem/_esm/actions/public/waitForTransactionReceipt.js:53) being exceeded, or by the configured app RPC failing while the wallet's own RPC succeeds.
findings.scenario:
1. User confirms an acquisition of 3 NFTs; the transaction is broadcast successfully.
2. HyperEVM routes it to the big-block queue, or the app's RPC endpoint (`NEXT_PUBLIC_HYPEREVM_RPC_URL`) rate-limits the caller (see the enumeration amplification above), so no receipt is observed within 180 s.
3. viem throws `WaitForTransactionReceiptTimeoutError`. `followReceipt`'s catch (line 352) does not distinguish it: `normalizeWriteError` falls through to the default branch and returns `REVERTED`, and the tx is written to phase `"reverted"` with the title "The on-chain call failed. Open technical details for the revert."
4. `executeWrite` then rethrows `REVERTED`, so `useProtocolAction` renders a red "transaction failed" alert and, in DepositFlow, `if (!tx) setSubmittedDeposit(null)` tears the success screen down.
5. The user, told the purchase failed, presses Confirm again and pays the acquisition + randomness fee a second time for a second, unwanted position.
Note `TxPhase` already defines `"timeout"` and DepositFlow treats it as terminal (DepositFlow.tsx:65, 88-89) — nothing in the codebase ever assigns it.
findings.impact: A succeeded-but-unconfirmed transaction is presented as a definitive failure. For `acquire` the retry is a real second spend of HYPE; for `settle`/`relist` it is a second payable call that reverts and burns gas. The transaction dock, which is the user's only record, records the wrong terminal state and `resumeTracking()` will not revisit it because `"reverted"` is not in the resumable set (line 1401).
findings.minimalFix: In `followReceipt`, catch `WaitForTransactionReceiptTimeoutError` and any transport/network error separately from a receipt with `status !== "success"`, and set phase `"timeout"` with copy such as "Still pending — we lost sight of it, check the explorer before retrying." Keep `"timeout"` in the set that `resumeTracking()` re-polls, and never rethrow it as `REVERTED` from `executeWrite`. Only a receipt whose `status` is literally `"reverted"` should produce phase `"reverted"`.
findings.regressionTest: Vitest: stub `pub.waitForTransactionReceipt` to reject with viem's `WaitForTransactionReceiptTimeoutError`, run `client.acquire(...)` with a stubbed wallet returning a hash, and assert the tracked transaction ends in phase `"timeout"` (not `"reverted"`), that the thrown ProtocolError code is not `REVERTED`, and that `resumeTracking()` re-polls it. Add a companion case where the receipt resolves with `status: "reverted"` and assert phase `"reverted"`.

refutationNotes.reason: SURVIVES, fully verified. viem's default timeout is 180_000 ms (node_modules/viem/_esm/actions/public/waitForTransactionReceipt.js, destructuring line). followReceipt's catch (352-357) maps every non-USER_REJECTED failure to phase 'reverted' via normalizeWriteError's default branch (328), executeWrite rethrows REVERTED (374-380), resumeTracking (1399-1403) only re-polls submitted/confirming, and grep confirms phase 'timeout' is assigned ONLY in the mock engine (mock/engine.ts:1400) even though it is defined (types.ts:310) and consumed by TxDock.tsx:25/29/119, DepositFlow.tsx:65/88-89 and DepositLaunchSequence.tsx:17. So a mined-but-unobserved acquire is presented as a definitive failure and is not resumable. Severity should be low rather than medium: the harm is an unintended second purchase (the user receives a second real position), not loss of funds; TxDock still renders the tx hash with an explorer link on the reverted card (75-79), so the user has a path to check; and reaching 180 s requires an RPC outage on top of the transport's own retryCount:2 (line 57) and waitForTransactionReceipt's internal retryCount:6. Real defect, cheap fix, worth doing before launch.

Fully confirmed and correctly rated at medium — the strongest finding in this set. viem's default `timeout = 180_000` verified at frontend/node_modules/viem/_esm/actions/public/waitForTransactionReceipt.js:53. `followReceipt` (ViemProtocolClient.ts:352-357) catches every error identically; `normalizeWriteError` (317-329) has no branch for `WaitForTransactionReceiptTimeoutError` or transport errors and falls through to `REVERTED` with 'The on-chain call failed. Open technical details for the revert.', and the tx is written to phase `'reverted'`. `executeWrite` (374-380) then rethrows `REVERTED`, so `useProtocolAction` (state/actions.ts:36-39) renders a failure alert and DepositFlow.tsx:382 (`if (!tx) setSubmittedDeposit(null)`) tears the success screen down. `resumeTracking` (1399-1403) only re-polls `submitted`/`confirming`, so the false terminal state is permanent. Grep confirms `TxPhase` `'timeout'` (types.ts:310) is consumed at DepositFlow.tsx:65/88/89, DepositLaunchSequence.tsx:17 and TxDock.tsx:25/29/119 but assigned only in the mock engine (mock/engine.ts:1400) — never by the live client, which is direct evidence the intended behaviour was designed and then not wired. The HyperEVM big-block routing argument makes >180 s plausible for a high-gas `acquireBatch`. Only nuance: the retry is a genuine second position rather than a loss to the protocol, and the wallet's own history contradicts the UI — but a UI that reports a mined transaction as failed is a real state-machine defect. Medium stands.

findings.lens: Release sequencing, fail-closed gates and admin powers (main
findings.title: Eight mutating deployment scripts have no positive chain-id allowlist
findings.lines: 37-40 (same pattern in ActivateNestMarket.s.sol:32-36, BindNestRewards.s.sol:33-37, BindSplitterHyperEVM.s.sol:31-35, ConfigureNestPool.s.sol:32-36, DeployNestModules.s.sol:55-59, DeployNestPlugin.s.sol:38-41, InitializeNestMarket.s.sol:26-29)
findings.preconditions: Operator supplies an --rpc-url other than hyperevm_mainnet/hyperevm_testnet, e.g. a mistyped alias, a stale foundry.toml rpc_endpoints entry, or a forked/aggregator endpoint that resolves to a different chain id.
findings.scenario: Every other mutating script in the tree opens with an unconditional `if (block.chainid != X) revert WrongChain(block.chainid)` - DeployHyperEVMMainnetCore.s.sol:55, ActivateHyperEVMMainnet.s.sol:42, DeploySplitterHyperEVM.s.sol:40-42, DeployNestToken.s.sol:46-48, ActivateHyperEVMCore.s.sol:33, and so on. These eight instead use only the conditional form `if (block.chainid == HYPEREVM_MAINNET_CHAIN_ID && !vm.envBool("NEST_MAINNET_DEPLOYMENT_CONFIRMED")) revert MainnetNotConfirmed();`. On any chain that is neither 998 nor 999 the confirmation predicate is vacuously satisfied and the script proceeds to vm.startBroadcast with zero chain checking. Because the mainnet-confirmation branch is correctly conditioned on 999, a genuine chain-999 broadcast is still flag-gated; the exposure is broadcasting onto an unintended third chain (and, on 998, running LaunchNestMarket/InitializeNestMarket/DeployNestPlugin with no gate at all).
findings.impact: An unintended-chain broadcast spends deployer funds and, where the environment addresses happen to have code, can execute one-shot actions on the wrong network. Most instances are saved incidentally by later address checks such as `token.owner() != deployer`, so this is defence-in-depth rather than a direct loss path - but it removes the single cheapest invariant the rest of the codebase relies on and is inconsistent with the project's own stated pattern.
findings.minimalFix: Add `if (block.chainid != HYPEREVM_TESTNET_CHAIN_ID && block.chainid != HYPEREVM_MAINNET_CHAIN_ID) revert WrongChain(block.chainid);` as the first statement of all eight scripts, matching DeploySplitterHyperEVM.s.sol:40-42.
findings.regressionTest: Add a Foundry test that vm.chainId(1) then expects a WrongChain revert from each of the eight script contracts' run(); assert via a directory-walking test or a CI grep that every script/*.s.sol containing startBroadcast also contains an unconditional chainid inequality check.

refutationNotes.reason: SURVIVES factually, severity overstated. I confirmed all eight by grepping every script/*.s.sol for `chainid`: ActivateNestMarket:34, BindNestRewards:35, BindSplitterHyperEVM:33, ConfigureNestPool:34, DeployNestModules:57, DeployNestPlugin:39, InitializeNestMarket:27, LaunchNestMarket:38 use only the conditional `== 999 && !flag` form, while 20 other scripts use an unconditional inequality. The inconsistency is real.
