Attacker needs only wHYPE and the public Nest router.
findings.scenario: beforeSwap only reverts when `isBuy && !externalBuysEnabled && recipient != address(TOKEN) && !TOKEN.isProtocolBuyer(recipient)`, and _afterTokenTransfer mirrors it with `to == address(this) || isProtocolBuyer[to]`. Neither looks at who initiated the swap. Out-of-tree PoC (compiled and run against the repo's own mocks, 4/4 passing): attacker 0xBADD calls router.exactInputSingle{tokenIn: wHYPE, tokenOut: FWA, recipient: address(token), amountIn: 0.01e18} while the market is closed — it SUCCEEDS and token.balanceOf(address(token)) increases by the output. The same call with recipient = any registered protocol buyer (e.g. FWARewardsHyperEVM, or in the PoC the adapter registered via setRewardsPool) also SUCCEEDS. Only recipient = the attacker reverts ExternalBuysDisabled. That the real Algebra pool passes the true output recipient into beforeSwap is already proven by the repo's own fork test: hyperevm-fork-test/NestDeployment.t.sol:118-123 executes token.buyback() successfully against the real Nest pool with externalBuysEnabled == false, which can only pass through the `recipient != address(TOKEN)` branch.
findings.impact: The stated bootstrap invariant — price driven purely by protocol/purchaser buys, no external or speculative buy-ins until the manual open — is not enforced. An outsider can move the closed-market price at will (their wHYPE ends up as irrecoverable principal in the locked LP and the FWA lands in the token or rewards contract, so this is griefing/donation, not theft — FWARewardsHyperEVM accounting is counter-based, not balance-based, so entitlements are not inflated). Concrete secondary damage: pushing the price ~10% past the launch-derived buybackSqrtPriceLimitX96 makes buyback() revert outright (Algebra rejects an already-crossed limitSqrtPrice), stalling protocol buybacks and piling up HYPE until the owner manually calls setBuybackSqrtPriceLimitX96. It also corrupts the plugin Trade feed the indexer and frontend consume. This is a direct regression against the Ethereum reference, whose hook gates on `sender` AND requires ITokenBuyer(sender).isBuying() precisely "so a registered-but-idle module can never be ridden" (FWA_ETHEREUM_REFERENCE/FWATokenHook/sources/src/FWATokenHook.sol:222-230).
findings.minimalFix: Restore the reference's handshake. Sender-gating alone cannot work here because the pool's msg.sender is Nest's shared router, so add a transient in-progress flag: FWATokenNest exposes protocolBuyInProgress() backed by transient storage, set true only across FWATokenNest.buyback() and across a call from the registered adapter serving FWARewards.buyFor. Then require in FWANestPlugin.beforeSwap `TOKEN.protocolBuyInProgress()` in addition to the recipient allowance, and apply the same condition to the `to == address(this) || isProtocolBuyer[to]` branch of _afterTokenTransfer.
findings.regressionTest: Add to test/FWANestIntegration.t.sol: with externalBuysEnabled == false, assert router.exactInputSingle(..., recipient: address(token)) reverts ExternalBuysDisabled, and assert the same for recipient = the registered rewards pool, while token.buyback() and rewards.buyFor still succeed.
findings.evidence: Scratchpad PoC NestGateBypass.t.sol: testOutsiderCanSwapClosedPoolByNamingTokenAsRecipient PASS, testOutsiderCanRideRegisteredProtocolBuyer PASS, testClosedMarketBlocksBuyToSelf PASS (baseline).

refutationNotes.reason: MECHANISM SURVIVES, SEVERITY OVERSTATED — low, not medium, and the title is materially wrong. The code path is exactly as described: FWANestPlugin.sol:125 only reverts when recipient is neither address(TOKEN) nor a registered protocol buyer, and FWATokenNest.sol:423 mirrors it, so router.exactInputSingle(recipient: address(token)) with externalBuysEnabled==false does complete. The port genuinely diverges from the parity oracle, which gates on sender AND ITokenBuyer(sender).isBuying() (FWATokenHook.sol:228-230) precisely against riding a registered module. But 'any outsider can trade the closed pool' is not what the code allows. The outsider can never RECEIVE $FWA: isProtocolBuyer is written only by setRewardsPool (:226) and owner setProtocolBuyer (:165), so the reachable recipient set is {token, FWARewardsHyperEVM} — never attacker-controlled. The attacker therefore pays wHYPE that becomes permanently locked LP principal and hands the $FWA to the protocol; FWA landing in the token contract is unrecoverable by anyone (burn() only burns msg.sender's balance, and buyback's _burn/_transfer amounts are derived from amountOut, never from the balance), and FWARewardsHyperEVM is accumulator-based (accTokenPerSqrt, purchaserEpochPot, tokenCredit), so a donated balance only over-collateralises existing claims. There is also no profitable sandwich: sells stay open while closed (:421), so any holder immediately arbitrages the donated pump back down, capturing most of the attacker's spend. What actually remains is a pure money-burning grief that can (i) distort the bootstrap price and (ii) push price past buybackSqrtPriceLimitX96 so buyback() reverts until one owner tx (setBuybackSqrtPriceLimitX96) resets it. Recoverable, self-financing for the protocol, and no fund or accounting impact — low. The proposed transient in-progress-flag fix is still the right hardening and the divergence is worth closing before launch.

SURVIVES at medium; impact framing partly wrong. Code confirmed verbatim: FWANestPlugin.sol:125-127 reverts only when `isBuy && !externalBuysEnabled && recipient != address(TOKEN) && !TOKEN.isProtocolBuyer(recipient)` - `sender` (param 1) is read and discarded; FWATokenNest.sol:423 mirrors it on `to`. The parity-regression claim is accurate: FWA_ETHEREUM_REFERENCE/FWATokenHook/sources/src/FWATokenHook.sol gates on `!isPool[sender] || !ITokenBuyer(sender).isBuying()` with the comment that the isBuying handshake exists 'so a registered-but-idle module can never be ridden'. Reachability is proven by the repo's own artefacts, not just the auditor's PoC: hyperevm-fork-test/NestDeployment.t.sol:114-118 runs token.buyback() through the REAL Nest router against the REAL pool with externalBuysEnabled == false, and the adapter passes `recipient: msg.sender` (FWANestSwapAdapter.sol:115), so the real Algebra pool demonstrably forwards the caller-chosen recipient into beforeSwap and the gate passes on it alone. Coverage gap is also real: test/FWANestIntegration.t.sol:78 only ever tries `recipient: USER`. Two corrections to the impact: (i) the distribution invariant is NOT broken - the attacker cannot obtain a single $FWA, so 'no speculative buy-ins during bootstrap' still holds; only the price invariant breaks, at strictly negative EV for the attacker (their wHYPE enters the permanently locked LP, their FWA lands in the token contract where nothing can ever move it, or over-funds the counter-based rewards module); (ii) 'pushing price past buybackSqrtPriceLimitX96 stalls buyback()' is the reference's explicitly INTENDED design ('bounding token-price appreciation during a buyback to roughly 10% until the owner deliberately updates it', FWAToken.sol:57), and the protocol's own 1-HYPE-per-block buybacks reach that ceiling unaided - an outsider only accelerates it. Net residual harm: an outsider can move the closed-market price, so protocol buybacks and claimAccruedTokens execute at a manipulated price. Recoverable griefing = medium. The proposed transient in-progress flag is the right fix.

findings.title: LP fee collection is bricked for the entire closed-market phase; the fork test masks it by using the owner as fee recipient
findings.preconditions: FWA_NEST_FEE_RECIPIENT is a treasury address that is neither the token owner nor a registered distributor. No script registers it — `grep -rn setDistributor script/ scripts/` returns nothing, and the only writes to isDistributor are setAdapter and setRewardsPool. externalBuysEnabled == false (the whole phase-7 window, and any later re-close).
findings.scenario: Sells into the pool are permitted while the market is closed (_afterTokenTransfer line 422: `if (to == marketPool) return;`), and rewards claimants who receive FWA from the distributor can sell immediately. Algebra takes swap fees from the input token, so those sells accrue FWA-denominated fees to the locked position. locker.collectFees() then calls positionManager.collect(tokenId, recipient = feeRecipient, uint128.max, uint128.max); the resulting pool -> feeRecipient FWA transfer falls through to `revert InvalidTransfer()` because feeRecipient is not a distributor, not the owner, not address(token) and not a protocol buyer. Because collect is atomic across both tokens, the wHYPE-side fees become uncollectable too. Verified: PoC testFeeRecipientCannotReceivePoolFeesWhileClosed passes (vm.prank(pool); token.transfer(FEE_RECIPIENT, 1e18) reverts InvalidTransfer). The fork test hyperevm-fork-test/NestDeployment.t.sol:86 and :125-126 only passes because it constructs the locker with feeRecipient = address(this), which is also the token owner and therefore exempt.
findings.impact: All protocol LP revenue is uncollectable for the entire bootstrap window, and again any time the owner re-closes public buys. NEST_DEPLOYMENT_RUNBOOK.md:77 explicitly makes "collecte de fees ... alors que les achats externes restent fermés" a phase-7 acceptance criterion — that step will fail on mainnet with a real treasury address. Recoverable (fees keep accruing and can be collected once the market opens), no permanent loss.
findings.minimalFix: Register the fee recipient as a distributor at deploy time — add token.setDistributor(feeRecipient, true) to DeployNestToken/DeployNestModules — and assert it in VerifyNestModules. Alternatively relax the token rule: allow `from == pool && to == FWANestLiquidityLocker(liquidityLocker).feeRecipient()` unconditionally.
findings.regressionTest: Integration test with feeRecipient != owner and not a distributor: launch, have a non-owner sell FWA into the pool while closed, then assert locker.collectFees() succeeds and pays the fee recipient.
findings.evidence: Scratchpad PoC NestGateBypass.t.sol: testFeeRecipientCannotReceivePoolFeesWhileClosed PASS. test/mocks/MockNestAlgebra.sol collect() returns (0,0) and performs no transfer, so no in-repo test can catch this.

refutationNotes.reason: MECHANISM SURVIVES, SEVERITY OVERSTATED — low, not medium, and the category is external-config (deployment wiring), not contract-bug. The trace is right: NFPM.collect passes recipient straight through to pool.collect, so the pool->feeRecipient FWA leg hits FWATokenNest.sol:428 revert InvalidTransfer whenever feeRecipient is not a distributor/owner/protocol buyer and externalBuysEnabled is false, and because collect is atomic the wHYPE leg is blocked with it. I confirmed the wiring gap independently: grep over script/ and scripts/ returns zero setDistributor calls, DeployNestToken.s.sol:57,78 passes FWA_NEST_FEE_RECIPIENT only to the locker constructor, and .env.mainnet.example ships FWA_NEST_FEE_RECIPIENT and FWA_OWNER as separate zero-addressed variables with nothing requiring them to be equal. The masking claim also holds — test/mocks/MockNestAlgebra.sol:241-250 returns (0,0) and performs no transfer, so no in-repo test can catch it, and NestDeployment.t.sol:86 uses feeRecipient == address(this) == the owner. But the impact is much smaller than 'all protocol LP revenue is uncollectable'. Fees are not lost, they keep accruing in the position; the condition needs an FWA-side fee to be owed (i.e. at least one sell) since Algebra only transfers non-zero legs; and the owner clears it with a single tx — token.setDistributor(feeRecipient,true) or locker.setFeeRecipient(owner) (FWANestLiquidityLocker.sol:54-58) — with no irreversible step in between. It is also surfaced by the team's own gate: NEST_DEPLOYMENT_RUNBOOK.md:77 makes fee collection while closed a phase-7 acceptance criterion that must pass before NEST_E2E_CONFIRMED, so the rehearsal is designed to catch exactly this. Worth fixing in DeployNestModules and asserting in VerifyNestModules, at low.

SURVIVES; severity and category both wrong. Mechanism confirmed: FWANestLiquidityLocker.sol:63-67 hardcodes amount0Max/amount1Max = uint128.max so collect is all-or-nothing; the resulting FWA leg lands at `from == pool, to == feeRecipient`, which falls through FWATokenNest.sol:415-428 to revert InvalidTransfer whenever externalBuysEnabled == false and feeRecipient is not a distributor/owner. Precondition is realistic: FWA_NEST_FEE_RECIPIENT is a standalone env var (.env.mainnet.example:59) distinct from FWA_OWNER (:5), DeployNestToken.s.sol:78 passes it straight into the constructor, DeployNestModules.s.sol:106 hands token ownership to finalOwner, and `grep -rn setDistributor script/ scripts/` genuinely returns nothing - the only isDistributor writes are setAdapter/setRewardsPool. Sells during the closed window are permitted (FWATokenNest.sol:421) so FWA-side fees do accrue. Test-blindness confirmed: test/mocks/MockNestAlgebra.sol:241-250 collect() returns (0,0) and transfers nothing. TWO CORRECTIONS. First, the fork-test 'masking' explanation is wrong: hyperevm-fork-test/NestDeployment.t.sol:125 passes not because feeRecipient == owner but because only buys ran, so the FWA fee leg is zero and no FWA transfer is attempted at all - the guard is never touched. Second, and decisive for severity: this is fail-CLOSED, fully recoverable in one owner transaction (token.setDistributor(feeRecipient, true) or locker.setFeeRecipient(owner)), loses nothing (fees keep accruing in the position and are collected later), and risks no user funds or NFTs. That is low, not medium. Category should be external-config / deployment-script gap, not contract-bug - the token behaves exactly as its transfer lock specifies.

findings.title: Permissionless pool.initialize between Nest's createPool and the plugin install; the only protection is a sentence in the handoff document
findings.lines: 18-31 ("personne n'appelle `initialize` avant l'action 2"); NEST_DEPLOYMENT_RUNBOOK.md:44-50; script/DeployNestPlugin.s.sol:48-54; src/hyperevm/FWANestPlugin.sol:57-58
findings.preconditions: Phase A complete, so the FWA token address is public on-chain. Nest broadcasts createPool(wHYPE, FWA) as a separate transaction from setPlugin/setPluginConfig, exactly as the handoff document splits Action 1 and Action 2. Any mempool observer suffices; no privilege required.
findings.scenario: Live read-only probes on chain 999 show the asymmetry precisely: pool.initialize(uint160) from 0x…dEaD reverts alreadyInitialized() (0x52669adc) — it cleared authorization and failed only on state, so initialize has NO access control — while setPlugin/setPluginConfig/setCommunityFee/setTickSpacing all revert notAllowed() (0x932984d2) and createPool reverts with a missing AccessControl role. The factory also exposes defaultPluginFactory() = 0x9F0B3984cE2496bDf9DB89701dF6BAc425FaAdD8, so a freshly created pool carries Nest's permissive default plugin until Action 2 lands. Attack: right after Nest's createPool tx confirms, an observer sends pool.initialize(<arbitrary price>). Nest's default plugin's beforeInitialize accepts it. Now globalState().price != 0, so (a) `new FWANestPlugin(...)` reverts PoolAlreadyInitialized (FWANestPlugin.sol:58), (b) DeployNestPlugin reverts PoolAlreadyInitialized, (c) token.setMarketInfrastructure can never be called, and (d) since Algebra Integral keys exactly one pool per pair via poolByPair, this FWA token address is permanently unlaunchable — phase A must be redone with a fresh token.
findings.impact: Cheap, repeatable denial of the mainnet launch by an unprivileged observer, timed to the scheduled window. No funds at risk (no LP exists yet), but each attempt burns a token deployment and the attack can be repeated indefinitely at gas cost. This is exactly the pattern where an off-chain gate stands in for an on-chain invariant: the Ethereum reference removes the window entirely by making pool init part of the token's own atomic launch() under a transient latch.
findings.minimalFix: Make Action 1 and Action 2 a single atomic transaction on Nest's side — a Safe batch or multicall performing createPool -> setPlugin(FWANestPlugin) -> setPluginConfig(7) — or have Nest register FWANestPlugin with the plugin factory so createPool attaches it directly. Update NEST_ADMIN_HANDOFF.md to state atomicity as a hard acceptance criterion rather than "personne n'appelle initialize". If atomicity is genuinely impossible, submit the pair as a private/bundled transaction and treat a griefed pool as an expected retry path.
findings.regressionTest: Fork test on 999: vm.prank(factory.owner()) createPool(wHYPE, token); then vm.prank(address(0xBADD)) pool.initialize(uint160(1<<96)) and assert it succeeds and that `new FWANestPlugin(pool, token, wHYPE)` subsequently reverts PoolAlreadyInitialized. Add the batched variant asserting the window is closed.
findings.evidence: cast call 0xBE512f…D696 "initialize(uint160)" 79228162514264337593543950336 --from 0x…dEaD → 0x52669adc (alreadyInitialized). cast call same pool "setPlugin(address)"/"setCommunityFee(uint16)"/"setTickSpacing(int24)"/"setPluginConfig(uint8)" --from 0x…dEaD → 0x932984d2 (notAllowed). cast call factory "createPool" --from 0x…dEaD → AccessControl missing role.

refutationNotes.reason: SURVIVES at medium, and I can confirm the core mechanism from the repo alone without trusting the RPC probes. The repo's own code proves initialization is unprivileged: FWATokenNest.initializeMarket (:273) reaches the pool through POSITION_MANAGER.createAndInitializePoolIfNecessary, and FWATokenNest is not a Nest admin — NestDeployment.t.sol:94 executes that call successfully against real chain-999 contracts with no impersonation, so any address can initialize an existing price==0 pool by the same route. The kill is confirmed too: FWANestPlugin.sol:57-58 reverts PoolAlreadyInitialized in the CONSTRUCTOR, and FWATokenNest.sol:269 requires currentPrice == 0, and there is no path to set marketInitialized other than initializeMarket, so a griefed pair is permanently unlaunchable for that token address even with a hand-rolled plugin. The window is in fact WIDER than the finding states: it opens at Nest's createPool and only closes when pool.setPlugin(FWANestPlugin) lands, because Algebra invokes beforeInitialize unconditionally whenever plugin != address(0) (mirrored at test/mocks/MockNestAlgebra.sol:97) — so the whole cross-org gap covering DeployNestPlugin (phase B) and Action 2 is exposed, not just the createPool-to-setPlugin hop. No funds are at risk (no LP, no users yet) and the cost is a redeployed token plus a fresh Nest-admin pool creation, which is why this is recoverable griefing rather than high: but each retry needs Nest's admin to act again, so a watcher can stall a scheduled launch repeatedly at gas cost. Medium is correct. Citing a markdown file as the primary location is unusual but justified here — the only control today is NEST_ADMIN_HANDOFF.md:31 asking that nobody call initialize.

SURVIVES; severity overstated. The window is real and the consequence is correctly traced in-repo: FWANestPlugin.sol:57-58 reverts PoolAlreadyInitialized in the CONSTRUCTOR if globalState().price != 0, DeployNestPlugin.s.sol:50-51 re-checks it, FWATokenNest.sol:269 requires currentPrice == 0 in initializeMarket, and poolByPair is one-pool-per-pair - so an initialize landing between Nest's Action 1 and Action 2 does permanently strand that token address. Once FWANestPlugin IS installed the window closes correctly (beforeInitialize:74-79 requires TOKEN.launching()), so the exposure is exactly the createPool -> setPlugin gap the handoff splits (NEST_ADMIN_HANDOFF.md:18-31). BUT the rubric does not support medium. It fails closed; zero funds, NFTs or LP exist at that phase; the attacker gains nothing and pays gas; recovery is a redeploy of the token + locker only - I verified the expensive bindings come LATER and are therefore untouched (FWA.setRewards, which one-shots both `rewards` and `token`, is FWA.sol:2347-2358 and runs at runbook phase 6, after the pool launch at phase 5). The audit mandate's own escalation rule ('an off-chain gate is a finding when the consequence is loss of funds or an irreversible open') is not met - neither applies. Low. The recommended fix (Nest-side atomic batch, or registering FWANestPlugin with the plugin factory) is correct and cheap, and NEST_ADMIN_HANDOFF.md:31 should indeed state atomicity as an acceptance criterion rather than a request. Note the finding's live-chain probe evidence is unverifiable from this workspace (no network, read-only audit); I confirmed the in-repo half only.

findings.title: Read-only state always blames a missing deployment manifest, even when the manifest is present and valid
findings.lines: 28-35; identical copy at SwapPanel.tsx:284, DepositFlow.tsx:158, PurchaseSidebar.tsx:183
findings.preconditions: `manifestState.status === "ready"` with `features.writesEnabled: false` — the normal mainnet pre-promotion state.
findings.scenario: `EnvBanner`'s reason ladder only handles `wrong-chain` and `invalid`; the `ready`-but-flag-off case falls through to the `else` and renders `READ-ONLY — writes disabled (no deployment manifest)`. The three write panels repeat the same claim verbatim ("No deployment manifest for this chain."). An operator or support engineer looking at a mainnet frontend during the §6 canary is told the manifest is missing when it is in fact loaded, validated and correct — sending them to debug the wrong system.
findings.impact: Misleading operational telemetry during the highest-risk phase of the launch. No fund impact.
findings.minimalFix: Add a fourth branch: when `manifestState.status === "ready"`, the reason is `"writes disabled by the deployment manifest (features.writesEnabled=false)"`. Update the three panel strings to match.
findings.regressionTest: Component test rendering `<EnvBanner>` with `manifestState = {status:"ready", manifest:{...features:{writesEnabled:false}}}` and asserting the banner text contains "features.writesEnabled" and does NOT contain "no deployment manifest".

refutationNotes.reason: SURVIVES exactly as written; severity low is correct. EnvBanner.tsx:29-34 handles only wrong-chain and invalid, so manifestState.status === 'ready' with writesEnabled:false falls through to 'no deployment manifest' -- and this is the normal mainnet pre-promotion state produced by WriteMainnetManifest.ps1:68. The identical claim is repeated verbatim at PurchaseSidebar.tsx:183 ('No deployment manifest for this chain.'), SwapPanel.tsx:284 (same string, confirmed), DepositFlow.tsx:156 ('No valid deployment manifest for this chain') and in errors.ts describeError's WRITES_DISABLED branch. Misleading operational telemetry during the sec.6 canary with no fund impact -- textbook low. Nothing to correct.

findings.title: "RPC unreachable — transactions are paused" banner is false: read-free writes still submit through the wallet's own provider
findings.preconditions: `getConnectionHealth()` returns `rpc: "down"` (the app's configured RPC is unreachable) while the user's injected wallet has a working provider.
findings.scenario: The banner asserts "quotes and transactions are paused". Quotes genuinely are — `acquire`, `listNFT` and `approveNFT` all perform pre-flight `this.pub.readContract` calls that throw when the RPC is down, so those three fail closed correctly. But `settle` (all 7 kinds), `withdrawListing`, `recoverStuckNFT`, `withdrawEarnings`, `withdrawAcquisitionRefund`, `claimListingFees`, `claimCrown` and `claimRewards` perform no reads at all: they call `connectedWallet()` (which only inspects wagmi state) and then `wallet.writeContract` on `custom(window.ethereum)`, i.e. the wallet's RPC, not the app's. Those transactions submit and mine normally.
findings.impact: The banner understates what the user can still do (arguably good) while stating something untrue, and it pairs badly with the previous finding: the write goes through but `followReceipt` — which does use the down RPC — then reports it as reverted.
findings.minimalFix: Reword to "RPC unreachable — quotes, pool data and confirmation tracking are paused; wallet transactions still go through your wallet's own network", or actually gate all writes on RPC health if the pause is the intended behaviour. Do not claim a pause the code does not implement.
findings.regressionTest: Component test for `<EnvBanner>` asserting the rpc-down copy, plus a Vitest case asserting that with `pub` stubbed to reject on every read, `client.withdrawEarnings()` still reaches `wallet.writeContract` — pinning the actual behaviour so the copy and the code cannot drift apart again.

refutationNotes.reason: Technically correct: EnvBanner.tsx:47-52 claims transactions are paused, while settle (1301-1340), withdrawListing (1243), recoverStuckNFT (1342), withdrawEarnings (1349), withdrawAcquisitionRefund (1356), claimListingFees (1363), claimCrown (1370) and claimRewards (1377) perform zero this.pub reads -- connectedWallet (302-315) inspects wagmi state only and the wallet client uses custom(injected). But the practical divergence is near zero, so this is an info-level copy nit rather than a low defect: with the app RPC down, getUserPositions (863-870) fails, so PositionsScreen renders skeletons (121-126) and none of those buttons are reachable on a cold load; getPoolSnapshot, getListing and getSettlementInfo fail the same way, so the surfaces that host those writes do not render either. The banner's summary is imprecise, not materially deceptive. Its real value is the pairing it names with verdict 6 (the write lands, then followReceipt reports it reverted) -- fix that one and reword this string alongside.

REFUTED: the stated discrepancy has no user-reachable manifestation. The client-layer claim is technically right — `connectedWallet()` (ViemProtocolClient.ts:302-315) touches only wagmi state and `window.ethereum`, and viem's `sendTransaction` for a `json-rpc` account (node_modules/viem/_esm/actions/wallet/sendTransaction.js:92-126) issues `eth_sendTransaction` plus `getChainId` on the wallet client's own `custom(injected)` transport, never on `this.pub`. But the banner is user-facing copy, and when `getConnectionHealth` reports `rpc: 'down'` (lines 680-706, which requires `pub.getBlockNumber()` to throw) every screen hosting those buttons is itself blocked on `this.pub` reads: `getUserPositions` (863-870) rejects, so PositionsScreen.tsx:121 (`isLoading || !positions`) stays on the skeleton branch forever and the Settle / Reclaim / Finalize / Claim / Withdraw controls are never mounted; `AcquisitionResultScreen` needs `usePurchaseStats` and `useListing`, both of which reject; PurchaseBox is blocked by `!snapshot`; the deposit picker is blocked by `useOwnedNfts`. So with the app RPC down the user cannot reach a single one of the writes the finding lists, and the banner statement is accurate as experienced. What remains is an inaccuracy only for a caller who invokes the client from a console — a copy nit at info level, not a defect. Note the finding's own pairing argument is also weakened: since the buttons cannot be pressed, the 'write goes through then followReceipt reports it as reverted' scenario cannot arise from this state.

findings.title: Protocol parameters documented as "always read on-chain" are hardcoded on the Positions screen and in two client computations
findings.lines: 1-6 (the claim); violations at PositionsScreen.tsx:214-215, 224, 247-250 and ViemProtocolClient.ts:1108, 1206
findings.preconditions: The owner retunes `settlementWindow`, `finalizeWindow`, `settlementDiscountBps` or `ownerSettlementFeeBps` on-chain after launch (all four are owner-settable at FWA.sol:2269-2277).
findings.scenario: params.ts states "in testnet/mainnet mode every one of these is read on-chain and the on-chain value always wins". I verified that is false in four places. PositionsScreen computes both settlement windows from the hardcoded `FWA_PARAMS.settlementWindowSec = 86_400` / `finalizeWindowSec = 604_800` and the standing bid from `FWA_PARAMS.bidPayoutBps = 8_500`, and those constants decide which *buttons* render (lines 266, 292). `getSettlementInfo` hardcodes the owner cut as `100n` bps rather than reading it. `listNFT` enforces `FWA_PARAMS.minBacking` client-side. If the owner raises `settlementWindow` to 48 h, a depositor is offered "Reclaim backing" / "Reclaim NFT" 24 h early and the transaction reverts; meanwhile `SettlementDrawer`, which *does* use the on-chain `settlementWindow` via `getSettlementInfo`, shows a different countdown for the same listing. (`minBacking`, `surchargeBps` and `acquisitionsEnabled` are genuinely `internal` in FWA.sol and cannot be read — only `settlementWindow`, `finalizeWindow` and `settlementDiscountBps` are public.)
findings.impact: Two screens disagree about the same listing's windows; users are offered actions that revert (gas loss only). Also a documentation claim that an auditor or a future maintainer will reasonably trust.
findings.minimalFix: Thread the already-fetched on-chain values into PositionsScreen (either extend `PoolSnapshot` with `settlementWindowSec`/`finalizeWindowSec`/`bidPayoutBps` or call `useSettlementInfo` per allocated row) and read `ownerSettlementFeeBps` in `getSettlementInfo` instead of the literal `100n`. Amend the params.ts docstring to name exactly which constants are unreadable on-chain (`minBacking`, `surchargeBps`, `acquisitionsEnabled` — all `internal`) and are therefore display fallbacks only.
findings.regressionTest: Vitest: stub `pub.readContract` so `settlementWindow` returns `172800n` and `settlementDiscountBps` returns `9000n`, then assert `getSettlementInfo` reports `purchaserWindowEndsAt = allocatedAt + 172800` and `bidPayoutBps = 9000`; plus a component test asserting PositionsScreen hides the depositor-reclaim buttons at t = allocatedAt + 86_401 when the on-chain window is 48 h.

refutationNotes.reason: SURVIVES; low is correct. Every claim checked out. params.ts:4-5 does assert 'in testnet/mainnet mode every one of these is read on-chain and the on-chain value always wins'. PositionsScreen.tsx:214-215/224 and 247-250 compute both windows and the standing bid from FWA_PARAMS constants, and those values gate which buttons render at 266 and 292. getSettlementInfo (1092-1109) correctly reads settlementWindow, finalizeWindow and settlementDiscountBps on-chain but hardcodes the owner cut as `100n` at 1108 -- and ownerSettlementFeeBps IS public (FWA.sol:347), so that one is readable and simply is not read. listNFT:1206 enforces FWA_PARAMS.minBacking client-side. The visibility split in the finding is exactly right: settlementWindow (FWA.sol:319), finalizeWindow (324), settlementDiscountBps (314) and ownerSettlementFeeBps (347) are public; minBacking (331), surchargeBps (306) and acquisitionsEnabled (281) are internal. All four are owner-settable (2266-2282). The two-screen disagreement is real: SettlementDrawer.tsx:31/40/138 uses on-chain info.purchaserWindowEndsAt while PositionsScreen uses the constant, so the same listing can show two different countdowns. Impact is gas on a reverting call plus a false docstring -- low.

Confirmed at every cited line. params.ts:4-5 does claim 'in testnet/mainnet mode every one of these is read on-chain and the on-chain value always wins'. PositionsScreen.tsx:214-215 and 247-248 compute both windows from `FWA_PARAMS.settlementWindowSec`/`finalizeWindowSec`, line 224 uses `FWA_PARAMS.bidPayoutBps`, and those constants gate which buttons render (line 266 `!purchaserExclusive && !canFinalize`, line 292 `canFinalize`), so a retuned window really does offer depositor-reclaim actions that revert. `getSettlementInfo` hardcodes the owner cut as `100n` at ViemProtocolClient.ts:1108 while correctly reading `settlementWindow`/`finalizeWindow`/`settlementDiscountBps` at 1095-1097 — which is exactly the two-screens-disagree case described. `listNFT` enforces `FWA_PARAMS.minBacking` client-side at line 1206. Contract visibility checks out: `settlementDiscountBps` (FWA.sol:314), `settlementWindow` (:319), `finalizeWindow` (:324) and `ownerSettlementFeeBps` (:347) are all `public`; `minBacking` (:331), `surchargeBps` (:306) and `acquisitionsEnabled` (:281) are `internal`. One small internal inconsistency in the write-up: it lists only three params as public and omits `ownerSettlementFeeBps`, though its own fix correctly assumes that one is readable. Severity low is correct — display divergence plus reverting transactions (gas only), conditioned on an owner retune that is not currently planned.

findings.title: Purchaser settlement panel renders without checking that the connected wallet is the listing's purchaser
findings.lines: 112; gate logic at InlineSettlementPanel.tsx:29-49; indexer origin at ViemProtocolClient.ts:829-860, 1151-1156
findings.preconditions: Live mode with an indexer configured, and the Goldsky subgraph compromised, misconfigured or serving a forked/incorrect dataset.
findings.scenario: `getPurchaseStats` builds its history from `indexedAcquisitionTickets(account)`, whose `listingId` comes straight from the subgraph row. `AcquisitionResultScreen` looks that id up on-chain (`useListing`, good) and hands the resulting listing to `PurchaseResultSurface`, which renders `<InlineSettlementPanel listing={listing} />` at line 112. `InlineSettlementPanel` guards only on `listing.status !== "allocated"` — it never compares `listing.purchaser` to `account.address`. So a subgraph returning `{requestId: 999, purchaser: <victim>, listingId: <a stranger's allocated listing>, status: "fulfilled"}` makes the victim's /acquisitions/999 page display someone else's genuine on-chain NFT, backing and odds as their win, with live Keep NFT / Auto-relist / Accept HYPE buttons. The same indexer row drives `useRevealQueue`, so it can also fire the full-screen "you won" reveal. Every button reverts on-chain (the contract checks the purchaser), so the loss is gas plus a payable `relistNFT` value that is returned on revert.
findings.impact: No unauthorised state change — the contract is the authority and holds. But the indexer, explicitly documented as untrusted discovery infrastructure, can drive a convincing win-notification phishing surface and induce reverting signatures. Note PositionsScreen does not have this gap: it filters `allocated` by on-chain `purchaser` (ViemProtocolClient.ts:875).
findings.minimalFix: In `InlineSettlementPanel`, add `if (!sameAddress(listing.purchaser, account.address)) return <NotYourPosition/>` alongside the existing status check, and have `AcquisitionResultScreen` refuse to render the surface when `listing.purchaser` does not match the connected account. Same guard before enqueuing a reveal in `useRevealQueue`.
findings.regressionTest: Component test: render `<PurchaseResultSurface>` with a listing whose `purchaser` is a different address from the connected account and assert none of `settle-keep`, `settle-relist`, `settle-acceptBidHype`, `settle-acceptBidTokens` are in the document. Plus a Vitest case feeding `useRevealQueue` a ticket whose listing's on-chain purchaser is a stranger and asserting no reveal is queued.

refutationNotes.reason: SURVIVES; low is correct, and the exposure is slightly wider than reported. InlineSettlementPanel.tsx:29 guards only on listing.status !== 'allocated' and never compares listing.purchaser to the connected account; PurchaseResultSurface.tsx:112 renders it unconditionally; AcquisitionResultScreen.tsx:17-18 takes record.listingId from usePurchaseStats, and getPurchaseStats (1151-1153) calls acquisitionTickets, which at 753-754 short-circuits to indexedAcquisitionTickets whenever an indexer is configured -- with NO on-chain revalidation of the requestId to listingId mapping (contrast the non-indexed branch at 762-805, which reads `acquisitions(requestId)` and enforces sameAddress(acquisition[0], account) at 768). Additional exposure the finding did not state: getUserPositions.pendingAcquisitions (881-887) cross-checks only `listing.id === ticket.listingId && status === 'allocated'`, not the purchaser, and hydrateIndexedListing (204-217) re-reads the listing by id without verifying the account is a party -- so useRevealQueue.ts:93-100 can indeed be driven to fire a full-screen reveal on a stranger's position. Severity stays low: the contract is the authority, every button reverts, relistNFT's value is returned on revert, and PositionsScreen.tsx does hold the line via the on-chain filter at ViemProtocolClient.ts:875. Worth adding the guard.

Confirmed. `InlineSettlementPanel` (frontend/src/components/positions/InlineSettlementPanel.tsx:29-39) guards only on `listing.status !== 'allocated'` and never compares `listing.purchaser` to the connected account; PurchaseResultSurface.tsx:112 renders it unconditionally; AcquisitionResultScreen.tsx:17-18 takes `record.listingId` straight from `usePurchaseStats` → `indexedAcquisitionTickets` (ViemProtocolClient.ts:829-860), whose `listingId` is a raw subgraph field. The `useRevealQueue` half also checks out: it consumes `positions.pendingAcquisitions`, and the allocated branch at ViemProtocolClient.ts:881-887 requires only `listing.status === 'allocated'`, unlike `positions.allocated` at line 875 which does filter on the on-chain purchaser — so the full-screen reveal can indeed fire for a stranger's listing. The contrast with PositionsScreen is stated correctly. Severity low is right: the contract is the authority and every button reverts; the residual is a convincing win-notification phishing surface plus induced reverting signatures, conditioned on the explicitly-untrusted indexer being wrong or hostile.

findings.title: Confirm-in-wallet silently does nothing when the refreshed quote breaches the signed guard
findings.preconditions: The acquisition quote has aged past `QUOTE_FRESH_MS` (20 s) and the pool fee has risen above `maxAcquisitionFeePerItem` in the interim.
findings.scenario: `onAcquire` refetches the stale quote and, if `fresh.data.totalPerItem > quote.data.maxAcquisitionFeePerItem + fresh.data.serviceFeePerItem` (which reduces correctly to `freshFee > oldMaxFee`), calls `setReviewing(false)` and returns. No `action.error` is set, no toast, no message. From the user's point of view they pressed "Confirm in wallet", the review block vanished, no wallet popup appeared, and nothing explains why. Repeated presses reproduce it.
findings.impact: The single most safety-relevant refusal in the acquisition flow is invisible. Users will assume the app is broken and either hammer the button or raise the drift tolerance blindly.
findings.minimalFix: Set an explicit error before returning, e.g. `action.setError({title: "Price moved past your guard", detail: "The pool fee rose above the maximum you approved. Review the refreshed quote and confirm again."})`, and keep the review block open showing the new numbers rather than collapsing it. `useProtocolAction` needs a small `setError` escape hatch for this.
findings.regressionTest: Component test for `<PurchaseBox>`: freeze the quote, mock `refetch` to return a quote whose `poolFeePerItem` exceeds the original `maxAcquisitionFeePerItem`, click `acquire-confirm`, and assert (a) `client.acquire` was not called and (b) a `role="alert"` node mentioning the guard is rendered.

refutationNotes.reason: SURVIVES; low is correct. PurchaseSidebar.tsx:189-195 refetches on a stale quote and, when fresh.data.totalPerItem > quote.data.maxAcquisitionFeePerItem + fresh.data.serviceFeePerItem, calls setReviewing(false) and returns with no action.error, no toast and no message -- and useProtocolAction (state/actions.ts:20-51) exposes no setError, so the component genuinely cannot report it today. The arithmetic reduction is right: quoteAcquisition (662-673) defines totalPerItem = fee + vrf, so the test collapses to freshPoolFee > oldMaxFee. One small correction to 'silently does nothing': the review block collapses back to the CTA, which re-renders with the refreshed higher total (293-299) and a reset freshness badge, so there is a visible change -- just no explanation of why the confirm was refused. That is still the defect. Low.

Confirmed at PurchaseSidebar.tsx:187-198: the stale branch calls `setReviewing(false); return;` with no error, and `action.clearError()` was called on entering review (line 289), so nothing at all is rendered. The condition does reduce to `freshPoolFee > oldMaxFee` given `totalPerItem = poolFeePerItem + serviceFeePerItem` (types.ts:283-296). The branch is reachable: `QUOTE_FRESH_MS = 20_000` vs `QUOTE_REFRESH_MS = 8_000` (params.ts:38-40) with `retry: 0` on the quote query (queries.ts:194) means a failing refetch leaves stale data with `isFetching` false. Severity low is correct. The impact statement is overstated, though: this is not 'the single most safety-relevant refusal' — `ViemProtocolClient.acquire()` re-runs the identical guard at lines 1266-1271 and throws `PRICE_DRIFTED`, which `useProtocolAction` surfaces in a `role="alert"` block (PurchaseSidebar.tsx:246-251), and the real protection is the on-chain `maxAcquisitionFee` check in FWA.sol `_validateAcquisition` (:1364). The defect is precisely that this redundant pre-check suppresses an error path that would otherwise be visible.

findings.title: Production CSP allows `script-src 'unsafe-inline'`; no HSTS header
findings.preconditions: Production build; headers are emitted by Next itself unless an upstream CDN overrides them.
findings.scenario: Line 18 sets `script-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline'` in production (only `unsafe-eval` is dev-gated). `connect-src 'self' https: wss:` and `img-src 'self' data: blob: https:` are host-wide, and there is no `Strict-Transport-Security` header at all — only the CSP's `upgrade-insecure-requests`, which does not protect the first plaintext navigation or a bookmark. I verified the app's actual XSS exposure is low today: the only `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` is the static theme literal (layout.tsx:26), all untrusted metadata flows through `sanitizeLabel` and React text nodes, image URLs are constrained by the proxy to allowlisted HTTPS / gateway / `data:image/(png|jpeg|gif|webp)` (SVG correctly excluded), and `NFTImage` uses a plain `` with `referrerPolicy="no-referrer"`.
findings.impact: No exploitable path found. But `'unsafe-inline'` removes the structural defence that would contain a future injection in a UI whose entire purpose is producing wallet signatures, and missing HSTS leaves a downgrade window. Defence in depth only.
findings.minimalFix: Adopt Next 16's nonce-based CSP via middleware and drop `'unsafe-inline'` from `script-src` in production. Add `Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=63072000; includeSubDomains; preload`. Tighten `connect-src` to the concrete RPC, indexer and manifest origins, and `img-src` to `'self' data: blob:` plus the allowlisted metadata/CDN hosts and the IPFS gateway — the same list already required in `NFT_METADATA_ALLOWED_HOSTS`.
findings.regressionTest: Playwright test asserting the response headers for `/`: `content-security-policy` contains `nonce-` and does not contain `'unsafe-inline'` inside the `script-src` directive, and `strict-transport-security` is present with `max-age >= 31536000`.

refutationNotes.reason: SURVIVES; low is correct and the finding is honest about having found no exploitable path. next.config.ts:18 does set script-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline' in production (only 'unsafe-eval' is dev-gated), connect-src and img-src are host-wide (23/25), and no Strict-Transport-Security header is emitted (35-41) -- only upgrade-insecure-requests. Two caveats worth carrying into the report rather than dropping the finding: Next's App Router requires either 'unsafe-inline' or a nonce middleware for its inline bootstrap, so this is a known trade-off with a real but non-trivial fix; and HSTS is commonly injected at the edge by the hosting platform, so the action item is 'verify the deployed response headers at the CDN', not 'assume it is absent in production'. The corroborating XSS-surface review the auditor did (single static dangerouslySetInnerHTML, sanitizeLabel on all untrusted text, SVG excluded from the data:image allowlist at route.ts:99) matches what I read. Defence in depth: low.

Confirmed verbatim at next.config.ts:17-44: production `script-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline'` (only `unsafe-eval` is dev-gated, line 18), host-wide `img-src 'self' data: blob: https:` and `connect-src 'self' https: wss:` (lines 23, 25), and no `Strict-Transport-Security` in the header list (35-41). The finding's own exposure assessment is accurate and I verified the mitigations it credits: the metadata route's `safeImageURL` (api/nft-metadata/route.ts:93-102) restricts images to IPFS / allowlisted HTTPS / `data:image/(png|jpeg|gif|webp)` with SVG excluded, and untrusted labels go through `sanitizeLabel`. It states plainly that no exploitable path was found and that this is defence in depth, which is exactly the `low` band — severity is correctly assigned, not inflated. Two caveats for the report: Next App Router hydration requires inline scripts, so the nonce-via-middleware remedy is the right (and only) fix rather than a simple directive removal; and HSTS is commonly emitted by the CDN/host rather than by `next.config.ts`, so 'no HSTS' is a property of this config that should be confirmed against the actual edge configuration before it is written up as a deployed gap.

findings.title: Indexer chooses the NFT name and artwork attached to on-chain listings and to the deposit picker
findings.lines: 204-234 (hydrateIndexedListing) and 1038-1081 (getIndexedOwnedEligibleNFTs); the unused on-chain fragment is at abi.ts:298-304
findings.preconditions: Live mode with a configured indexer that is compromised, forked or simply wrong.
findings.scenario: `hydrateIndexedListing` re-reads every economically meaningful field on-chain (`getListing`), which is correct — but then overwrites `listing.nft.name` and `listing.nft.imageUrl` from metadata resolved via `row.tokenURI`, a string supplied by the subgraph. The ERC-721 `tokenURI(uint256)` fragment exists in `abi.ts` but is never called anywhere. Same pattern in `getIndexedOwnedEligibleNFTs` (line 1062). So a hostile indexer can attach any allowlisted-host or IPFS artwork and any 120-character name to any listing id and to any token in the user's deposit picker. Ownership, approval, collection allowlisting and every amount are revalidated on-chain (verified: lines 1046-1061, 1209-1230), so no unauthorised or mis-parameterised transaction is possible — the deception is limited to *which asset the user believes they are handling*, e.g. relabelling a junk token as the valuable one in the deposit grid so the wrong NFT gets escrowed.
findings.impact: A user can be induced to deposit or settle the wrong NFT of their own. No theft, no wrong recipient, no wrong amount. Also: `metadataCache` (line 144) is an unbounded `Map` keyed by tokenURI, so a hostile indexer returning many unique URIs grows browser memory without limit.
findings.minimalFix: Read `tokenURI(tokenId)` from the collection contract for any token the user is about to act on (the deposit picker and the settlement surfaces), and treat the indexer's `tokenURI` as a pre-fetch hint only — or drop the field from the query entirely and always resolve from chain, since the contract read is already batched alongside `ownerOf`/`getApproved`. Bound `metadataCache` with an LRU (e.g. 500 entries).
findings.regressionTest: Vitest: stub the indexer to return `tokenURI` pointing at metadata named "Rare #1" for a token whose on-chain `tokenURI` resolves to "Common #7", and assert the `OwnedNFT` surfaced to the deposit picker carries the on-chain name. Add a case asserting `metadataCache.size` stays bounded after 2,000 distinct URIs.

refutationNotes.reason: SURVIVES; low is correct. hydrateIndexedListing (204-217) re-reads every economic field via getListing but then overwrites nft.name and nft.imageUrl from metadata resolved off the subgraph-supplied row.tokenURI (211-215); getIndexedOwnedEligibleNFTs does the same at 1062 after correctly revalidating ownerOf/getApproved/isApprovedForAll on-chain (1046-1061). The ERC-721 tokenURI fragment exists at abi.ts:300 and grep confirms it is never called anywhere in src. The 'wrong NFT' scenario is reachable: the deposit picker tile (DepositFlow.tsx:234-244) and the step-2 confirmation card (267-276) both render only sanitizeLabel(name) plus the collection, with the tokenId appearing only as the fallback when the indexer supplies no name -- so a relabelled grid gives the user no independent identifier. Bounded correctly by the finding: no theft, no wrong recipient, no wrong amount, and the mistake is recoverable via withdrawListing while the listing is still active. The unbounded metadataCache (line 144, a Map with no eviction) is real but is per-page-session and grows only as fast as the indexer returns distinct URIs. Low.

Confirmed. `hydrateIndexedListing` (ViemProtocolClient.ts:204-217) re-reads every economic field via `getListing` but then overwrites `listing.nft.name` and `listing.nft.imageUrl` from metadata resolved off `row.tokenURI`, a subgraph-supplied string (query at line 197); `getIndexedOwnedEligibleNFTs` does the same at line 1062. The ERC-721 `tokenURI(uint256)` fragment exists at abi.ts:298-304 and a tree-wide grep shows zero call sites — the on-chain read genuinely is never performed. The revalidation the finding credits is real: ownership/approval at lines 1046-1061 and 1217-1230, whitelist at 1209-1215, so the deception is confined to which asset the user believes they are handling. `metadataCache` at line 144 is an unbounded `Map` keyed by tokenURI, confirming the memory-growth note. Severity low is correct — no theft, no wrong recipient, no wrong amount, and rendering is bounded by `safeName`/`safeImageURL` in the metadata route plus `sanitizeLabel` in the components, so there is no injection path either.

findings.title: BindSplitterHyperEVM has no chain-id guard and its 'core not ready' gate is satisfiable at any time on a live protocol, so it can re-point PAYOUT_ADDRESS to a different snapshot after fees have accrued
findings.preconditions: Possession of the FWA owner key (the script requires `fwa.owner() == vm.addr(PRIVATE_KEY)`), plus `FWA_SPLITTER_BINDING_CONFIRMED=true` in the loaded env file.
findings.scenario: Unlike `DeploySplitterHyperEVM.s.sol:40-42`, which requires chain 998 or 999, `BindSplitterHyperEVM.run()` has no `block.chainid` restriction at all - it only special-cases 999 to additionally demand `NEST_MAINNET_DEPLOYMENT_CONFIRMED`. Its safety gate is `fwa.activeListingCount() != 0 || fwa.unsettledAcquisitionCount() != 0` (line 42), which reads like 'the core is fresh and unused' but is in fact satisfied by any live protocol at a moment when every listing happens to be settled. It also never checks `fwa.accruedOwnerFees()`, never verifies the new splitter's `NFT_ADDRESS()` or `SNAPSHOT_SUPPLY()`, and never records what the previous `payoutAddress` was. Sequence: fees accrue under splitter A (whose snapshot is collection X), the owner runs this script pointing at splitter B (snapshot collection Y) during a settled moment, then anyone calls `payoutFees()`; fees earned across collection X's tenure are split under collection Y's snapshot. Nothing in the script or its emitted event surfaces the substitution.
findings.impact: No capability the FWA owner does not already have via `setAddr(PAYOUT_ADDRESS, …)`, so this is a hardening/tooling issue rather than a privilege escalation. The concern is that the script's gate reads as a stronger safety property than it is, that it runs on any chain, and that a mis-scoped env file (998 values against a 999 RPC, or the reverse) is caught only incidentally by the `code.length` and `owner()` checks.
findings.minimalFix: Add the same `block.chainid` allowlist used by `DeploySplitterHyperEVM.s.sol:40-42`. Replace the ambiguous readiness gate with an explicit assertion of the expected current state - require `fwa.payoutAddress() == vm.envAddress("FWA_SPLITTER_PREVIOUS_PAYOUT")` and `fwa.accruedOwnerFees() == 0` - and verify the incoming splitter's `NFT_ADDRESS()` matches `FWA_SPLITTER_SNAPSHOT_NFT` and its `MAX_TOKEN_ID()` matches `FWA_SPLITTER_MAX_TOKEN_ID` before broadcasting. Include the previous payout address in `SplitterHyperEVMBound`.
findings.regressionTest: Add to `release/script-self-test/`: a case asserting `BindSplitterHyperEVM` reverts on an unexpected chain id, a case asserting it reverts when `fwa.accruedOwnerFees() != 0`, and a case asserting it reverts when the target splitter's `NFT_ADDRESS()` differs from the configured snapshot collection.

refutationNotes.reason:
The observation is accurate but the framing overstates it into a defect it is not.

(1) The missing chain-id allowlist is not a gate that can fail open. Every target is env-supplied, and BindSplitterHyperEVM.s.sol:41-43 fails closed on any chain where FWA_ADDRESS resolves to a contract whose owner() is not vm.addr(PRIVATE_KEY) or where the splitter has no code — a wrong-chain run reverts on the extcodesize check inside the `fwa.owner()` view call before any broadcast. The sibling script BindNestRewards.s.sol:34-37 uses the identical `block.chainid == 999 -> require NEST_MAINNET_DEPLOYMENT_CONFIRMED` pattern with no allowlist, so this is the codebase's binding-script convention, not an oversight unique to the splitter path.

(2) The headline scenario grants no capability. The finding itself concedes 'No capability the FWA owner does not already have via setAddr(PAYOUT_ADDRESS, ...)'. The owner can re-point PAYOUT_ADDRESS in one transaction with no script, no env file and no confirmation flag. A tool that is strictly more constrained than the raw power it wraps is not an attack surface. It also over-reaches on consequence: HYPE already received by splitter A stays in A and remains claimable under A's snapshot; only FWA-side accruedOwnerFees follows the new address.

(3) The 'core not ready' gate reading as stronger than it is (activeListingCount()==0 && unsettledAcquisitionCount()==0) is a naming/readability opinion.

What is worth keeping is the small hardening list — assert `fwa.accruedOwnerFees() == 0`, assert the expected previous payoutAddress, and re-verify the incoming splitter's NFT_ADDRESS()/MAX_TOKEN_ID() against the configured env before broadcast — which is genuinely cheap and closes the accrued-fee misdirection window. That is info-level tooling hardening, not low.

The facts hold but the severity is one notch high because the script is off the release path entirely. Verified: run() has no block.chainid allowlist (lines 31-35 only special-case 999 for an extra env gate), unlike DeploySplitterHyperEVM.s.sol:40-42; the readiness gate `activeListingCount() != 0 || unsettledAcquisitionCount() != 0` (line 42) is satisfied by any live protocol in a fully-settled moment; and it checks neither accruedOwnerFees(), NFT_ADDRESS(), MAX_TOKEN_ID(), nor the previous payoutAddress. Material correction the finding misses: `grep -rn BindSplitterHyperEVM` across every .md, .ps1 and .sol in the tree returns only its own definition at script/BindSplitterHyperEVM.s.sol:19 - the mainnet runbook never invokes it, no PowerShell release script calls it, no test covers it, and the actual mainnet path binds PAYOUT_ADDRESS at core construction (DeployHyperEVMMainnetCore.s.sol:97). It is unreachable dead tooling on the 999 sequence. Combined with the finding's own concession that it grants no capability the FWA owner lacks via setAddr, and that on a wrong chain `fwa.owner()` reverts on a codeless address (line 41), the realistic exposure is an operator running a script nothing tells them to run. Keep it as a hardening note at info, and prefer the stronger minimal fix: delete the script or chain-guard it to 998 only, rather than growing its gate surface.

findings.lens: Release sequencing, fail-closed gates and admin powers (main
findings.title: TestReleaseCandidate.ps1 reports status: passed and broadcastPerformed: false regardless of which gate steps were skipped, and never records its invocation flags
findings.preconditions: Operator runs the release gate with -SkipFork and/or -SkipE2E, or without -CleanInstall/-VerifyLiveTestnet, then hands release/release-gate-last-run.json to a reviewer.
findings.scenario: The runbook's section 3 acceptance criterion is literally "Ne poursuivre que si le rapport JSON termine avec status: passed et broadcastPerformed: false". A run invoked as `TestReleaseCandidate.ps1 -SkipFork -SkipE2E` omits the Nest mainnet fork simulation and the Playwright suite entirely, yet the finally block at lines 91-98 emits `status = "passed"` because $failed was never set. The report records only the steps that ran; it does not record $CleanInstall/$SkipFork/$SkipE2E/$VerifyLiveTestnet, nor an expected step list, nor a test count (the runbook claims 91 Solidity tests but nothing asserts that number). broadcastPerformed is a hardcoded literal, not a derived fact.
findings.impact: A reviewer applying the documented criterion cannot distinguish a full gate run from a partial one without manually diffing the steps array against an unwritten expected list. No direct fund impact; it weakens the primary pre-launch quality gate.
findings.minimalFix: Record the switch values in the report (`options = @{ cleanInstall = [bool]$CleanInstall; skipFork = [bool]$SkipFork; skipE2E = [bool]$SkipE2E; verifyLiveTestnet = [bool]$VerifyLiveTestnet }`), add a `completeRun` boolean that is true only when no skip switch was used and -VerifyLiveTestnet was supplied, and have the runbook's acceptance criterion require completeRun. Parse the `forge test` summary and record the passing test count.
findings.regressionTest: Add a self-test that invokes TestReleaseCandidate.ps1 -SkipFork -SkipE2E against a trivial fixture and asserts the emitted report has completeRun = false and options.skipFork = true.

refutationNotes.reason: SURVIVES, severity correct. Verified: switches at lines 2-7, conditional steps at 51 (fork), 70 (Playwright) and 76 (live 998), and the finally block at 90-98 emitting status = if($failed){'failed'}else{'passed'} with broadcastPerformed hardcoded to $false and no record of $CleanInstall/$SkipFork/$SkipE2E/$VerifyLiveTestnet. Runbook line 49 does state the acceptance criterion as exactly 'status: passed et broadcastPerformed: false'. Partially mitigating, and worth stating so the fix is scoped correctly: the `steps` array (line 30) records the name of every step that actually ran, so a reviewer who knows the expected list CAN detect a partial run by inspection; and the runbook's own documented invocation at line 44 is `-CleanInstall -VerifyLiveTestnet` with no skip switches. So this is a report-completeness gap, not a silently-lying report. Low is the right severity.

Verified line by line and correctly rated low. $failed is set only inside the catch (line 88); the finally block writes status='passed' (94) and a hardcoded broadcastPerformed=$false (96); the report carries only the steps array with no record of -CleanInstall/-SkipFork/-SkipE2E/-VerifyLiveTestnet, no expected-step list and no test count. -SkipFork omits lines 55-57 and -SkipE2E omits line 70 with no trace in the report. Runbook section 3's acceptance criterion is verbatim 'status: passed et broadcastPerformed: false' and the same section claims '91 tests Solidity' with nothing asserting that number. Supporting evidence for the fix: the committed release/release-gate-last-run.json records 'Solidity full tests' at 0.92 s, which is consistent with a fully cached run — precisely the case a recorded test count would expose. No severity change.
