findings.title: TestReleaseScripts.ps1 only exercises the happy path of the promotion gate, so the -Confirm* switches could silently become cosmetic
findings.preconditions: A future edit to PromoteMainnetManifest.ps1 line 12 weakens or removes the confirmation check.
findings.scenario: The self-test calls PromoteMainnetManifest.ps1 with all five switches present and asserts the manifest was promoted. It never asserts the negative: that omitting any one switch throws. I verified empirically that the current implementation does gate correctly (a [switch] evaluates to $false inside -and when absent, and Test-Gate returned BLOCKED for the absent and explicit -B:$false cases), so today the gate is real - but the invariant is untested and a regression that made the switches cosmetic would pass the release gate silently. The same gap applies to WriteMainnetManifest's zero-address/empty-collection rejections and PrepareSourceVerification's -Submit/-ConfirmPublicSubmission pairing.
findings.impact: No current defect; the release gate cannot detect a future weakening of the fail-closed promotion, source-publication or manifest-validation guards.
findings.minimalFix: Add negative cases to TestReleaseScripts.ps1: assert PromoteMainnetManifest.ps1 throws when each -Confirm* switch is individually omitted and when -PublicIndexerUrl is http://; assert WriteMainnetManifest.ps1 throws on a zero address, an empty CollectionsJson and a collection missing deploymentBlock; assert PrepareSourceVerification.ps1 throws with -Submit but without -ConfirmPublicSubmission.
findings.regressionTest: The fix is the test. Wrap each negative case in try/catch and fail the self-test if no exception was raised.

refutationNotes.reason: SURVIVES but severity overstated. Verified: TestReleaseScripts.ps1:39-46 asserts only the positive case, and PromoteMainnetManifest.ps1:12-15 does gate correctly today (an absent [switch] is $false inside the -and chain, and the HTTPS check at line 15 is real). The finding states in its own impact field 'No current defect'. A missing negative test over an implementation the author confirmed is correct is an observation about future regression risk, not a defect at any severity band — 'low' is reserved for hardening with an actual present weakness. Reclassify as info and, in practice, merge it into the report's test-coverage recommendations rather than carrying it as a numbered finding.

Verified: TestReleaseScripts.ps1:39-46 passes all five -Confirm* switches and asserts only the positive outcome, and PromoteMainnetManifest.ps1:12 does gate correctly today (single -and chain over five [switch] values, plus the HTTPS check at line 15). The proposed negative cases are reasonable. But the finding states outright 'No current defect', which by the stated rubric is info ('observation worth recording, no action strictly required'), not low. Downgrading rather than refuting because the suggestion is sound and cheap.

findings.lens: Indexer (Goldsky subgraph) correctness and its consumption b
findings.title: Activity rows for allocations and settlements carry no collection, so the collection filter silently hides them
findings.preconditions: User selects a collection in the Activity screen's "Filter by collection" select (frontend/src/components/activity/ActivityScreen.tsx:110-126), or switches scope to "Mine".
findings.scenario: Only three handlers ever set `Activity.collection`: `handleListingStaged` (mapping.ts:134), `handleNFTListed` (170) and `handleNFTDeliveryFailed` (441). `handleNFTAllocated`, `handleNFTKept`, `handleNFTRelisted`, `handleDepositorBidAccepted(AsTokens)`, `handleUnsettledFinalized`, `handleStuckNFTRecovered` and the refund handlers all leave it null, even though every one of them carries a `listingId` from which the collection is known. `getActivity` builds `where: { collection_in: [...] }` (ViemProtocolClient.ts:714-718), so selecting "Hypurr" returns only deposits/activations/delivery-failures and drops every allocation and settlement of a Hypurr NFT. Symmetrically, `Activity.address` is unset by `handleNFTRelisted` (402-408) and `handleRandomnessCached` (282-284), so the "Mine" scope (`where: { address: … }`, ViemProtocolClient.ts:712) never shows the user their own relists or their own randomness events. Separately, `handleRandomnessCached` writes `activity.listingId = event.params.requestId` (mapping.ts:283) — a request id stored in the listing-id column, which `ActivityRow` renders as a listing reference.
findings.impact: Filtered activity views are silently and materially incomplete, and one row type displays a request id as a listing id. No fund impact, but the screen is presented as "ON-CHAIN TAPE — A readable event trail" (ActivityScreen.tsx eyebrow/description), so users will reasonably read an empty filtered result as "nothing happened".
findings.minimalFix: In every listing-scoped handler, copy the collection and token id from the already-loaded `Listing` entity onto the activity (`activity.collection = listing.collection; activity.tokenId = listing.tokenId;`). Set `activity.address` on relist (use the new listing's depositor, available from the subsequent `NFTListed`, or index `NFTRelisted.newListingId` into a new schema field) and on `randomness_cached` (load `Acquisition.purchaser`). Add a `requestId: BigInt` field to `Activity` and stop overloading `listingId` at mapping.ts:283.
findings.regressionTest: Matchstick: run `handleNFTListed` then `handleNFTAllocated` for listing 1 of collection `0xAA…`, and assert the `allocation` activity has `collection == 0xAA…` and `tokenId` set. Second case: `handleRandomnessCached(requestId=99, sequence=1)` after `handleAcquisitionRequested(requestId=99, purchaser=0xBB…)` asserts `Activity.address == 0xBB…` and `Activity.listingId == null`.

refutationNotes.reason: Fully confirmed and correctly rated low. Activity.collection is set only in handleListingStaged (mapping.ts:134), handleNFTListed (171) and handleNFTDeliveryFailed (441); handleNFTAllocated, the four settlement handlers, handleStuckNFTRecovered and the refund handlers leave it null while getActivity builds `collection_in` (ViemProtocolClient.ts:714-718) and the select is reachable at ActivityScreen.tsx:110-124. Activity.address is likewise unset by handleNFTRelisted (402-408) and handleRandomnessCached (282-284) while the Mine scope filters on it (line 712). And handleRandomnessCached does write a requestId into activity.listingId (mapping.ts:283), which ActivityRow renders as a `/?listing=<id>` link (ActivityScreen.tsx:203-207) — a genuinely wrong link target. schema.graphql leaves all three fields optional, so nothing catches it. No fund impact; low is right.

Verified line by line and accurate. Activity.collection is set only at mapping.ts:134 (handleListingStaged), 171 (handleNFTListed) and 441 (handleNFTDeliveryFailed); handleNFTAllocated (375-379), handleNFTKept (395-399), handleNFTRelisted (404-407), handleDepositorBidAccepted(AsTokens) (412-426), handleUnsettledFinalized (431-434) and handleStuckNFTRecovered (447-450) all leave it null despite each carrying a listingId. getActivity builds `collection_in` (ViemProtocolClient.ts:714-718) driven by the collection <select> at ActivityScreen.tsx:110-126, so a filtered view really does drop every allocation and settlement. Activity.address is likewise unset by handleNFTRelisted and handleRandomnessCached, breaking the "Mine" scope (`address:` filter at ViemProtocolClient.ts:712). The listingId overload is confirmed and slightly worse than described: mapping.ts:283 writes the requestId into Activity.listingId, and ActivityRow renders it as a clickable deep link `/?listing=<requestId>` (ActivityScreen.tsx:203-207), which opens the detail drawer on an unrelated or nonexistent listing. Severity low is right — no fund impact, and only filtered views are affected.

findings.lens: Indexer (Goldsky subgraph) correctness and its consumption b
findings.title: Paginated indexer loops are unbounded — a hostile or misbehaving endpoint hangs the browser
findings.preconditions: The configured indexer endpoint returns a full page on every request — a compromised or substituted Goldsky endpoint, a caching proxy that replays one page, or an operator misconfiguration. indexer/README.md:42 explicitly declares the endpoint "untrusted, cacheable read infrastructure".
findings.scenario: Every paginated read is `for (let skip = 0; ; skip += N) { … if (page.length < N) break; }` with no iteration cap and no total-rows cap. `indexedAcquisitionRows` and `getIndexedOwnedEligibleNFTs` request `first: 1000` and break only on `length < 1000`; `getIndexedListingsForAccount` uses `INDEXER_PAGE_SIZE = 200`. An endpoint that always answers with exactly `first` rows drives an infinite request loop. In `getIndexedOwnedEligibleNFTs` each row additionally fans out three `readContract` calls (lines 1046-1060) inside `Promise.all` over the accumulated array, so memory and RPC load grow without bound. Concrete: connect a wallet, the deposit flow calls `useOwnedNfts()`, the endpoint replays 1000 rows → the tab allocates until it is killed and the user's RPC quota is exhausted.
findings.impact: Denial of service against every user of the app from a single compromised read endpoint, plus RPC-quota exhaustion. No funds at risk directly, but it is the cheapest way to take the front end down and it contradicts the stated "untrusted infrastructure" posture.
findings.minimalFix: Bound each loop by both iteration count and accumulated rows, and require strict progress: e.g. `const MAX_PAGES = 25; const MAX_ROWS = 5_000;` break when `rows.length >= MAX_ROWS || pages >= MAX_PAGES`, and additionally break if a page returns an id already seen (proving the endpoint is not advancing). Also delete the unused `getAllListings()` (line 539) — it is dead code and its `skip` growth would hit the Graph's `skip` ceiling anyway.
findings.regressionTest: Vitest: stub `fetch` to always return 1000 `ownedTokens` rows and assert `getIndexedOwnedEligibleNFTs` resolves (does not hang) with at most `MAX_ROWS` rows and that `fetch` was called at most `MAX_PAGES` times.

refutationNotes.reason: The four loops are as cited and the dead-code note is right (grep finds no caller of getAllListings other than its own definition at line 539). But 'infinite' only holds against a substituted or hostile endpoint: a real graph-node/Goldsky enforces the Graph query API's skip ceiling, so the loop terminates with a query error that indexerQuery converts to a thrown INDEXER_DOWN (lines 168-180) and the loop exits by exception — at most ~6 pages at first:1000 and ~26 at 200. Under the stated precondition (endpoint compromised or replaced), that same endpoint has strictly simpler ways to hang the tab — an unbounded response body, a never-resolving fetch (there is no timeout on the fetch either) — so the loop bound is not the interesting control. No privilege, no funds, no data corruption. Keep as an info-level hardening item (bound pages/rows and add a fetch timeout), not a finding.

Confirmed as written. All four loops are `for (let skip = 0; ; skip += N)` breaking only on a short page: getAllListings (ViemProtocolClient.ts:541-546, INDEXER_PAGE_SIZE = 200 at line 51), getIndexedListingsForAccount (556-566), indexedAcquisitionRows (810-825, first: 1000) and getIndexedOwnedEligibleNFTs (1025-1037, first: 1000). The last one does fan out three readContract calls per accumulated row inside Promise.all (1044-1060), so an endpoint that always replays a full page grows memory and RPC load without bound. getAllListings is indeed dead code — the only reference in the file is its own definition at line 539. Low is the right severity: a real graph-node rejects skip beyond its 5000 ceiling, which surfaces as a thrown INDEXER_DOWN and terminates the loop, so this needs a substituted or compromised endpoint — and an attacker holding NEXT_PUBLIC_INDEXER_URL already controls the whole discovery surface, while every row remains revalidated on-chain before any signature. Bounding the loops is cheap hardening consistent with the README's stated untrusted-endpoint posture.

findings.lens: Indexer (Goldsky subgraph) correctness and its consumption b
findings.title: Activity feed is silently capped at 200 rows and the "Show more" counter always reads "1 left"
findings.preconditions: More than ~200 indexed activity events, and the user clicks "Show more" repeatedly.
findings.scenario: ActivityScreen never passes a cursor; it grows `limit` by 30 (`setLimit((n) => n + PAGE)`, line 178). `getActivity` computes `first = Math.min(200, query.limit + 1)` (line 720) and `hasNext = data.activities.length > query.limit` (line 730). At `limit = 200`, `first` clamps to 200, so `200 > 200` is false: `nextCursor` becomes undefined and the button disappears at 200 rows regardless of how much history exists. Separately `total = offset + items.length + (hasNext ? 1 : 0)` (line 748) with `offset = 0`, so `page.total - page.items.length` is always exactly `1` — the button literally renders "Show more (1 left)" at every step, from 30 events to 199.
findings.impact: The event tape is capped at 200 rows with no indication, and the pagination affordance displays a fixed, meaningless count. The known-limits disclosure covers approximate *listing* totals; this is the activity feed rendering that approximation as a concrete, always-wrong number.
findings.minimalFix: Switch ActivityScreen to cursor-based pagination (append pages using `page.nextCursor` rather than growing `limit`), and drop the numeric count from the button — render "Show more" alone, or expose a real `totalCount` from an aggregate entity in the schema.
findings.regressionTest: Vitest on `getActivity`: with a stub returning 31 rows for `limit: 30`, assert `nextCursor === "30"` and that `total` is not used as a remaining-count. Component test: render ActivityScreen with a 30-item page carrying `nextCursor` and assert the button text does not contain "1 left".

refutationNotes.reason: Both halves verified. getActivity sets first = Math.min(200, limit+1) (line 720) and hasNext = activities.length > limit (730), so once ActivityScreen's growing limit reaches 200 the comparison is 200 > 200 = false and the button disappears with no indication. total = offset + items.length + (hasNext?1:0) (line 748) with offset always 0 because ActivityScreen never passes a cursor, so `page.total - page.items.length` at ActivityScreen.tsx:177 is exactly 1 every time the button renders. One thing the finding missed and should be folded in: PoolScreen.tsx:295 renders the identical expression, so the pool grid shows the same fixed '(1 left)'. Low is correct.

Both mechanics reproduce exactly. ActivityScreen holds `const [limit, setLimit] = useState(PAGE)` with PAGE = 30 (line 18, 61), passes limit but never a cursor into useActivity (70-76), and grows it via `setLimit((n) => n + PAGE)` (178). getActivity computes `first = Math.min(200, query.limit + 1)` (ViemProtocolClient.ts:720) and `hasNext = data.activities.length > query.limit` (730), so at limit = 200 the clamp makes `200 > 200` false, nextCursor goes undefined and the button vanishes at exactly 200 rows regardless of history depth. With offset pinned at 0, `total = offset + items.length + (hasNext ? 1 : 0)` (748) makes `page.total - page.items.length` exactly 1 whenever the button renders at all — the label is literally always "Show more (1 left)". Low is correct: cosmetic pagination defect, no fund or accounting impact, and it is not covered by the disclosed "bounded listing-search window" limit, which concerns listing totals rather than the activity feed.

findings.lens: Indexer (Goldsky subgraph) correctness and its consumption b
findings.title: GraphQL queries are assembled by string concatenation; orderBy/orderDirection/first/skip are interpolated unquoted
findings.preconditions: None reachable today — see impact. Becomes reachable the moment a sort, direction, status, cursor or limit is sourced from a URL parameter, a saved view, or any other runtime-typed input.
findings.scenario: Every query is a template literal. Filter *values* are escaped with `JSON.stringify` (lines 605, 609, 558, 712-717, 817, 1032), which does produce a valid GraphQL string literal, so those are currently safe. But four positions are interpolated with no quoting and no runtime validation: `orderBy: ${orderBy}`, `orderDirection: ${direction}`, `first: ${first}`, `skip: ${skip}` (lines 196, 724, 814, 1029). `direction` originates from `e.target.value.split(":") as [ListingsQuery["sort"], ListingsQuery["direction"]]` in `frontend/src/components/pool/FiltersBar.tsx:150-151` — a TypeScript *cast*, not a runtime check. I traced every producer and found no path from a URL parameter or free-text input into these positions today (`PoolScreen.tsx:67` reads only `?listing=` and validates it with `/^\d+$/`; `search` is applied client-side at lines 625-637 and never sent; statuses and activity types come from module-level constants; cursors are only ever produced internally by `String(offset + n)`), so this is a latent primitive rather than a live bug. The blast radius if it did become reachable is also bounded: a subgraph exposes no mutation root and holds no privilege, so the worst case is reading other entities and forcing an expensive query.
findings.impact: No exploitable path today. Recorded because the query builder gives the compiler, not the runtime, responsibility for a trust boundary the README declares untrusted, and because a single future feature (shareable filtered URLs, persisted views) turns it into a live injection point.
findings.minimalFix: Move to typed GraphQL variables: send `{ query, variables }` with `query($first: Int!, $skip: Int!, $orderBy: Listing_orderBy!, $orderDirection: OrderDirection!, $where: Listing_filter)` and build `where` as a JS object serialised by `JSON.stringify`. That eliminates all interpolation and lets the subgraph's own schema reject bad enum values. As an interim measure, validate at runtime: `const dir = input.direction === "asc" ? "asc" : "desc"` and an allowlist check on `orderBy`.
findings.regressionTest: Vitest: call `getListings({ view: "pool", sort: "value", direction: "desc) { id } } query evil { _meta { block { number } } " as any, limit: 24 })`, capture the stubbed `fetch` body, and assert the request uses a `variables` object and that the query string contains no attacker-supplied substring.

refutationNotes.reason: The finding states its own defeater — 'No exploitable path today' — and my trace confirms it is stronger than that. Three of the four cited positions are provably constrained, not merely unreached: orderBy is produced by a 4-way ternary over string constants (ViemProtocolClient.ts:612-613) and typed as a union at 187; first is Math.max(1, Math.min(..., 1000)) (line 190) and Math.min(200, limit+1) (720); skip is `Number.parseInt(cursor) || 0` (614, 719) — all numbers by construction. Only `direction` is a raw string passthrough, and its sole producer is a 7-option `<select>` (FiltersBar.tsx:146-161); every other call site hardcodes `desc`. Reaching it requires a user to tamper with their own DOM, aimed at a read-only subgraph with no mutation root and no privilege — self-inflicted, zero gain. Migrating to typed variables is reasonable hygiene, but as written this is a hardening preference, not a defect, and shipping it as a `low` in a production audit costs credibility.

Accurate and honestly scoped — the finding states outright that there is no reachable path today, and I confirmed that. The four unquoted positions exist (ViemProtocolClient.ts:196, 724, 814, 1029) but every producer is closed: `direction` and `sort` come from a fixed <select> whose option values are literals (FiltersBar.tsx:150-160), so the `as [ListingsQuery["sort"], ListingsQuery["direction"]]` cast can only ever see one of six hardcoded strings; `orderBy` is chosen from a ternary over a closed union (601-602); `first` is numerically clamped (183-184, 720); `skip` is `Number.parseInt(cursor ?? "0", 10) || 0` (614, 719), which cannot emit a non-number; the only URL parameter read on the pool page is `?listing=` and it is validated with /^\d+$/ (PoolScreen.tsx:67); filter values are JSON.stringify'd. So this is not a live injection point. It sits squarely in this rubric's `low` band — "hardening, defence in depth" — and the recommended move to typed GraphQL variables is the right fix, but the team should read it as latent-risk hygiene, not a bug to hotfix before launch.

findings.lens: Indexer (Goldsky subgraph) correctness and its consumption b
findings.title: VrfServiceFeePaid overwrites rather than accumulates, understating the per-ticket service fee when one transaction calls acquire twice
findings.preconditions: A single transaction produces more than one `VrfServiceFeePaid` event — i.e. a router/aggregator/multicall contract that calls `acquire()` or `acquireBatch()` more than once in one transaction.
findings.scenario: `AcquisitionTransaction` is keyed on the transaction hash (mapping.ts:42-44) and `handleVrfServiceFeePaid` performs `context.serviceFeeTotal = event.params.amount` — an assignment, not `+=` (line 230). FWA emits the event once per `_acquire` with `vrf` and once per `_acquireBatch` with `vrfTotal` (FWA.sol:1285 and 1338), so the assignment is correct for a direct user call. For a contract that calls `acquire()` twice in one transaction the mapping sees `VrfServiceFeePaid(vrf)`, `AcquisitionRequested`, `VrfServiceFeePaid(vrf)`, `AcquisitionRequested`: `serviceFeeTotal` ends at `vrf` while `requestCount` reaches 2. `handleNFTAllocated` then computes `serviceFee = serviceFeeTotal / requestCount = vrf / 2` (line 369) and writes `listing.acquiredFor = acquisitionFee + vrf/2` (line 371). The frontend divides identically at ViemProtocolClient.ts:850.
findings.impact: Indexed cost basis is understated by up to 50% of the VRF service fee for those tickets, which inflates the displayed profit in `PurchaseStats.netListingPL` (ViemProtocolClient.ts:1159, 1171-1177) and in the purchase-history table. Accounting only — no contract or solvency impact — and only for users transacting through a batching contract.
findings.minimalFix: Accumulate instead of assigning: `context.serviceFeeTotal = context.serviceFeeTotal.plus(event.params.amount);` at mapping.ts:230. Since the entity is created fresh per transaction hash this is correct for both the single and the batch case.
findings.regressionTest: Matchstick: emit `VrfServiceFeePaid(purchaser, 100)`, `AcquisitionRequested(1, …)`, `VrfServiceFeePaid(purchaser, 100)`, `AcquisitionRequested(2, …)` all under one transaction hash, then `NFTAllocated(1, listing 1, …)`, and assert `Listing["1"].acquiredFor == acquisitionFee + 100` (not `+ 50`).

refutationNotes.reason: Confirmed, and correctly rated low. mapping.ts:230 is an assignment, not an accumulation; FWA emits VrfServiceFeePaid once per _acquire with `vrf` (FWA.sol:1285) and once per _acquireBatch with `vrfTotal` (1338); the precondition is reachable because FWA imposes no EOA restriction on acquisition (no tx.origin comparison anywhere in FWA.sol, and nonReentrant does not prevent sequential calls in one transaction), so a router calling acquire() twice — or acquireBatch(n) then acquire() — leaves serviceFeeTotal at the last value while requestCount keeps climbing, and handleNFTAllocated divides at mapping.ts:369 (mirrored in the frontend at line 850). Display-only cost-basis understatement, narrow population, one-word fix that is correct as proposed.

Confirmed on both sides. mapping.ts:230 is `context.serviceFeeTotal = event.params.amount` — a plain assignment into a per-transaction-hash entity (transactionKey at 42-44) — while requestCount increments per AcquisitionRequested (245). The contract emits one VrfServiceFeePaid(msg.sender, vrf) per _acquire (FWA.sol:1285) and one VrfServiceFeePaid(msg.sender, vrfTotal) per _acquireBatch (FWA.sol:1338), so the assignment is correct for a direct call and for a batch, and wrong only when one transaction makes two or more separate acquire calls — reachable because nonReentrant blocks nesting, not sequential calls, and nothing restricts msg.sender to an EOA (NFTDeliveryFailed exists precisely because contracts can be purchasers). The consequence propagates as described: handleNFTAllocated divides at mapping.ts:369 and writes acquiredFor at 371, and the frontend repeats the division at ViemProtocolClient.ts:850, feeding allInPaid and netListingPL in getPurchaseStats (1158, 1173). Display-only accounting for users routing through a batching contract — low is right, and the one-character `.plus()` fix is correct.

findings.lens: Indexer (Goldsky subgraph) correctness and its consumption b
findings.title: Governance, earnings-accrual and crown-funding events are not indexed at all
findings.preconditions: None — this is the shipped handler set.
findings.scenario: I enumerated the FWA ABI against the manifest. All 25 declared handlers match their ABI signatures exactly, but 13 emitted events have no handler, and several are material to the trust story: `ConfigSet(indexed uint256,uint256)` (every owner `setUint`/`setBool`/`setAddr`, including `settlementWindow`, `selectionSlippageBps`, `callbackGasLimit`), `CollectionWhitelistSet(indexed address,bool)`, `OwnershipTransferred`/`OwnershipHandoverRequested`/`OwnershipHandoverCanceled`, `EarningsAccrued(indexed address,indexed uint256,uint256)`, `TopListingFunded`, `OwnerFeesAccrued`, `FeesPaidOut`, `ProtocolFeesToToken`, `FulfillmentIgnored`, `UnfulfilledVrfReconciled`. `EarningsAccrued` is the one FWA's own NatSpec calls out as indexer-facing ("An indexer can track each address's claimable balance as Σ EarningsAccrued − Σ EarningsWithdrawn", FWA.sol:659-660); the subgraph indexes only the `EarningsWithdrawn` half, so the tape shows withdrawals with no matching accruals. Independently, `frontend/src/protocol/types.ts:236-256` declares two `ActivityType` values the mapping can never emit — `reward_claim` (the FWARewardsHyperEVM contract has no data source at all) and `depositor_resolved` — and both are wired into the "Claims & refunds" and "Settlements" filter chips (ActivityScreen.tsx:26-29).
findings.impact: The screen presented as the product's "ON-CHAIN TAPE" contains no governance record: an owner changing an economic parameter, de-allowlisting a collection or initiating an ownership handover leaves no trace in the app. Two filter chips promise event classes that cannot appear. No fund impact, but for a product whose pitch is verifiable on-chain mechanics, the admin surface is the one thing the tape omits.
findings.minimalFix: Add handlers for `ConfigSet`, `CollectionWhitelistSet`, `OwnershipTransferred`, `OwnershipHandoverRequested`/`Canceled` and `EarningsAccrued`, writing them as `Activity` rows with a `governance`/`earnings_accrued` type, and surface a "Protocol changes" filter group. Add an FWARewards data source for reward claims, or remove `reward_claim` and `depositor_resolved` from `ActivityType` and from the filter groups so the UI does not offer unreachable filters.
findings.regressionTest: Matchstick: emit `ConfigSet(key, value)` and assert an `Activity` row of the new governance type exists with the key and value. Add a build-time assertion that every member of the frontend `ActivityType` union is produced by at least one mapping handler (a small script over `mapping.ts` string literals versus `types.ts`).

refutationNotes.reason: The enumeration is accurate — I diffed abis/FWA.json against the manifest: 38 events, 25 handled, and the 13 unhandled ones are the ones listed (plus RewardsConfigured). But not indexing an event is a product-scope decision, not a defect: nothing displayed becomes wrong, the subgraph is declared discovery/history-only (indexer/README.md:40-46), and 'add handlers for governance' is a feature request. The one concrete sub-claim is inert on inspection: reward_claim and depositor_resolved appear only as extra members of multi-type filter GROUPS (ActivityScreen.tsx:27 and :29), so 'Settlements' and 'Claims & refunds' still return their other five and two types respectively — the unreachable members silently match nothing and produce no user-visible breakage. Worth recording as an info observation (and removing the two dead union members), not a finding.

Half defect, half scope opinion; low is the right severity for the half that is a defect. Verified: none of ConfigSet (FWA.sol:668), CollectionWhitelistSet (671), EarningsAccrued (661, whose own NatSpec at 659-660 explicitly names indexers as the consumer), OwnerFeesAccrued (674), FeesPaidOut (676), TopListingFunded (681), ProtocolFeesToToken (687), FulfillmentIgnored (587) or UnfulfilledVrfReconciled (588) appears in the 25 eventHandlers of subgraph.template.yaml:26-76. The concrete defect is the unreachable filter chips: TYPE_GROUPS at ActivityScreen.tsx:24-29 wires `depositor_resolved` into "Settlements" and `reward_claim` into "Claims & refunds", both declared in types.ts:247, 245, and no mapping handler can ever emit either (there is no FWARewards data source at all) — so two chips are guaranteed to return empty. The rest is a product-scope argument rather than a defect: nothing in the README or INTEGRATION_NEEDS claims governance is indexed, and the EarningsAccrued omission costs nothing because the frontend reads feeCredit on-chain (ViemProtocolClient.ts:866). Fix the two dead chips; treat the governance tape as a feature request.

findings.lens: FWA core, parity and liability conservation (HyperEVM mainne
findings.title: Gelato coordinator targets a drand round only 1-3 seconds ahead on chain 999 and does not enforce FWA's requestConfirmations axiom
findings.preconditions: Chain 999 (`block.chainid != 1`), ~1 second block times, and a block whose `timestamp` is not ahead of wall clock.
findings.scenario: `_nextRound()` computes `currentRound = ((block.timestamp - 1692803367) / 3) + 1` and then `requestedRound = currentRound + (block.chainid == 1 ? 4 : 1)`. On Ethereum that is a 12-second (4 round) lead; on 999 it is a single round, i.e. `3 - ((t - genesis) mod 3)` seconds — between 1 and 3 seconds ahead of the request block's timestamp. The derived word is `keccak256(randomness, address(this), block.chainid, requestId)` with `requestId = nextRequestId++`, so both the round and the ID are fully predictable; only the drand beacon is not. Separately, `request.requestConfirmations` and `request.requestedAtBlock` are stored (lines 123-125) but never read: nothing prevents `fulfillRandomness` landing in the very next block, so FWA's stated security axiom ('no VRF word can exist before this many blocks', FWA.sol:230-232) is substituted by the drand round's futurity rather than preserved. I could not construct an exploit under normal operation — the target round is strictly in the future of the request block's timestamp, and the pool is frozen between request and settlement by `_requireExitUnlocked` and the request-time reserved batch — so this is a margin/hardening finding, not a live break.
findings.impact: The safety margin against block-timestamp skew is 1-3 seconds instead of Ethereum's 12. If HyperEVM block timestamps ever run behind wall clock (catch-up after an outage, or proposer latitude), `currentRound + 1` can be a round whose beacon is already public, at which point a purchaser wrapping `acquire()` in a contract can compute the exact derived word and the resulting `_selectSlot` outcome and abort the transaction on an unfavourable draw — selecting outcomes by refusal.
findings.minimalFix: Scale the round lead to the target chain rather than special-casing chain 1: use a constructor-set `ROUND_LEAD` (e.g. 4-8 rounds on 999, so the beacon is unpublished for 12-24 seconds) and enforce `block.number >= request.requestedAtBlock + request.requestConfirmations` inside `fulfillRandomness` so the stored confirmation count is load-bearing.
findings.regressionTest: `testTargetRoundIsUnpublishedByAtLeastNSeconds`: fuzz `block.timestamp` and assert `roundTimestamp(_nextRound()) - block.timestamp >= MIN_LEAD_SECONDS` for a configured floor; and `testFulfillmentBeforeRequestConfirmationsIsRejected`.

refutationNotes.reason: SURVIVES, CORRECTLY RATED LOW. _nextRound (GelatoVRFCoordinator.sol:215-221) verified: currentRound = ((t - 1692803367)/3)+1 has a timestamp <= t, so requestedRound = currentRound + 1 on chain 999 leads wall clock by exactly 3 - ((t-genesis) mod 3) seconds, i.e. strictly in (0,3], versus 4 rounds / 12 s on chain 1. Confirmed that request.requestConfirmations and request.requestedAtBlock are written at lines 123-125 and never read again - fulfillRandomness (140-168) checks only round, consumer, callbackGasLimit and the payload hash, so FWA's stated axiom at FWA.sol:230-232 ('no VRF word can exist before this many blocks') is substituted by drand futurity, not preserved. Corroborating evidence the finding did not cite, which strengthens it: the sibling DrandRelayCoordinator takes an explicit immutable MIN_ROUND_DELAY_SECONDS constructor parameter (line 47, set to 6 s live on 998) and computes roundAtOrAfter(block.timestamp + delay), proving the team already knows how to parameterise the lead and simply did not do so for the 999 coordinator. The finding is honest that no exploit is constructible under normal operation (the target beacon is unpublished at request time), and the timestamp-lag precondition is speculative. Hardening / margin issue with no demonstrated break: low is right. The 'exploitation-risk' category label is slightly generous but the body is appropriately hedged.

Both factual halves verified. GelatoVRFCoordinator.sol:218 is `currentRound + (block.chainid == 1 ? 4 : 1)`, so chain 999 gets a one-round lead. Given round r's timestamp is DRAND_GENESIS_TIME + (r-1)*3 and currentRound = floor((t - genesis)/3) + 1, the requested round's timestamp lands in (t, t+3] - strictly future under honest timestamps, which is exactly why the finding correctly concedes it could not build an exploit. Separately, Request.requestConfirmations and Request.requestedAtBlock are written at lines 123-125 and echoed in the event at 134, but grep shows they are never read anywhere in fulfillRandomness or requestPayload, so FWA's stated security axiom at FWA.sol:230-232 ('no VRF word can exist before this many blocks') is genuinely not preserved by this coordinator - on Ethereum the Chainlink coordinator enforced it. That is a real, verifiable port divergence.

The finding is honestly scoped: it is filed as low/hardening, it states no live break, and both proposed fixes (a constructor-set round lead and a block.number >= requestedAtBlock + requestConfirmations check) are cheap and correct. Severity low is right; I would not raise it, because the residual risk requires HyperEVM block timestamps to run behind wall clock, and even then the purchaser cannot determine the selected slot at acquire time - selection runs against the pool state at ordered processing (_settleReadyAcquisition / _selectSlot), not at request time. Keep as filed.

findings.title: DrandRelayCoordinator has no on-chain chain-id guard; 'no drand on mainnet' is enforced only by three deployment scripts
findings.preconditions: Someone deploys DrandRelayCoordinator on 999 by any route other than the provided scripts (bespoke script, cast send, a copied deploy pipeline) and the FWA owner points `VRF_COORDINATOR` at it.
findings.scenario: The three drand scripts do gate `block.chainid != 998` in code, which I verified — the runbook's claim 'Il n'existe aucun fallback silencieux vers drand sur mainnet' (DRAND_GELATO_RANDOMNESS_RUNBOOK.md:58) holds for the scripted paths. But the contract itself contains no chain-id restriction: `block.chainid` appears only inside the word derivation (line 171). Deployed on 999 it would function identically, reducing mainnet randomness to a single unverified relayer key with no BLS check at all — strictly weaker than the Gelato path. Symmetrically, GelatoVRFCoordinator has no guard preventing deployment on 998, where Gelato VRF does not exist and every request would hang forever.
findings.impact: No exploit path without owner action, but the stated 'testnet exclusively' property (line 16 of the runbook, line 14-18 of the contract header) is a documentation and tooling property rather than a contract invariant. Given the no-expiry finding, an accidental mainnet drand deployment would also be unrecoverable.
findings.minimalFix: Constructor guards: in DrandRelayCoordinator, `if (block.chainid == 999) revert MainnetForbidden();` (or an allowlist of {998, 31337}); in GelatoVRFCoordinator, `if (block.chainid == 998) revert TestnetForbidden();`. One line each, no runtime cost.
findings.regressionTest: `testDrandRelayCannotBeDeployedOnMainnet`: `vm.chainId(999); vm.expectRevert(DrandRelayCoordinator.MainnetForbidden.selector); new DrandRelayCoordinator(relayer, owner, 6);` and the mirror for GelatoVRFCoordinator on 998.

refutationNotes.reason: SURVIVES at low as stated. Verified both halves: DrandRelayCoordinator's constructor (95-106) contains no chain-id restriction and block.chainid appears only in the word derivation at line 170; GelatoVRFCoordinator likewise has no 998 guard, using block.chainid only for the round offset at 218. The script-side gates the finding credits are real — DeployDrandRelayCoordinator.s.sol:43, ActivateDrandRelayCoordinator.s.sol:48 and FulfillDrandRelay.s.sol:28 all revert WrongChain when block.chainid != 998 (DeployHyperEVMCore.s.sol:48 too) — so the runbook's 'aucun fallback silencieux vers drand sur mainnet' does hold for every scripted path. This is therefore pure defence in depth requiring a deliberate off-script deployment plus a deliberate owner setAddr, and the finding says so honestly rather than inflating it. One-line constructor guards are cheap and correct; low is the right rating.

REFUTED as a defect — at most an info-level style preference. The factual observation is accurate (constructor 95-106 has no chain-id check; I verified the gates exist at DeployDrandRelayCoordinator.s.sol:43, ActivateDrandRelayCoordinator.s.sol:48 and FulfillDrandRelay.s.sol:28). But the proposed guard would create no invariant. `FWA.setAddr(FWAConfigKeys.VRF_COORDINATOR, value)` (FWA.sol:2318-2325) accepts ANY non-zero address with no interface, chain, or behavioural validation whatsoever. An owner capable of deploying DrandRelayCoordinator on 999 by a bespoke route and wiring it in can equally wire in any other weak or malicious coordinator, of which there is an unbounded supply; blocking one named implementation in its constructor removes one member of that set and changes nothing about the trust model. The precondition is therefore an owner error with no attacker-reachable path, and the mitigation is cosmetic rather than an invariant. This is defence-in-depth commentary on a hypothetical operator mistake, not a verified defect in the shipped system.

findings.title: Frontend calls the draw 'verifiable randomness' and asserts the word 'is requested before it exists', with no disclosure of the single-operator trust boundary
findings.preconditions: Mainnet 999 with `randomnessMode: "gelato-vrf"`.
findings.scenario: RandomnessFlightDeck.tsx:64 labels the wait state 'awaiting verifiable randomness' and line 114 states 'The NFT remains unknown until the authenticated drand word is received'. The docs Callout (docsContent.tsx:278-283, 'No outcome is known in advance') asserts 'The random word is requested before it exists and decides the outcome afterwards.' On 999 the word is authenticated (operator identity is checked) but not verified (no signature or beacon check), and the 'before it exists' margin is one drand period of wall-clock with no on-chain enforcement. Nothing in the UI or the docs discloses that one Gelato key can choose the outcome or force a timeout. Separately, `manifest.ts:38,44` gives `randomnessMode` a default of `"drand-relay-testnet"`, so a mainnet manifest that omits the field silently mislabels the source rather than failing validation.
findings.impact: Users are told the draw carries a cryptographic guarantee it does not have on 999. No direct fund impact from the copy alone, but it materially misstates the trust boundary in the one place users actually read before signing.
findings.minimalFix: Replace 'verifiable randomness' with 'authenticated randomness' in the aria-label; add one sentence to the docs randomness section naming the operator dependency ('the beacon is delivered by a dedicated Gelato operator and is not verified on-chain; every delivery is publicly auditable against drand after the fact'); and make `randomnessMode` a required field in the manifest schema (drop `.default(...)`) so an ambiguous mainnet manifest fails closed.
findings.regressionTest: Extend the manifest schema test to assert a mainnet manifest missing `randomnessMode` fails validation, and add a component assertion that the flight-deck copy for `randomnessMode === "gelato-vrf"` contains the operator disclosure string.

refutationNotes.reason: Half SURVIVES at info; the manifest half is REFUTED. Strings verified: RandomnessFlightDeck.tsx:64 aria-label '…awaiting verifiable randomness', :114 'until the authenticated drand word is received', docsContent.tsx:280 'The random word is requested before it exists and decides the outcome afterwards'. The manifest sub-claim is factually defeated by the release pipeline: scripts/WriteMainnetManifest.ps1:70 always emits randomnessMode = 'gelato-vrf', and scripts/PromoteMainnetManifest.ps1:21 refuses promotion unless chainId is 999 AND randomnessMode is 'gelato-vrf' AND dexMode is 'nest' — the z.default at manifest.ts:38 is unreachable through any sanctioned mainnet path, so no mainnet manifest can 'silently mislabel the source'. 'Verifiable' is also more defensible than stated: RandomnessFulfilled (GelatoVRFCoordinator.sol:63-69) emits both gelatoRandomness and round, so every delivery genuinely is verifiable against drand — just off-chain and after the fact, which is what the word means in ordinary use. Note too that these strings are inherited product copy from the Ethereum reference where the proof IS checked on-chain, which is the actual parity point. Residual: a one-line operator-dependency disclosure in the docs randomness section is worth adding. Info, not low, and the aria-label rewrite is optional.

findings.title: FWAVRFService is never funded by any deploy or activation script, so the first acquisition after activation reverts InsufficientVrfCoverage
findings.preconditions: Mainnet activation with the example coverage parameters and no manual pre-funding of the FWAVRFService address.
findings.scenario: With `FWA_MIN_RANDOMNESS_BUFFER_WEI = FWA_MAX_RANDOMNESS_COST_WEI = 1e16` (0.01 HYPE), the first `acquire()` drives `FWAVRFService.prepareRequests -> _ensureSubscriptionCoverage(1)`, which computes `required = 0.01 + (0 + 1) * 0.01 = 0.02 HYPE`, reads `current = coordinator.nativeSubscriptionBalance = 0`, and needs to move 0.02 HYPE. The service's balance at that instant is only the just-received `requestFee() = 800_000 * tx.gasprice * 1.3` — about 1.04e14 wei (0.0001 HYPE) at 0.1 gwei. `if (amount > address(this).balance) revert InsufficientVrfCoverage();` (FWAVRFService.sol:250) therefore reverts. Neither DeployHyperEVMMainnetCore nor ActivateHyperEVMMainnet transfers value to the service or asserts its balance, and ActivateHyperEVMMainnet checks fifteen other wiring invariants (lines 65-76) but not this one.
findings.impact: Fail-closed, no loss — but the runbook's post-activation canary ('Exécuter une acquisition réelle de faible montant', DRAND_GELATO_RANDOMNESS_RUNBOOK.md:56) will revert with a message that points at randomness coverage rather than at an unfunded treasury, inviting an ad-hoc change to the coverage parameters under launch pressure — exactly the parameters that underwrite callback safety.
findings.minimalFix: Add to ActivateHyperEVMMainnet before the broadcast: `if (address(service).balance < service.requiredSubscriptionBalance(1)) revert VrfServiceUnderfunded();` and add an explicit pre-activation funding step to the runbook and to .env.mainnet.example.
findings.regressionTest: `testFirstAcquisitionRequiresPreFundedService`: deploy the mainnet wiring with a zero-balance FWAVRFService, enable acquisitions, expect `acquire` to revert `InsufficientVrfCoverage`; then `vm.deal` the service to `requiredSubscriptionBalance(1)` and assert `acquire` succeeds and `coordinator.nativeSubscriptionBalance() == 0.02 ether`.

refutationNotes.reason: SURVIVES at low exactly as rated, and the corroboration is stronger than the finding claims. Arithmetic verified end to end: DeployHyperEVMMainnetCore.s.sol:84 constructs FWAVRFService(1e16, 1e16) from .env.mainnet.example:28-29, so requiredSubscriptionBalance(1) = 1e16 + (0+1)*1e16 = 2e16 (FWAVRFService.sol:210-214); the coordinator starts at nativeSubscriptionBalance == 0; the service's only balance at that instant is requestFee() = 800_000 * tx.gasprice * 13000/10000 (line 191-193 with .env values 800000 / 3000 bps / 0 flat), i.e. 1.04e6 * gasprice, which needs ~19.2 gwei to self-cover — far above HyperEVM's normal gas price — so `if (amount > address(this).balance) revert InsufficientVrfCoverage()` at line 250 fires. Neither DeployHyperEVMMainnetCore (81-108) nor ActivateHyperEVMMainnet (63-81) transfers value to the service or asserts its balance, and grepping MAINNET_RELEASE_RUNBOOK_2026-07-26.md for any service-funding step returns nothing. Decisive corroboration the finding missed: the TESTNET path already solves this — script/PrepareDrandGameplayE2E.s.sol:134-142 `_prefundCoverage` computes requiredSubscriptionBalance(1), tops the service up and calls topUpSubscription. The step is known to the team and simply absent from the mainnet scripts and runbook. Fail-closed, no loss, real launch-sequencing gap: low.

SURVIVES, and I corroborated it by execution. The arithmetic is right: with .env.mainnet.example:28-29 both at 1e16, `requiredSubscriptionBalance(1) = 0.01 + (0+1)*0.01 = 0.02 HYPE` (FWAVRFService.sol:210-213), `subscriptionNativeBalance()` is 0 on a fresh coordinator, and `_ensureSubscriptionCoverage` reverts `InsufficientVrfCoverage` at line 250 because the only inflow at that instant is `requestFee() = 800_000 * tx.gasprice * 1.3` (191-193), which reaches 0.02 HYPE only around 19 gwei. Executable corroboration: the in-repo Gelato integration test passes ONLY because setUp deliberately tunes the fee to the requirement — `new FWAVRFService(1,1)` plus `setFeeConfig(1, 0, 2)`; the -vvvv trace shows `prepareRequests{value: 2}` -> `fundSubscriptionWithNative{value: 2}`, i.e. a 2-wei fee exactly covering a 2-wei requirement. That is not the mainnet ratio. I also confirmed nobody funds the service on 999: DeployHyperEVMMainnetCore.s.sol:81-108 and ActivateHyperEVMMainnet.s.sol:78-81 transfer no value, .env.mainnet.example has no funding variable, and MAINNET_RELEASE_RUNBOOK_2026-07-26.md mentions funding only the deployer wallet (line 23) and the Gelato Gas Tank (line 97). Decisive: the team already wrote `_prefundCoverage` for exactly this at script/PrepareDrandGameplayE2E.s.sol:134-142 for TESTNET, and there is no mainnet equivalent. Fails closed, so `low` is the right severity, and the suggested balance assertion in the activation script is the correct minimal fix.

findings.title: Pre-open buy gate keyed on `recipient` instead of the reference's `sender` + isBuying handshake, letting any third party execute buys and move the pre-open spot the go/no-go check relies on
findings.preconditions: Market launched, externalBuysEnabled == false (the deliberate window between ActivateHyperEVMMainnet and ActivateNestMarket).
findings.scenario: The gate is `if (isBuy && !TOKEN.externalBuysEnabled() && recipient != address(TOKEN) && !TOKEN.isProtocolBuyer(recipient)) revert ExternalBuysDisabled();` — it inspects only the swap's recipient. The Ethereum reference gates on the swap's `sender` AND a handshake flag: FWA_ETHEREUM_REFERENCE/FWATokenHook/sources/src/FWATokenHook.sol:228-230 `if (params.zeroForOne && !externalBuysEnabled) { if (!isPool[sender] || !ITokenBuyer(sender).isBuying()) revert ExternalBuysDisabled(); }`, with the in-source rationale that the isBuying flag exists "so a registered-but-idle module can never be ridden". The port dropped both the sender keying and the handshake (FWARewardsHyperEVM no longer has isBuying at all — see the diff against the reference). Result: while buys are officially closed, any address can call the Nest router with recipient = address(FWATokenNest) or recipient = address(FWARewardsHyperEVM) and the swap executes. I found no path for the caller to recover the FWA (the token contract's balance is only consumed for the exact amountOut of a buyback, and the rewards module's balance is only paid out from internal accounting), so this is a donation rather than a theft — but it does let an unprivileged party move the pool price arbitrarily during the closed window, which is exactly the price the mainnet runbook's pre-open checklist inspects ("Avant `open`, vérifier liquidité, route Nest, affichage du spot on-chain et comportement d'un swap canary", MAINNET_RELEASE_RUNBOOK_2026-07-26.md:171) and which the frontend displays as the $FWA spot.
findings.impact: The "closed market" state is weaker than the reference's: the pre-open spot price shown to operators and users is third-party controllable, and the anti-riding handshake that the reference documents as load-bearing was removed without an equivalent. Combined with the static buyback price limit this is the cheapest way to force the buyback DoS.
findings.minimalFix: Key the gate on the swap `sender` as the reference does — require sender to be the FWANestSwapAdapter — and add an equivalent handshake: have the adapter expose an `isBuying()` transient flag raised only across its own buyExactInput, and have beforeSwap require both `TOKEN.isProtocolBuyer(sender)` and `ITokenBuyer(sender).isBuying()`. Keep the recipient check as an additional constraint rather than the only one.
findings.regressionTest: test/FWANestIntegration.t.sol: with externalBuysEnabled false, assert that a router swap from an arbitrary EOA with recipient = address(token) reverts ExternalBuysDisabled after the fix (it currently succeeds), while token.buyback() and rewards.claimAccruedTokens still succeed.

refutationNotes.reason: SURVIVES AT THE STATED SEVERITY; THE PROPOSED FIX IS INFEASIBLE. Divergence confirmed on both sides: FWATokenHook.sol:228-230 gates on `sender` AND ITokenBuyer(sender).isBuying() (FWARewards.sol:162, 598, 608), while FWANestPlugin.sol:125 inspects only `recipient` and FWARewardsHyperEVM has no isBuying at all. The exploit path is real: FWATokenNest._afterTokenTransfer:423 returns for `to == address(this)`, so a third party can route a Nest router buy with recipient = the token while externalBuysEnabled is false. Two corrections. (1) 'Key the gate on the swap sender as the reference does — require sender to be the FWANestSwapAdapter' would break the protocol's own buys: FWANestSwapAdapter.sol:111-121 goes through ROUTER.exactInputSingle, so the `sender` Algebra passes to beforeSwap is the Nest router, not the adapter. Keying on recipient is a forced consequence of using a shared router; the v4 reference could key on sender only because FWAToken and FWARewards call poolManager.swap from their own unlockCallbacks. A workable fix is an adapter-side transient isBuying flag plus keeping the recipient check, not a sender==adapter requirement. (2) 'the cheapest way to force the buyback DoS' is unsupported — see my finding-5 verdict; and the donated FWA is genuinely unrecoverable (from==token to==EOA reverts at _afterTokenTransfer:428; the token's only outbound FWA paths consume the buyback's amountOut). Low is the right rating: a documented parity weakening of the closed window with a purely donative attacker cost.

SURVIVES at the stated severity, with one important correction to the fix.

The divergence is real and I traced it end to end. FWANestPlugin.sol:125 gates on `recipient` only. The reference gates on the swap sender plus a handshake: FWA_ETHEREUM_REFERENCE/FWATokenHook/sources/src/FWATokenHook.sol:228-230 `if (params.zeroForOne && !externalBuysEnabled) { if (!isPool[sender] || !ITokenBuyer(sender).isBuying()) revert ExternalBuysDisabled(); }`, with the in-source rationale at :225-227 that the flag exists 'so a registered-but-idle module can never be ridden'. FWARewards.sol:162/598/608 carries `isBuying`; FWARewardsHyperEVM has no such flag anywhere. Reachability confirmed: router.exactInputSingle with recipient = address(FWATokenNest) passes the plugin at :125, then FWATokenNest._afterTokenTransfer(from = pool, to = address(this)) returns at :423 via the `to == address(this)` branch. And the FWA is unrecoverable by the buyer (the token's balance is only ever burned or routed for a buyback's own amountOut), so it is a donation, exactly as stated.

CORRECTION TO THE FIX — the proposed remedy would brick the protocol. 'Key the gate on the swap sender ... require sender to be the FWANestSwapAdapter' cannot work: FWANestSwapAdapter.sol:111 executes through ROUTER.exactInputSingle, so the pool sees msg.sender = the Nest router for protocol buybacks and for every external buyer alike. Sender-keying is architecturally unavailable on a router-mediated Algebra pool; recipient-keying is the only workable equivalent, so that half of the divergence is forced, not a lapse. The genuinely restorable half is the handshake: FWANestSwapAdapter could expose a transient isBuying() and FWANestPlugin could staticcall it on the recipient. That is the correct minimal fix.

Impact is correctly rated low and should not be inflated by pairing it with the buyback finding: post-open, any buyer moves the same price with the same capital and keeps the tokens, so the closed window is not 'the cheapest way' to anything.

findings.title: Docs and rewards UI describe purchaser epochs as cadence-driven; the contract uses fixed 1-day wall-clock epochs and counts every settled acquisition as exactly one unit
findings.preconditions: Rewards module live.
findings.scenario: RewardsScreen.tsx:173-175 tells the user "Each epoch's pot splits across its acquisitions once the epoch closes ({coldGapSec/60}m cold gap). Acquisitions after a cold gap take a bonus share.", and the "Epoch mode HOT/COLD" card (lines 94-110) is driven purely by `lastAcquisitionAt + hotGapSec`; docsContent.tsx:483-486 says "An epoch stays hot while acquisitions keep arriving within 60s of each other; a gap of 60 min closes it cold." Neither statement matches the contract. FWARewardsHyperEVM.currentEpoch() (lines 375-379) is `(block.timestamp - emissionStart) / 1 days` — epochs are fixed 24h wall-clock windows and coldGap plays no role in closing them. claimEpochTokens (lines 505-525) pays `purchaserEpochAmount(epoch) * userAcquisitionsInEpoch[epoch][msg.sender] / acquisitionsInEpoch[epoch]`, i.e. every settled acquisition is worth exactly 1 unit regardless of the gap that preceded it. The hot/cold curve (tokenShareBps, lines 382-388) affects only the surcharge slice that becomes tokenBuyAllowance — a different bucket entirely. The UI also never reads pendingAcquisitionsInEpoch, so it cannot model the EpochStillPending revert (line 511) that blocks a claim until every request registered that day is terminal, nor the EpochNotClosed revert (line 510).
findings.impact: Users are told epoch-pot share depends on acquisition cadence and that waiting out a cold gap earns a bonus share of the pot — both false. They will mis-time claims (seeing "COLD" and expecting a claimable epoch that is hours away) and hit two unexplained reverts the UI does not model. No fund loss.
findings.minimalFix: Split the two concepts in the copy: describe epochs as fixed 24h windows measured from emissionStart with a countdown to the next boundary, and describe the hot/cold gap solely as the fraction of an acquisition's surcharge routed into that purchaser's FWA buy allowance. Read pendingAcquisitionsInEpoch and render "settling" for epochs that are closed but still pending.
findings.regressionTest: Component test asserting the epoch card renders a boundary countdown derived from emissionStart + (currentEpoch+1)*86400 rather than from lastAcquisitionTs, and that an epoch with pendingAcquisitionsInEpoch > 0 renders as not-yet-claimable.

refutationNotes.reason: FULLY CONFIRMED AT THE STATED SEVERITY. currentEpoch() is (block.timestamp - emissionStart) / 1 days (FWARewardsHyperEVM.sol:375-379) — coldGap plays no role in closing an epoch. claimEpochTokens pays purchaserEpochAmount(epoch) * userAcquisitionsInEpoch / acquisitionsInEpoch (505-525): every settled acquisition is worth exactly one unit, with no gap-derived bonus. tokenShareBps (382-388) feeds only the surcharge slice that becomes tokenBuyAllowance via registerAcquisition (306-316) and settleAcquisition (342-346) — a different bucket. RewardsScreen.tsx:173-175 ('Each epoch's pot splits across its acquisitions once the epoch closes ({coldGapSec/60}m cold gap). Acquisitions after a cold gap take a bonus share.') and docsContent.tsx:483-486 ('a gap of 60 min closes it cold') are both wrong about epoch closure and about what the bonus applies to. The client never reads pendingAcquisitionsInEpoch (absent from fwaRewardsAbi), so the UI cannot model EpochStillPending (511) or EpochNotClosed (510). One nuance: the HOT/COLD card's sub-copy 'next acquisition may take the cold bonus' is defensible — a cold-gap acquisition really does get a larger tokenShareBps; the defective copy is specifically the sentence tying the cold gap to how the epoch pot splits. No fund impact; low is correct.

SURVIVES at low. The contract semantics are exactly as described and I confirmed they are also exact parity with the reference (FWARewards.sol:399-402 is the same `(block.timestamp - start) / 1 days`), so this is purely an HWA copy defect, not a port defect — which is the right place to file it since the copy is newly written.

Verified: currentEpoch (FWARewardsHyperEVM.sol:375-379) is a fixed 24h wall-clock window from emissionStart; coldGap appears nowhere in it. claimEpochTokens (:518) pays purchaserEpochAmount(epoch) * userAcquisitionsInEpoch / acquisitionsInEpoch — one unit per settled acquisition, no cadence weighting. tokenShareBps (:382-388) feeds only the surcharge slice that becomes tokenBuyAllowance at :344. RewardsScreen.tsx:173-175 does say the pot 'splits across its acquisitions once the epoch closes ({coldGapSec/60}m cold gap)', and docsContent.tsx:483-486 does say 'a gap of 60 min closes it cold' — both conflate the cold gap with the epoch boundary, which is false. The screen never reads pendingAcquisitionsInEpoch, so the EpochStillPending (:511) and EpochNotClosed (:510) reverts are unmodelled.

One nuance to soften in the write-up: 'Acquisitions after a cold gap take a bonus share' is imprecise rather than false — a post-cold-gap acquisition does route 100% of its surcharge to that purchaser's FWA buy allowance, a real bonus, just to a different bucket than the epoch pot. No fund impact, so low is correct.

findings.title: The entire rewards claim, buyback-routing and rescue surface has zero test coverage, and the mainnet adapter is never tested with the rewards module
findings.preconditions: None — coverage finding, verified by exhaustive grep across test/, fork-test/ and hyperevm-fork-test/.
findings.scenario: FWARewardsHyperEVM has 5 tests: constructor wiring, a tokenShareBps fuzz vs the reference, listing-activation accounting vs the reference, register/settle/claimAccruedTokens, and buyFor. Grepping the whole repo for onTokenReceived, claimEpochTokens, claimDepositorTokens, withdrawTokens, sweepEmptyEpoch, rescueTokens, withdrawTokenBuyAllowanceAsETH and refundAcquisition returns exactly one hit — a mock router in test/mocks/MockHyperSwapV3.sol:283 used by the legacy token test. So none of these are exercised: the buyback→rewards routing callback (FWARewardsHyperEVM.sol:561-580, including the sqrtBackingTotal == 0 burn branch), the depositor claim path and its floor/ceil tokenDebt checkpointing (473-492), the tokenCredit withdrawal (495-502), the epoch pot pro-rata split and its EpochNotClosed / EpochStillPending / AlreadyClaimed guards (505-525), the empty-epoch sweep (608-619), the destructive rescue (623-633), the ETH escape hatch (460-470), and the refund terminal hook (352-360). Separately, test/FWANestIntegration.t.sol:117-132 exercises buyback() with rewardsPool unset (destination == address(0), full burn), so the 40/40/20 routing is never run against FWATokenNest at all — only against the legacy FWATokenHyperEVM with a mock router (test/FWATokenHyperEVM.t.sol:122-155). And the mainnet pairing FWARewardsHyperEVM + FWANestSwapAdapter exists in no test; the rewards test binds the testnet-only FWAHyperSwapAdapter instead.
findings.impact: The paths that move the 300M FWA reward budget and the ones that let the owner sweep or rescue it are entirely unverified on a release that will custody real value, and the exact contract pair that will run on chain 999 has never been executed together.
findings.minimalFix: Add a FWANest+rewards integration suite covering: buyback routing into FWARewardsHyperEVM (both sqrtBackingTotal == 0 and > 0), depositor claim/reprice/remove checkpointing including the deposit-then-immediately-withdraw no-farm property, the epoch claim happy path plus each of the three revert guards plus a duplicate-epoch array, sweepEmptyEpoch on an empty vs non-empty epoch, rescueTokens gated by canRescueRewards, withdrawTokenBuyAllowanceAsETH, and refundAcquisition draining pendingAcquisitionsInEpoch. Add an emission-solvency invariant test asserting the module never pays out more FWA than it was funded.
findings.regressionTest: An invariant test with fail_on_revert=false over registerAcquisition/settle/refund/onListingActivated/reprice/removed/onTokenReceived plus all claim paths, asserting `sum(all payouts) <= initial funding + sum(buyback deposits)` and `address(rewards).balance >= tokenBuyAllowanceTotal` at every step.

refutationNotes.reason: CONFIRMED IN FULL AT THE STATED SEVERITY. I re-ran the exhaustive grep across test/, fork-test/ and hyperevm-fork-test/ for onTokenReceived|claimEpochTokens|claimDepositorTokens|withdrawTokens|sweepEmptyEpoch|rescueTokens|withdrawTokenBuyAllowanceAsETH|refundAcquisition: exactly one hit, test/mocks/MockHyperSwapV3.sol:283 (the MockFWABuybackRouter used by the legacy token test). test/FWARewardsHyperEVM.t.sol has exactly 5 tests and binds FWAHyperSwapAdapter at lines 46-48 — the testnet-only adapter — so the chain-999 pair FWARewardsHyperEVM + FWANestSwapAdapter is exercised nowhere. test/FWANestIntegration.t.sol:117-132 runs buyback() with rewardsPool unset and asserts totalSupply == supplyBefore - amountOut, i.e. only the full-burn branch; the 40/40/20 routing is exercised solely against the legacy FWATokenHyperEVM with a mock router (test/FWATokenHyperEVM.t.sol:122-155), exactly as the finding states. All 15 tests in the two suites pass, and none touch the depositor tokenDebt checkpointing (473-492), tokenCredit withdrawal (495-502), the epoch pro-rata split and its three revert guards (505-525), sweepEmptyEpoch (608-619), rescueTokens (623-633), withdrawTokenBuyAllowanceAsETH (460-470), refundAcquisition (352-360), or the sqrtBackingTotal == 0 burn branch of onTokenReceived (564-567). If anything low is conservative for the code paths that move a 300M-token program; I would not object to medium, but low is defensible under the rubric's 'hardening / defence in depth'.

SURVIVES, and the grep result is even starker than claimed. Running the search across test/, fork-test/ and hyperevm-fork-test/ for onTokenReceived, claimEpochTokens, claimDepositorTokens, withdrawTokens, sweepEmptyEpoch, rescueTokens, withdrawTokenBuyAllowanceAsETH, refundAcquisition and claimAccruedTokens returns exactly TWO hits in the entire repository: test/mocks/MockHyperSwapV3.sol:283 (a mock's own onTokenReceived, used by the legacy token test) and test/FWARewardsHyperEVM.t.sol:133 (claimAccruedTokens). Every other listed function is executed by no test at all. FWARewardsHyperEVM.t.sol has 154 lines and 5 tests (testConstructorAndCoreWiring, testFuzzHotColdCurveMatchesReference, testListingEmissionAccountingMatchesReference, testAcquisitionAccountingMatchesThenClaimsThroughHyperSwap, testCoreBuyForUsesExactInputAdapterAndTransfersRecipient) and its setUp binds FWAHyperSwapAdapter, not the mainnet FWANestSwapAdapter. setRewardsPool appears in no test except FWATokenHyperEVM.t.sol:131 (the legacy token with a mock router), so FWANestIntegration.t.sol:117-132 does indeed exercise buyback only with rewardsPool unset, i.e. the full-burn branch — the 40/40/20 routing has never run against FWATokenNest.

This is not covered by the disclosed known limits, which mention only the subgraph's missing Matchstick tests. The release gate's '91 tests Solidity' is a count, not coverage.

Low is right (it is an assurance gap, not an exploitable defect), but the category should be 'test-coverage' rather than 'exploitation-risk'.

findings.title: LaunchNestMarket computes a tickLower below the initial price whenever the price's tick is a multiple of the spacing, aborting the launch
findings.preconditions: FWA sorts as token0 (address(token) < wHYPE — roughly half of deployments), and the operator-chosen FWA_INITIAL_SQRT_PRICE_X96 maps to a tick that is a multiple of POOL_TICK_SPACING (60) without being exactly that tick's boundary price.
findings.scenario: _floorToSpacing(t, 60) returns t when t % 60 == 0, so the token0 branch sets tickLower = floorTick == currentTick ? currentTick : floorTick + spacing → tickLower = currentTick. But TickMath.getTickAtSqrtPrice floors, so getSqrtPriceAtTick(currentTick) <= sqrtPriceX96 with equality only at an exact boundary. finalizeLaunch then hits `if (sqrtPriceX96 > TickMath.getSqrtPriceAtTick(tickLower)) revert InvalidRange()` (FWATokenNest.sol:313). Concrete case, verified: sqrtPriceX96 = TickMath.getSqrtPriceAtTick(60) + 1 → currentTick == 60, floorTick == 60, tickLower == 60, and sqrtPriceX96 > getSqrtPriceAtTick(60), so the launch transaction reverts. The existing tests never hit this because every test uses INITIAL_PRICE = 1 << 96, which is exactly the tick-0 boundary — the one class of value that survives.
findings.impact: Fails closed: a wasted mainnet transaction and a stalled launch phase on the day, no loss of funds or NFTs. Probability is roughly 1 in 60 for an arbitrarily chosen initial price, on the token0 half of deployments.
findings.minimalFix: script/LaunchNestMarket.s.sol:62 → `tickLower = (floorTick == currentTick && sqrtPriceX96 == TickMath.getSqrtPriceAtTick(floorTick)) ? currentTick : floorTick + spacing;`
findings.regressionTest: Unit test over both cases: sqrtPriceX96 = getSqrtPriceAtTick(60) (must yield tickLower == 60 and pass finalizeLaunch's guard) and sqrtPriceX96 = getSqrtPriceAtTick(60) + 1 (must yield tickLower == 120).

refutationNotes.reason: SURVIVES at low. The arithmetic checks out: _floorToSpacing (LaunchNestMarket.s.sol:78-82) returns t unchanged when t % spacing == 0, so line 62 sets tickLower = currentTick; TickMath.getTickAtSqrtPrice floors, so getSqrtPriceAtTick(currentTick) <= sqrtPriceX96 with equality only at an exact tick boundary; therefore for any spacing-aligned tick whose price is not the exact boundary, FWATokenNest.sol:313 (fwaIsToken0 branch) sees sqrtPriceX96 > getSqrtPriceAtTick(tickLower) and reverts InvalidRange. The token1 branch (:314) is safe because floorTick <= currentTick always satisfies the >= comparison, so the finding correctly scopes it to the FWA-as-token0 half. Test-blindness claim verified: every call site uses 1<<96 (test/FWANestIntegration.t.sol:21, test/NestTestnetHarness.t.sol:64, hyperevm-fork-test/NestDeployment.t.sol:94), which is exactly the tick-0 boundary that survives. One mitigating fact the finding does not mention and that keeps this at low rather than anything higher: .env.mainnet.example ships FWA_INITIAL_SQRT_PRICE_X96=79228162514264337593543950336, i.e. 1<<96 — the shipped operational value is the surviving case, so the bug only bites if the operator picks a different price whose tick happens to be a multiple of 60. It fails closed (a reverted, non-broadcast-costly launch tx), no funds or NFTs at risk. The one-line fix at :62 is correct as written.

SURVIVES exactly as written, at the stated severity. Verified end to end. _floorToSpacing (LaunchNestMarket.s.sol:78-82) returns t unchanged when t % 60 == 0, so line 62's ternary `floorTick == currentTick ? currentTick : floorTick + spacing` sets tickLower = currentTick for any spacing-aligned tick. TickMath.getTickAtSqrtPrice is documented in the vendored source (vendor/fwa-reference-union/lib/v4-core/src/libraries/TickMath.sol:116-121) as 'the greatest tick value such that getSqrtPriceAtTick(tick) <= sqrtPriceX96', i.e. it floors, so equality holds only at an exact boundary price. FWATokenNest.sol:313 then reverts InvalidRange for the token0 orientation whenever sqrtPriceX96 > getSqrtPriceAtTick(tickLower). The worked case (getSqrtPriceAtTick(60) + 1) is correct. I also checked the token1 branch (lines 65-66 vs FWATokenNest.sol:314) and it is sound in every case, which matches the finding's scoping. The claim that existing tests miss it is right: every test uses 1<<96, the exact tick-0 boundary, the single surviving value. Probability ~1/60 on the token0 half of deployments; fails closed with a wasted mainnet transaction and no fund impact. The one-line fix at :62 is correct. Low is the right severity.

findings.title: The production path that opens public trading carries none of ActivateNestMarket's wiring checks
findings.preconditions: Mainnet ownership held by a Safe, which the runbook says is the intended production configuration ("Safe owners use PrepareMainnetOwnerActions.ps1 instead", ActivateNestMarket.s.sol:22).
findings.scenario: ActivateNestMarket gates setExternalBuysEnabled(true) behind sixteen on-chain assertions (adapter/rewardsPool/rewardsBuyer wiring, fwa.rewards, fwa.token, splitter shares, pool.plugin, pluginConfig, fee, communityFee, tickSpacing, owner identity) plus the NEST_E2E_CONFIRMED env gate. But PrepareMainnetOwnerActions.ps1 emits manualTradingControls.open as a bare `setExternalBuysEnabled(bool) true` calldata against the token, with no preconditions whatsoever. A Safe signer executing that payload opens public trading regardless of whether VerifyNestModules passed, whether the rewards module is bound, or whether the pool configuration has drifted since phase E.
findings.impact: Public trading can be opened into a half-wired protocol. It is reversible (setExternalBuysEnabled(false) exists), so not an irreversible open, but the sequencing guarantees the team believes are enforced are absent from the path they will actually use — the classic case of an off-chain gate substituting for an on-chain invariant.
findings.minimalFix: Move the preconditions into the contract: make FWATokenNest.setExternalBuysEnabled(true) require adapter != address(0), rewardsPool != address(0) and a passing _assertLivePoolConfiguration, while leaving the `false` direction unconditional so the kill switch is never blocked. The Safe calldata then inherits the guarantee for free.
findings.regressionTest: Assert setExternalBuysEnabled(true) reverts when adapter == address(0) or rewardsPool == address(0), and that setExternalBuysEnabled(false) still succeeds under a drifted pool configuration.

refutationNotes.reason: SURVIVES at low, as filed. The asymmetry is exactly as described: ActivateNestMarket.s.sol:33 gates on NEST_E2E_CONFIRMED and :46-55 asserts sixteen on-chain conditions (adapter, rewardsPool, adapter.rewardsBuyer, rewards.fwa, fwa.rewards, fwa.token, fwa.payoutAddress, splitter shares, pool.plugin, pluginConfig, fee, communityFee, tickSpacing, owner identity) before setExternalBuysEnabled(true), whereas PrepareMainnetOwnerActions.ps1:54-61 emits manualTradingControls.open as bare setExternalBuysEnabled(bool) true calldata with no preconditions at all — and ActivateNestMarket.s.sol:22 itself states the Safe path is the intended production route, so the unguarded path is the one that will actually be used. FWATokenNest.setExternalBuysEnabled (:171-175) enforces only launched(). The severity is correctly held at low rather than high: the action is fully reversible via the sibling close calldata that the same script emits, so this is not 'a launch step that irreversibly opens the product early'. The proposed fix is well-shaped — the asymmetric guard (require wiring on true, leave false unconditional) is the right pattern so the kill switch can never be blocked by a drifted pool, which matters given how easily _assertLivePoolConfiguration can start reverting.

SURVIVES as written, at low. Verified on both sides. ActivateNestMarket.s.sol:33 gates on NEST_E2E_CONFIRMED and :46-55 asserts the full wiring set (adapter, rewardsPool, adapter.rewardsBuyer, rewards.fwa, fwa.rewards, fwa.token, fwa.payoutAddress, splitter shares 7000/3000, pool.plugin, pluginConfig, fee, communityFee, tickSpacing, owner identity) before calling setExternalBuysEnabled(true) at :58. PrepareMainnetOwnerActions.ps1:54-61 emits `manualTradingControls.open` as bare `setExternalBuysEnabled(bool) true` calldata against the token with no preconditions of any kind, and ActivateNestMarket.s.sol:22 confirms the Safe path is the intended production route ('Safe owners use PrepareMainnetOwnerActions.ps1 instead'). On-chain, setExternalBuysEnabled (FWATokenNest.sol:171-175) checks only `launched`. So the sixteen guarantees exist solely on the path the team will NOT use in production - the exact off-chain-gate substitution the mandate flags. Correctly held at low: the action is reversible via the paired `close` calldata, the runbook sequences VerifyNestModules ahead of it, and no funds are at risk. The proposed fix (require adapter != 0, rewardsPool != 0 and _assertLivePoolConfiguration on the true direction only, leaving false unconditional so the kill switch never blocks) is sound and is the cheapest way to make the Safe payload inherit the guarantee. This is the best-calibrated finding in the set.

findings.title: setOwnerShareBps lets the owner take 100% of any incoming deposit with no floor, no timelock and no delay, and payoutFees() is permissionless with a publicly readable accrual - so the '70/30' split is an owner-controlled parameter, not a protocol guarantee
findings.preconditions: Control of the Splitter owner key, which `VerifyHyperEVMCore.s.sol:68-70` and `ActivateHyperEVMMainnet.s.sol:70-72` require to be the same `finalOwner` that owns FWA.
findings.scenario: `ownerShareBps` is mutable at any time up to 10,000 with immediate effect on the next deposit; only already-checkpointed allocations are protected (correctly verified by `testSplitUpdateOnlyAffectsFutureDeposits`). `FWA.accruedOwnerFees` is public and `payoutFees()` is permissionless, so the owner can watch the accrual grow, send `setOwnerShareBps(10_000)`, then call `payoutFees()` in the same block: the entire payout is booked to `ownerAllocated` and the NFT side receives nothing, after which the owner can restore 7,000 so every point-in-time verification (`ownerShareBps != 7_000` in VerifyHyperEVMCore and ActivateHyperEVMMainnet) still passes.
findings.impact: Holders' 30% is discretionary. This is exact parity with the verified Ethereum `Splitter` (same code path, same lack of a floor) and the Ethereum deployment has the same owner on FWA and the Splitter (0x019817ad… in both `FWA_ETHEREUM_REFERENCE/roles-state.json` and `Splitter/state-snapshot.json`), so it is not a port divergence. Recorded because the runbook and FWA_PARITY_MANIFEST present '70/30' as a property of the release and every automated check that asserts 7,000 bps is a snapshot that a two-transaction sequence defeats.
findings.minimalFix: No change needed for parity. If a stronger guarantee is wanted at launch, add an immutable `MAX_OWNER_SHARE_BPS` floor to the constructor (e.g. reject `newOwnerShareBps > 7_000`), or route `setOwnerShareBps` through the timelock rather than the Safe's immediate-execution path, and state the current discretion explicitly in the public docs.
findings.regressionTest: `testOwnerCanFrontRunADepositWithASplitFlip()` - set 10,000 bps, deposit 100 ether, assert `nftAllocated == 0` and `claimablePerToken() == 0`, restore 7,000 bps and assert the view checks used by VerifyHyperEVMCore pass again. Pinning this makes the discretion visible in CI instead of implicit.

refutationNotes.reason:
Survives, and the severity (info) is correct. Verified end to end: SplitterHyperEVM.sol:85-92 accepts newOwnerShareBps up to BPS=10_000 with no floor and no delay, and receive() (94-104) prices each deposit at the value of ownerShareBps at that instant; vendor/fwa-reference-union/src/FWA.sol:451 makes accruedOwnerFees public and 1988-2003 makes payoutFees() permissionless, so the set-10000 / payoutFees / restore-7000 sequence is executable and atomically composable by the owner.

The 'every automated check is a point-in-time snapshot' observation is the valuable part and checks out: VerifyHyperEVMCore.s.sol:68-70 and ActivateHyperEVMMainnet.s.sol:70-72 both assert `splitter.ownerShareBps() != 7_000` as a revert condition, and both are defeated by a two-transaction restore.

It is exact parity with FWA_ETHEREUM_REFERENCE/Splitter/sources/src/Splitter.sol:125-132 (same missing floor, same owner on both contracts per roles-state.json / state-snapshot.json 0x019817ad...), so it is correctly filed as an observation rather than a port defect. Keep it in the trust-boundary section of the report; do not escalate.

Survives at the stated severity (info). Every mechanical step verified: setOwnerShareBps accepts up to BPS with immediate effect and no floor (SplitterHyperEVM.sol:85-92); receive() then computes nftAllocation = fullMulDiv(msg.value, 10000-10000, 10000) = 0 so the whole deposit books to ownerAllocated (line 96-101); FWA.accruedOwnerFees is public (vendor/fwa-reference-union/src/FWA.sol:451) and payoutFees() is external nonReentrant with no auth (line 1988), so the flip and the payout are composable in one block; and the flip-and-restore genuinely defeats both automated checks, since VerifyHyperEVMCore.s.sol:70 and ActivateHyperEVMMainnet.s.sol:72 assert `splitter.ownerShareBps() != 7_000` as a point-in-time read. Correctly classified as exact parity with reference Splitter.sol:125-132 rather than a port divergence, and correctly rated info. One accuracy correction for the report: payoutFees first routes a protocolFeeToTokenBps slice to the token buyback reserve (FWA.sol:1993-1996), so the amount diverted is the payout-address portion `accrued - tokenPortion`, not the entire accrual. Keep it - it is the only finding in this set that documents a real, undisclosed limitation of two release-gate assertions.
