findings.title: DeploySplitterHyperEVM requires NEST_MAINNET_DEPLOYMENT_CONFIRMED on mainnet, which the runbook's splitter step does not mention and which consumes the Nest gate before the Nest phase begins
findings.preconditions: Operator follows MAINNET_RELEASE_RUNBOOK section 4.1 verbatim.
findings.scenario: Runbook section 4.1 says only "Dry-run puis broadcast avec FWA_SPLITTER_DEPLOYMENT_CONFIRMED=true". The script also demands NEST_MAINNET_DEPLOYMENT_CONFIRMED (line 44-46), so the first attempt fails closed with MainnetNotConfirmed - harmless in itself. The structural consequence is what matters and is captured in the separate one-shot-actions finding: to complete step 4.1, the operator must set the flag that is the sole mainnet gate for DeployNestPlugin, InitializeNestMarket and LaunchNestMarket, three steps that do not occur until section 4.3.
findings.impact: Documentation/code mismatch that fails closed, plus loss of the per-phase meaning of NEST_MAINNET_DEPLOYMENT_CONFIRMED. No direct risk on its own.
findings.minimalFix: Either drop the NEST_MAINNET_DEPLOYMENT_CONFIRMED requirement from DeploySplitterHyperEVM (FWA_SPLITTER_DEPLOYMENT_CONFIRMED plus the chain check already gate it), or document it in runbook section 4.1 and introduce genuinely per-phase Nest flags as described in the one-shot-actions finding.
findings.regressionTest: Add a self-test asserting DeploySplitterHyperEVM reverts MainnetNotConfirmed on chain 999 with only FWA_SPLITTER_DEPLOYMENT_CONFIRMED set, so the coupling is at least pinned and visible.

refutationNotes.reason: SURVIVES at info, which is the correct severity. Verified: DeploySplitterHyperEVM.s.sol:43-46 requires both FWA_SPLITTER_DEPLOYMENT_CONFIRMED and NEST_MAINNET_DEPLOYMENT_CONFIRMED on chain 999, while runbook section 4.1 (line 55) mentions only the former; and that same flag is the sole mainnet gate on DeployNestPlugin:39, InitializeNestMarket:27 and LaunchNestMarket:38, so completing 4.1 does consume it several phases early. Both halves are factually accurate and it fails closed, so there is no risk in the mismatch itself. Two caveats for the report editor: the structural half is the same observation already carried by the one-shot-actions finding, so it should be merged there rather than listed separately; and as a pure documentation/sequencing note with a fail-closed gate it is at the very bottom of what is worth a reviewer's attention.

Verified and correctly rated info. DeploySplitterHyperEVM.s.sol:43-46 requires both FWA_SPLITTER_DEPLOYMENT_CONFIRMED and NEST_MAINNET_DEPLOYMENT_CONFIRMED on chain 999, while MAINNET_RELEASE_RUNBOOK section 4.1 mentions only the former; the mismatch fails closed with MainnetNotConfirmed. findings.title: DrandRelayCoordinator ignores callbackGasLimit and does not validate extraArgs, forwarding unbounded gas to the consumer
findings.preconditions: Testnet 998 only.
findings.scenario: `requestRandomWords` accepts any `callbackGasLimit` including 0 and does not check `extraArgs` for the native-payment tag that the Gelato coordinator requires (GelatoVRFCoordinator.sol:110). The stored `callbackGasLimit` is then never applied: line 188 does a plain high-level `IDrandFWAConsumer(request.consumer).rawFulfillRandomWords(...)`, forwarding all remaining gas rather than `call{gas: request.callbackGasLimit}` as the mainnet coordinator does. The existing test consumer passes `extraArgs: ""` (test/DrandRelayCoordinator.t.sol:28), which the Gelato coordinator would reject.
findings.impact: Testnet only, and the consumer is FWA, so no realistic abuse. It is a behavioural divergence between the two coordinators used to validate the same core, which weakens the 998 rehearsal as evidence for 999: a callback that would be gas-capped on mainnet is not gas-capped on testnet.
findings.minimalFix: Mirror the mainnet coordinator: validate `numWords == 1`, non-zero `callbackGasLimit`, and the native-payment `extraArgs`, and deliver via `call{gas: request.callbackGasLimit}` with the same `!success -> revert` handling.
findings.regressionTest: `testDrandRelayEnforcesCallbackGasLimit`: consumer that burns more than `callbackGasLimit`; assert the fulfilment reverts and the request stays Pending, matching GelatoVRFCoordinator behaviour.

refutationNotes.reason: SURVIVES at info as rated. Verified: DrandRelayCoordinator.requestRandomWords validates only subId, numWords and keyHash (129-131) — no callbackGasLimit floor and no extraArgs check — while GelatoVRFCoordinator additionally requires requestConfirmations != 0, callbackGasLimit != 0 and the exact native-payment extraArgs (107-111); and delivery at line 188 is a plain high-level IDrandFWAConsumer(...).rawFulfillRandomWords, forwarding all remaining gas, versus `call{gas: request.callbackGasLimit}` with an explicit !success revert at GelatoVRFCoordinator.sol:162-165. test/DrandRelayCoordinator.t.sol:28 passing extraArgs "" confirms the mainnet coordinator would reject the testnet consumer's request shape. Testnet-only, the consumer is FWA, the relayer is supervised, and no abuse path exists — the substance is purely that the 998 rehearsal does not exercise the mainnet gas-capping semantics, which is a fair fidelity note. Info is correct; it should not be escalated.

SURVIVES at `info`, which is the correct level. Verified: DrandRelayCoordinator.sol:129-131 validates only `subId`, `numWords == 1` and a non-zero `keyHash`, so `callbackGasLimit` may be 0 and `extraArgs` is never inspected, whereas GelatoVRFCoordinator.sol:107-111 additionally requires a non-zero callback limit and an exact native-payment `extraArgs` match. Line 188 is a plain high-level `IDrandFWAConsumer(...).rawFulfillRandomWords(...)` forwarding all remaining gas, against `call{gas: request.callbackGasLimit}` at GelatoVRFCoordinator.sol:162-165. I confirmed the test consumer passes `extraArgs: ""` (test/DrandRelayCoordinator.t.sol:28), which the mainnet coordinator would reject with `InvalidRequest`. Testnet-only, the consumer is FWA, and there is no abuse path — but the point that this weakens 998 as a rehearsal for 999 is legitimate and correctly rated as an observation rather than a defect.

findings.title: Admin power enumeration for the rewards/token stack, including a two-call owner path that redirects 100% of buyback proceeds
findings.preconditions: Owner key (Safe) compromised or acting adversarially. All powers below are parity with the verified Ethereum reference except where noted.
findings.scenario: FWARewardsHyperEVM owner: setFWA (one-shot; binding a non-contract permanently bricks rescueTokens, which decodes a bool from canRescueRewards()); setEmission (no cap, no funding check, locked once emission starts); setColdGapBands and setForcedTokenShareBps (move the acquisition surcharge between purchaser token-buy allowances and depositors/protocol at will, 0-100%); sweepEmptyEpoch (takes an entire closed epoch's pot — up to the 10M daily pot plus all buyback-routed tokens — to any address whenever that day had zero settled acquisitions); rescueTokens (drains the module's entire FWA balance, including every unclaimed depositor and epoch reward, once the owner has set the core to withdrawOnly — a two-transaction confiscation of the whole unclaimed 300M program, documented in-source as deliberate). FWATokenNest owner: setDistributor (grants unlimited transfer freedom to any address, and can REVOKE the rewards module's distributor flag, which freezes every reward payout with no way for the rewards module to restore it); setProtocolBuyer (lets a named address buy from the locked pool before the public open — no reference equivalent, the reference hook requires an isBuying handshake); setExternalBuysEnabled (toggles public buying off again after opening); setRouteSplit (0-100% of every buyback to depositors, purchasers or burn); setBuybackSqrtPriceLimitX96; setAdapter and setRewardsPool (one-shot each, see the migration finding). Composite path worth noting: with acquisitions paused so acquisitionsInEpoch[e] stays 0, the owner sets setRouteSplit(0, 10000, 0), lets buybacks accumulate into purchaserEpochPot[e], then after the epoch closes calls sweepEmptyEpoch(e, ownerAddress) — 100% of the buyback proceeds are redirected to the owner instead of burned or redistributed, using only functions that exist in the reference. FWANestSwapAdapter owner: setRewardsBuyer (one-shot), recoverForcedHype (sweeps force-sent HYPE). FWANestLiquidityLocker owner: setFeeRecipient (redirects all LP fee income).
findings.impact: No unauthorised power was found relative to the reference except setProtocolBuyer, which has no reference analogue and grants pre-open buying to an owner-named address. The rest are parity but their aggregate blast radius — full confiscation of unclaimed rewards, full freeze of reward payouts, and full redirection of buyback proceeds — is not disclosed anywhere in the user-facing docs, which present rewards as an accruing entitlement.
findings.minimalFix: Publish the admin-power table (function, holder, blast radius, reversibility) in the public docs and in NEST_ADMIN_HANDOFF.md; put setDistributor, setRouteSplit, rescueTokens and sweepEmptyEpoch behind a timelock on the Safe; and consider removing setProtocolBuyer in favour of the reference's sender+handshake gate so pre-open buying cannot be granted to an arbitrary address.
findings.regressionTest: Add tests asserting each owner-only function reverts for non-owners and emits its event, and one explicitly documenting the setRouteSplit(0,10000,0) → sweepEmptyEpoch redirection so the behaviour is a recorded, intentional property rather than an emergent one.

refutationNotes.reason: SURVIVES AS INFO, BUT ITS ONE DISTINGUISHING CLAIM IS WRONG. The enumeration is accurate and the composite is reachable: setRouteSplit(0, 10_000, 0) satisfies the sum check (FWATokenNest.sol:232-238), buyback routes the whole amount to the module, onTokenReceived credits purchaserEpochPot[currentEpoch] (575-579), and sweepEmptyEpoch (608-619) requires only epoch-closed / no-pending / no-acquisitions, so an owner who keeps acquisitions paused can take the entire pot. Revoking the rewards module's distributor flag does freeze every payout (_afterTokenTransfer:415-428 leaves no other path for module->user). Both are worth publishing. However: 'setProtocolBuyer ... no reference equivalent' is FALSE — FWATokenHook.sol:68 declares `mapping(address => bool) public isPool` and 135-136 declares `function setPool(address _pool, bool allowed) external onlyOwner`, a direct analogue granting an owner-named address pre-open buying. The only delta is the extra isBuying handshake, which is already finding 7's subject. So the correct conclusion is 'no unauthorised power was found relative to the reference', full stop — and the setRouteSplit + sweepEmptyEpoch composite is likewise reference-native (FWAToken.setRouteSplit:208-214, FWARewards.sweepEmptyEpoch:672). Also, 'binding a non-contract permanently bricks rescueTokens' is true (setFWA:233-238 has no code check) but harmless: a module bound to an EOA can never be wired to a core (FWA.setRewards requires r.fwa() == address(this)), so it holds no user funds and is simply redeployed.

REFUTED. The enumeration is mostly accurate but its single differentiating claim is factually wrong, and what remains is a documentation recommendation rather than a defect.

The claim 'setProtocolBuyer ... no reference equivalent, the reference hook requires an isBuying handshake' and 'setProtocolBuyer, which has no reference analogue' is FALSE. FWA_ETHEREUM_REFERENCE/FWATokenHook/sources/src/FWATokenHook.sol:134-137 is `function setPool(address _pool, bool allowed) external onlyOwner { isPool[_pool] = allowed; ... }`, documented at :132-133 as 'Register/deregister a protocol buyer allowed while external buys are gated'. isProtocolBuyer IS isPool. The only element actually dropped is the isBuying handshake — which is finding 8's subject, correctly rated low there, and which as I showed cannot be restored by sender-keying on Algebra. So the finding's own headline conclusion ('No unauthorised power was found ... except setProtocolBuyer') collapses to 'no unauthorised power was found'.

The composite path is real — I verified sweepEmptyEpoch (FWARewardsHyperEVM.sol:608-619) pays purchaserEpochAmount = purchaserEpochPot[epoch] + purchaserDailyPot to an arbitrary `to` on any epoch with zero settled acquisitions, and setRouteSplit can steer 100% of buybacks into that pot — but both functions exist identically in the reference (FWARewards.sol:672 sweepEmptyEpoch, FWAToken.sol:207-214 setRouteSplit), so the composite is parity, not an emergent HyperEVM power. Same for rescueTokens (FWARewards.sol:687) and the setDistributor revocation freeze (reference _afterTokenTransfer :434-455 has the identical distributor gate, and the owner can re-grant in one tx).

Remaining content is 'publish the admin-power table and put the Safe behind a timelock' — a governance/documentation recommendation, already flagged as open gate #6 in FWA_PARITY_MANIFEST.md:255 ('Administration : multisig, timelock, operators et procédure d'urgence avant déploiement public'). Info.

findings.title: $FWA can only be bought through a route that names the buyer directly as the swap recipient
findings.preconditions: Market open (externalBuysEnabled == true).
findings.scenario: _afterTokenTransfer reverts on any transfer that touches neither the pool, the owner, nor a distributor. So a DEX aggregator or executor contract that receives FWA from the pool and then forwards it to the end user reverts on the forwarding leg. Only a direct single-hop exactInputSingle (or a one-pool exactInput) with recipient = the user works. The same follows for peer-to-peer transfers, CEX deposits and vault deposits: $FWA is permanently non-transferable between ordinary holders, who can only sell back into the pool.
findings.impact: No fund risk; it is the same property as the reference's transient-allowance model, so this is parity rather than a divergence. But it is a hard constraint on which trading UI the frontend may link to, and NEST_DEPLOYMENT_RUNBOOK.md:86 commits to redirecting users to a reviewed Nest URL — that URL must not route through an aggregator or a multi-pool path.
findings.minimalFix: No contract change required. Validate the exact Nest route on mainnet before opening, and state the constraint explicitly in the frontend token page and in the runbook.
findings.regressionTest: Frontend/e2e check that the configured external swap URL resolves to a direct wHYPE→FWA single-hop route with the connected wallet as recipient.

refutationNotes.reason: SURVIVES at info, and the parity call is correct — I checked it against the oracle rather than taking it on trust. FWATokenNest.sol:407-429 permits only mints/burns, distributor legs, owner legs, sells into the pool, and pool-out legs to the token or a protocol buyer (or anyone once open); every other transfer, including holder-to-holder, aggregator-executor-to-user, CEX deposits and vault deposits, falls through to revert InvalidTransfer at :428. The reference is the same shape — FWA_ETHEREUM_REFERENCE/FWAToken/sources/src/FWAToken.sol:434-453 allows mint/burn, distributor, owner, and PoolManager legs capped by the transient allowance, then reverts InvalidTransfer — so $FWA is deliberately non-transferable between ordinary holders on both chains. This is parity, not a port regression, and the finding says so. It is worth keeping in the report at info because the operational consequence is concrete and actionable: NEST_DEPLOYMENT_RUNBOOK.md:86 commits to redirecting users to a reviewed Nest URL, and that URL must resolve to a direct single-hop wHYPE->FWA route with the connected wallet as recipient — an aggregator or multi-pool path will revert on the forwarding leg and users will read it as a broken product. No contract change, no fund risk.

SURVIVES as an accurate info-level observation. Traced FWATokenNest.sol:407-428 exhaustively: a holder-to-holder transfer passes none of the exemptions (not mint/burn, not launching, neither side a distributor, neither side the owner, `to != pool`, `from != pool`) and falls to revert InvalidTransfer at :428; an aggregator or executor that takes delivery from the pool clears the `from == marketPool` branch at :422-423 but reverts on the forwarding leg. So single-hop exactInputSingle with recipient == the end user is indeed the only working retail buy route, and CEX/vault deposits are impossible. The parity claim is correct and I verified it directly rather than accepting it: FWA_ETHEREUM_REFERENCE/FWAToken/sources/src/FWAToken.sol:434-453 has the same structure ('Everything else reverts - the lock'), and its transient allowance is bumped only for PoolManager-side legs, so aggregator forwarding breaks there too. No divergence, no fund risk - correctly filed as info/ux-parity. Two small precisions for the write-up: it is not 'permanently non-transferable' in the absolute sense, since the owner can grant isDistributor to any address (FWATokenNest.sol:159-163), which is the intended escape for a listing or custody integration; and the operational consequence should be stated against NEST_DEPLOYMENT_RUNBOOK.md:86, which commits the frontend to a reviewed Nest URL that must be validated as a direct single-hop route with the connected wallet as recipient.

findings.title: Snapshot solvency invariant is only checked once, in the constructor; the port made the snapshot collection an unvalidated constructor parameter, so a collection that can mint/remint an ID <= MAX_TOKEN_ID drains the owner side and bricks claimOwner()
findings.preconditions: The address supplied as FWA_SPLITTER_SNAPSHOT_NFT is a collection whose admin (or any party) can, after the Splitter is deployed, make `ownerOf(id)` succeed for an id in [1, MAX_TOKEN_ID] that was NOT live when the constructor ran. That is exactly the case when `burnedTokenCount() > 0` at deploy time and the collection supports re-minting a burned id, or when the collection can mint non-sequential ids below the cap. `.env.mainnet.example:36-37` still has the collection and max id unset (0x0 / 0), so the choice is open. The only snapshot-collection contract the repo actually contains, `src/hyperevm/testnet/FWATestnetNFT.sol`, has exactly this capability (`remint`, lines 120-132).
findings.scenario:
Reproducible today with the shipped fixtures. Using `test/SplitterHyperEVM.t.sol` setUp: tokens 1,2 -> ALICE, 3 -> BOB, 4 minted then burned. Constructor reads getCurrentSupply()=3, burnedTokenCount()=1, so SNAPSHOT_SUPPLY=3 and MAX_TOKEN_ID=4 and the check on line 73 passes.
1. Deposit 100 ether -> ownerAllocated=70e18, nftAllocated=30e18, balance=100e18, _claimablePerToken()=30e18/3=10e18.
2. ALICE claims [1,2] -> 20e18. BOB claims [3] -> 10e18. Balance = 70e18. This is the intended end state.
3. The snapshot-collection admin restores id 4 (with the shipped mock this is literally `nft.seed(4, CHARLIE)`; `_ownerOf[4]` is address(0) after the burn so the call succeeds. With `FWATestnetNFT` it is `remint(CHARLIE, 4)`, which is owner-only and, notably, is NOT blocked by `closeMinting()`).
4. CHARLIE calls `claim([4])`. tokenId 4 <= MAX_TOKEN_ID passes (line 112), `ownerOf(4)` returns CHARLIE (line 114), `claimed[4]` is 0, so amount = 10e18 is paid. Balance = 60e18.
Total NFT-side outflow is now 4 x 10e18 = 40e18 against an nftAllocated of only 30e18. `claim()` has no aggregate accumulator and never compares the payout to `nftAllocated`; its only bound is `MAX_TOKEN_ID`, and the constructor's `snapshotSupply + burnedTokenCount == maxTokenId` check is a one-shot point-in-time assertion that nothing re-establishes afterwards.
5. `claimOwner()` now computes grossAmount = ownerAllocated - ownerClaimed = 70e18 and calls `SafeTransferLib.forceSafeTransferETH`, whose first statement is `if lt(selfbalance(), amount) { revert ETHTransferFailed() }` (vendor/fwa-reference-union/lib/solady/src/utils/SafeTransferLib.sol:150-156). Balance is 60e18 < 70e18, so `claimOwner()` reverts and stays reverting until enough new revenue arrives; the same revert hits any legitimate holder who claims last, so the drain is first-come-first-served.
At Ethereum reference scale the same shape gives 324 - 264 = 60 reclaimable ids against a claimablePerToken of 0.652954586925172557 ETH (FWA_ETHEREUM_REFERENCE/Splitter/state-snapshot.json), i.e. ~39.2 ETH diverted out of the owner side in one batch.
findings.impact: Protocol insolvency in the Splitter's core accounting invariant. Value allocated to the owner/secondary-owner side is paid out as if it were NFT-side allocation, and once the balance falls below the next requested amount both `claimOwner()` and the remaining honest holders' `claim()` calls revert with `ETHTransferFailed()` - a permanent DoS of the payout path that only unwinds if new revenue backfills the deficit or the owner waits out the 365-day `sweep()`. Because the snapshot collection's owner will in practice be the same Safe as the Splitter/FWA owner (`VerifyHyperEVMCore.s.sol:68-70` forces `splitter.owner() == fwa.owner() == finalOwner`), this is also an undisclosed admin power to mint claims against the 30% holder pool. On Ethereum this could not happen because `NFT_ADDRESS` is a hardcoded constant pointing at a known, verified collection that is part of the audited deployment; the HyperEVM port replaced that with a constructor parameter whose only validation anywhere in the pipeline is `snapshotNft_.code.length != 0` (SplitterHyperEVM.sol:67, DeploySplitterHyperEVM.s.sol:58, VerifyHyperEVMCore.s.sol:55). Nothing replaced the guarantee the hardcoded address used to provide, and the mainnet runbook step 4.1 asks only to 'Verifier snapshot, shares, owner et secondary owner'.
findings.minimalFix: Restore the invariant on-chain rather than by convention. Minimal and parity-preserving enough: in the constructor require `snapshotNft.burnedTokenCount() == 0`, which forces MAX_TOKEN_ID == SNAPSHOT_SUPPLY so every in-range id is live at deploy and the live-in-range count can never exceed SNAPSHOT_SUPPLY afterwards (burning can only lock funds, never over-issue). The 998 fixture already satisfies this (supply/cap 4/4, TESTNET_998_DEPLOYMENTS.md:19). If burned ids must be tolerated, add a defence-in-depth cap in `claim()` instead: track `uint256 nftClaimed` and require `nftClaimed + amount <= nftAllocated` before the transfer, so over-claim reverts on the NFT side instead of silently consuming the owner side. Additionally make `DeploySplitterHyperEVM.s.sol` assert the chosen collection is supply-frozen (e.g. require a `mintingClosed()`/equivalent to be true and record `highestMintedTokenId()`), and add an explicit line to MAINNET_RELEASE_RUNBOOK step 4.1 requiring proof that no party can mint or restore an id <= MAX_TOKEN_ID.
findings.regressionTest: Add to `test/SplitterHyperEVM.t.sol`, using only the existing `MockSplitterSnapshotNFT`: `testRestoredSnapshotIdCannotOverclaimTheOwnerSide()` - deposit 100 ether, have ALICE claim [1,2] and BOB claim [3], then `nft.seed(4, CHARLIE)` and assert that `vm.prank(CHARLIE); splitter.claim([4])` reverts (or, if the cap fix is chosen, that it reverts with the new error), and assert the standing invariant `address(splitter).balance >= (ownerAllocated - ownerClaimed) + (nftAllocated - totalNftClaimed)` after every claim. Also add `testConstructorRejectsCollectionWithBurnedTokens()` asserting the constructor reverts for the current setUp fixture once `burnedTokenCount() != 0` is rejected. There is currently no solvency assertion anywhere in the suite: `testFuzzEveryDepositIsFullyAllocated` (lines 159-169) only checks that a deposit is fully split.

refutationNotes.reason:
The arithmetic mechanism is real, but every load-bearing claim around it fails on the code.

(1) NOT a port divergence. FWA_ETHEREUM_REFERENCE/Splitter/sources/src/Splitter.sol:101-117 contains the byte-identical one-shot constructor invariant (`if (snapshotSupply + NFT.burnedTokenCount() != maxTokenId_) revert InvalidMaxTokenId();`) and lines 157-183 contain the identical `claim()` with only a MAX_TOKEN_ID bound and no aggregate accumulator. The finding asserts 'On Ethereum this could not happen because NFT_ADDRESS is a hardcoded constant' — but Splitter/state-snapshot.json shows the live Ethereum deployment running with SNAPSHOT_SUPPLY=264 and MAX_TOKEN_ID=324, i.e. 60 burned in-range ids. The audited reference therefore relies on exactly the same unenforced assumption ('the collection cannot restore an in-range id'), and its own NatSpec (Splitter.sol:19-21) states the burned-id semantics deliberately. The only real divergence is address-as-parameter, which FWA_PARITY_MANIFEST.md:206 documents as forced ('la collection Ethereum n'est pas consultable nativement sur HyperEVM').

(2) 'Reproducible today with the shipped fixtures' is misleading. The repro uses MockSplitterSnapshotNFT.seed() (test/mocks/MockSplitterSnapshotNFT.sol:9-13), an access-control-free test double that is never deployed, or FWATestnetNFT.remint(), which is hard chain-guarded to 998/31337 at src/hyperevm/testnet/FWATestnetNFT.sol:48-50 and therefore cannot exist on 999. No contract in this repo that is deployable on chain 999 has a restore/arbitrary-id mint path.

(3) The only actually-deployed configuration is immune. TESTNET_998_DEPLOYMENTS.md:19 records the 998 snapshot fixture at supply/cap 4/4, so burnedTokenCount()==0 and MAX_TOKEN_ID == SNAPSHOT_SUPPLY; at most SNAPSHOT_SUPPLY ids can ever answer ownerOf inside [1,MAX], and a burn+remint round trip cannot over-issue because claimed[tokenId] (SplitterHyperEVM.sol:39,120-121) is keyed by id and is never cleared.

(4) The 'undisclosed admin power' framing is inverted. The value consumed by the over-claim is ownerAllocated — which belongs to the very Safe the finding posits as the attacker (VerifyHyperEVMCore.s.sol:68-70 forces splitter.owner()==fwa.owner()). An owner running this steals from itself; the only coherent threat model is a snapshot collection controlled by a third party, and FWA_SPLITTER_SNAPSHOT_NFT is still 0x0 (.env.mainnet.example:36-37) with MAINNET_RELEASE_RUNBOOK_2026-07-26.md:24 already listing 'Splitter snapshot | collection, max token ID et secondary owner définitifs' as an open pre-launch decision.

(5) The proposed fix is not parity-preserving: `require(burnedTokenCount() == 0)` would reject the Ethereum reference's own configuration (264 + 60 = 324).

What survives is a low-severity deployment-configuration requirement, not a high contract bug: record in the runbook that the chosen 999 snapshot collection must have no path to make ownerOf succeed for an id <= MAX_TOKEN_ID that was not live at construction. The optional defence-in-depth `nftClaimed + amount <= nftAllocated` cap in claim() is reasonable hardening but is a deliberate divergence from a verified contract and should be priced as such.

The arithmetic is correct but the framing and severity are wrong on five verified points. (1) NOT a port divergence: FWA_ETHEREUM_REFERENCE/Splitter/sources/src/Splitter.sol:101-117 has the byte-identical one-shot constructor invariant `snapshotSupply + NFT.burnedTokenCount() != maxTokenId_`, and the *verified Ethereum deployment itself* shipped with SNAPSHOT_SUPPLY=264 and MAX_TOKEN_ID=324 (Splitter/state-snapshot.json:11-28), i.e. 60 ids of exactly the headroom the finding describes. The property is inherited, not introduced. (2) The load-bearing claim 'On Ethereum this could not happen because NFT_ADDRESS is a hardcoded constant' is false: hardcoding binds *which* collection, not whether that collection can re-mint a burned id. The reference is protected solely by the properties of the chosen collection - which is precisely the mitigation available on HyperEVM. (3) Not reachable in the audited artifact set: FWA_SPLITTER_SNAPSHOT_NFT is 0x0 in .env.mainnet.example:36, the only contract in the tree with `remint` (src/hyperevm/testnet/FWATestnetNFT.sol:121) is chain-guarded to 998/31337 at lines 48-50 and cannot exist on 999, and the live 998 snapshot fixture is supply 4 / highest id 4 / zero burns (TESTNET_998_DEPLOYMENTS.md:19), so its headroom is zero. The exploit depends entirely on a future, unaudited contract choice. (4) The actor is the snapshot collection's owner, in practice the same Safe that VerifyHyperEVMCore.s.sol:68-70 forces to own the Splitter - i.e. the same trust class this same auditor files as *info* in the setOwnerShareBps finding, where the owner can already book 100% of every future deposit to itself. Rating a strictly narrower self-rug as 'high' while rating the broader one 'info' is internally inconsistent. (5) Already disclosed and gated: FWA_PARITY_MANIFEST.md:148 and :154 name 'Adresse de collection snapshot configurable au constructeur' as the HyperEVM delta, list 'double claim' and 'mauvaise collection/owners' as its named risks, and mark the collection choice as an outstanding pre-launch gate; :206 gives the rationale. Also, the proposed fix (`require burnedTokenCount()==0`) is itself a divergence - the verified reference could not have been deployed under it. Residual and genuinely actionable: add an explicit 'prove no party can mint or restore an id <= MAX_TOKEN_ID' line to runbook step 4.1 and an assertion in DeploySplitterHyperEVM.s.sol. That is deployment-checklist hardening = low, not high.

findings.title: setRewardsPool made one-shot (the Ethereum reference setPool is rotatable): a rewards-module migration permanently strands 80% of all future buyback proceeds
findings.preconditions: Token launched and rewardsPool bound. Operators later migrate to a new FWARewardsHyperEVM — which the module's own NatSpec states is the intended migration path ("migration deploys a new module so stale and replacement pools cannot both create liabilities here", FWARewardsHyperEVM.sol:231-232) and which FWA.setRewards enforces by being one-shot on the core side too.
findings.scenario: 1) DeployNestModules binds rewardsPool = RewardsV1. 2) A bug, a core migration, or an owner rescueTokens retires RewardsV1; RewardsV2 is deployed against the same FWATokenNest and whitelisted with setDistributor so it can pay claims. 3) FWATokenNest.setRewardsPool(RewardsV2) reverts RewardsPoolAlreadySet (line 222) — there is no rotation and no clear. 4) Every subsequent buyback() still executes lines 387-398 against RewardsV1: it transfers toDep+toPurchaser (80% of amountOut at the default 4000/4000/2000 split) into the retired module and calls RewardsV1.onTokenReceived, which credits accTokenPerSqrt/purchaserEpochPot inside a module nobody is claiming from any more. Those tokens are recoverable only by RewardsV1's owner via rescueTokens, which itself requires the OLD core to report canRescueRewards() == true. The Ethereum reference deliberately allows rotation: FWA_ETHEREUM_REFERENCE/FWAToken/sources/src/FWAToken.sol:200-204 `function setPool(address g) external onlyOwner { if (g == address(0)) revert InvalidAddress(); pool = g; emit PoolSet(g); }`. The port removed that recovery path.
findings.impact: 80% of every future buyback is permanently routed to a dead contract after any rewards migration, and there is no on-chain way to redirect it. The same one-shot also means a single wrong address at deploy time (only `code.length != 0` is checked, line 223) permanently grants that address distributor + protocol-buyer status and permanently points the buyback router at it — if it does not implement onTokenReceived, buyback() reverts forever and all HYPE in the token is locked (see the no-rescue finding).
findings.minimalFix: Restore reference semantics: make setRewardsPool rotatable (keep the non-zero + code.length checks, drop the RewardsPoolAlreadySet guard), and revoke the old address's isDistributor/isProtocolBuyer flags on rotation. Additionally probe the candidate with a staticcall to a marker view (e.g. require IFWARewards(candidate).token() == address(this)) before binding, mirroring the check setAdapter already performs at lines 209-213.
findings.regressionTest: test/FWANestIntegration.t.sol: bind rewardsPool to RewardsV1, run a buyback and assert the routing lands there; deploy RewardsV2, rotate, run another buyback and assert the routing follows and that RewardsV1 lost its distributor/protocol-buyer flags. Add a negative test that binding a contract whose token() != address(this) reverts.

refutationNotes.reason: THE CODE ALREADY PROVIDES THE RECOVERY THE FINDING SAYS DOES NOT EXIST. The parity divergence is real (reference FWAToken.sol:200-204 setPool is rotatable; FWATokenNest.sol:222 reverts RewardsPoolAlreadySet). The asserted consequence is not. (1) 'no on-chain way to redirect it' — setRouteSplit is NOT one-shot (FWATokenNest.sol:232-238). setRouteSplit(0, 0, 10_000) makes toDep + toPurchaser == 0, so buyback (391-398) never transfers to and never calls the stale module; it burns 100%, which is precisely the reference's own behaviour when `pool` is unset. That single owner call also refutes the second half of the finding — 'if it does not implement onTokenReceived, buyback() reverts forever and all HYPE in the token is locked'. (2) 'recoverable only by RewardsV1's owner via rescueTokens, which requires the OLD core to report canRescueRewards()' is incomplete: in a retired module sqrtBackingTotal == 0, so onTokenReceived BURNS the depositor slice (FWARewardsHyperEVM.sol:564-567) rather than stranding it, and the purchaser slice lands in purchaserEpochPot[e] for epochs with acquisitionsInEpoch[e] == 0, which sweepEmptyEpoch (608-619) recovers with NO canRescueRewards gate. (3) The migration premise is weak: FWA.setRewards is one-shot on the core too (FWA.sol:2347-2348), so 'RewardsV2 against the same core' is impossible — a rewards migration is necessarily a core migration in which the token binding is one of many deliberate re-wirings. Worth an info note ('rotatable upstream, one-shot here; setRouteSplit(0,0,10000) is the recovery lever, and consider a token() marker staticcall at bind time mirroring setAdapter:209-213'), not a medium.

The DIVERGENCE is real — FWATokenNest.sol:222 reverts RewardsPoolAlreadySet where FWA_ETHEREUM_REFERENCE/FWAToken/sources/src/FWAToken.sol:200-204 rotates freely — but the stated IMPACT is false, and the impact is what makes it medium.

'80% of every future buyback is permanently routed to a dead contract ... there is no on-chain way to redirect it' is refuted by setRouteSplit, which the finding itself enumerates in finding 13 and then forgets here. One owner transaction, setRouteSplit(0, 0, 10000), makes toDep = toPurchaser = 0 at FWATokenNest.sol:391-392, so the guard `if (toDep + toPurchaser != 0)` at :395 is never taken: no transfer to the stale module, no onTokenReceived call, and toBurn = amountOut is burned at :394. That is byte-for-byte the behaviour of the `rewardsPool == address(0)` branch at :388-389. Buyback proceeds are therefore never stranded in a dead contract — they are burned, which accrues to every holder.

The same one-liner refutes the secondary claim that a wrong bind 'permanently grants distributor + protocol-buyer status and ... buyback() reverts forever and all HYPE in the token is locked'. It does not: split-to-burn restores buyback immediately. And in the scripted path the address cannot be wrong — DeployNestModules.s.sol:88-92 deploys FWARewardsHyperEVM inline and passes that exact address.

Also note the migration premise is thinner than presented: FWA.setRewards is one-shot on the core (FWA.sol:2347), so a rewards migration already requires a new core deployment; carrying the same FWATokenNest across it and losing buyback routing to the new module is a real but bounded cost.

Divergence worth recording at low (restore rotation, revoke flags on rotation, probe token()==address(this) as setAdapter already does at :209-213). Not medium.

findings.title: Buyback price limit is a static absolute anchored to the launch price; ~+10% appreciation permanently reverts every buyback until an owner re-arm, and a third party can force that state cheaply through the recipient-keyed buy gate
findings.preconditions: Market launched; HYPE flowing to the token (requires PROTOCOL_FEE_TO_TOKEN_BPS to be set, see the separate finding).
findings.scenario: finalizeLaunch (lines 357-363) sets buybackSqrtPriceLimitX96 once, to launch sqrtPrice scaled by DEFAULT_BUYBACK_SQRT_LIMIT_BPS=9535 — a price band of exactly ±~10% (computed: (10000/9535)^2 = 1.0999, (9535/10000)^2 = 0.9092). It is never recomputed. buyback() (line 383) passes minOut=0 and relies solely on this absolute limit. Two ways it becomes unreachable: (a) organic appreciation — any sustained move above ~1.10x launch puts the market price on the wrong side of the limit, and Algebra's pool.swap rejects a limitSqrtPrice that is not strictly beyond the current price (and even if it filled zero, FWANestSwapAdapter.buyExactInput lines 124-127 revert PartialFill on any unspent wHYPE), so buyback() reverts; (b) deliberately — FWANestPlugin.beforeSwap gates pre-open buys on `recipient`, not sender (line 125), so while externalBuysEnabled is false ANY address can route a router buy with recipient = address(TOKEN) and push the price past the limit at the cost of donating the bought FWA. Either way buyback() reverts every block. Because FWATokenNest has no HYPE rescue (line 439 receive() with no counterpart), the protocol-fee HYPE piles up unspendable until the owner manually calls setBuybackSqrtPriceLimitX96 — an absolute value that must be re-set by hand every time the price moves, indefinitely. Note the port also inherits BUYBACK_DELAY_BLOCKS=1 unchanged from an Ethereum contract with 12s blocks; on HyperEVM's ~1s small blocks the reserve drains and the caller bounty is paid roughly 12x more often per unit time, a divergence FWA_PARITY_MANIFEST.md:154 flags as a risk ("« un bloc » a autre durée") but no code change addresses.
findings.impact: Buybacks fail closed with the HYPE trapped rather than merely delayed, permanently unless an owner intervenes; a griefer can force that state for the cost of a donated buy; and the correct operating procedure (continuously re-arming an absolute sqrt price) is not documented in any runbook.
findings.minimalFix: Replace the absolute limit with a relative bound computed at call time from the pool's current sqrtPrice (e.g. `limit = currentSqrt * BAND_BPS / TOTAL_BIPS` read from globalState() inside buyback()), keeping the owner override for emergencies; and add an owner-only rescueHype so a stalled buyback path never traps funds. Separately, re-derive BUYBACK_DELAY_BLOCKS for HyperEVM block time (or switch to a timestamp-based delay) so the drain cadence matches the reference's economic intent.
findings.regressionTest: test/FWANestIntegration.t.sol: after launch, execute buys that raise the price above the launch limit and assert buyback() reverts today; assert it succeeds with a relative limit after the fix. Add a test that a third party calling the router with recipient == address(token) while externalBuysEnabled is false succeeds (documenting the gate) and moves the pool price.

refutationNotes.reason: THIS IS EXACT ETHEREUM-REFERENCE BEHAVIOUR, NOT A PORT DIVERGENCE. FWAToken.sol:55-57 declares the same DEFAULT_BUYBACK_SQRT_LIMIT_BPS = 9_535 with the comment 'bounding token-price appreciation during a buyback to roughly 10% until the owner deliberately updates it'; 257-259 sets the same static limit exactly once in launch(); 332-352 passes no minOut and relies solely on that limit plus a PartialFill revert; 218-224 is the same owner-only re-arm. On Ethereum the identical stall arises after ~10% appreciation because v4 rejects a sqrtPriceLimitX96 on the wrong side of spot. The port reproduces it (direction-aware at FWATokenNest.sol:357-363, PartialFill enforced at FWANestSwapAdapter.sol:124-127). Per the audit mandate, reference behaviour is a finding only if the port diverges — it does not. Three further errors: (a) 'the HYPE trapped rather than merely delayed' — the reserve is empty and stays empty because protocolFeeToTokenBps is 0 and no script sets it (the same auditor's finding 6), matching the reference snapshot (balanceWei 0, lastBuybackBlock 0). (b) 'a griefer can force that state cheaply' — forcing >10% against a single-sided 500M position spanning 3600 ticks (~1.43x) consumes roughly a quarter of the sqrt-range, i.e. on the order of 100M+ FWA bought and then donated: the market value of ~10-12% of supply, to move a limit the owner resets in one transaction. (c) BUYBACK_DELAY_BLOCKS — the block-duration divergence is explicitly recorded in FWA_PARITY_MANIFEST.md's 'Buybacks et Splitter' row (Divergence: « un bloc » a autre durée; Risque: cadence accélérée), i.e. a disclosed accepted item, and the economic sub-claim is wrong: CALLER_REWARD_BPS is 50 bps of each slice, so total bounty is 0.5% of all HYPE spent regardless of cadence.

REFUTED as a port defect: every element is exact parity with the verified Ethereum deployment, which the mandate designates as the parity oracle.

(1) Static launch-anchored limit: FWA_ETHEREUM_REFERENCE/FWAToken/sources/src/FWAToken.sol:257 sets buybackSqrtPriceLimitX96 = sqrtPriceX96 * 9535 / 10000 exactly once inside launch() and never recomputes it. FWATokenNest.sol:357-363 is the same computation with the token0/token1 ordering handled. Identical design.

(2) 'Permanently reverts until an owner re-arm' is self-contradictory and is the reference's documented operating model: FWAToken.sol:216-217 NatSpec calls setBuybackSqrtPriceLimitX96 'the hard execution-price floor used by every permissionless buyback ... a protocol bound, not caller-supplied slippage, so a searcher cannot weaken it when poking'. Re-arming is the intended knob, not a defect.

(3) The PartialFill claim is fully parity, and this is the decisive one. FWAToken.sol:349-351 already contains `if (amountSpent != buyAmount) revert PartialFill();` with the identical in-source rationale ('Revert the entire buyback in that case so no ETH becomes untracked and the caller bounty is never calculated from an amount the swap did not actually spend'). FWANestSwapAdapter.sol:124-127 reproduces it. The port did not add a fail-closed behaviour here.

(4) 'No HYPE rescue so funds are trapped rather than delayed' — parity again, FWAToken.sol:456 `receive() external payable {}` with no rescue.

(5) BUYBACK_DELAY_BLOCKS=1 on ~1s blocks is explicitly disclosed in FWA_PARITY_MANIFEST.md:154 ('« un bloc » a autre durée', risk 'cadence accélérée'), which the finding cites itself.

(6) The 'third party forces the DoS cheaply' vector is strictly dominated. Pre-open the griefer must DONATE the entire purchased FWA to address(TOKEN); post-open any ordinary buyer can push the same price with the same capital AND keep the tokens. The closed window therefore offers no cheaper attack than simply buying after open. And with protocolFeeToTokenBps = 0 at launch (finding 7) there is no reserve to strand in the first place.

findings.title: protocolFeeToTokenBps is never configured anywhere in the release, so the buyback engine has no funding source while the product states protocol revenue routes into buybacks
findings.preconditions: Mainnet launch executed as scripted.
findings.scenario: FWA.payoutFees computes `tokenPortion = token == address(0) ? 0 : accrued * protocolFeeToTokenBps / BPS` (FWA.sol:1993) and only that portion is forwarded to the token's buyback reserve (line 1999). `protocolFeeToTokenBps` is declared `uint256 internal protocolFeeToTokenBps;` (line 496) with no initializer, i.e. 0, and is settable only through setUint(FWAConfigKeys.PROTOCOL_FEE_TO_TOKEN_BPS = 23). A repo-wide search across script/, scripts/, all runbooks and the frontend finds zero references to PROTOCOL_FEE_TO_TOKEN_BPS or protocolFeeToTokenBps. DeployHyperEVMMainnetCore sets only WHITELIST_MANAGER, PAYOUT_ADDRESS and TOP_LISTING_SHARE_BPS (lines 97-99); BindNestRewards, ActivateHyperEVMMainnet and ActivateNestMarket set none. So at launch 100% of protocol fees go to the Splitter, 0 HYPE ever reaches FWATokenNest, and buyback() reverts NoHype on every call — the 40/40/20 routing, the burn and the 50 bps caller bounty are all inert. Meanwhile TokenScreen.tsx:64 renders the flat claim "Buy pressure — protocol revenue routes into buybacks (40/40/20 with burn)" and RewardsScreen.tsx:52 repeats it; the docs (docsContent.tsx:488-490) say "Protocol revenue routes into permissionless buybacks". The variable is `internal` with no public getter, so neither VerifyNestModules nor ActivateHyperEVMMainnet can even read it to attest the intended value.
findings.impact: Either the buyback mechanic silently does not exist at launch while the product asserts it does (misleading users about $FWA buy pressure), or an operator sets it ad hoc post-launch with no runbook step, no gate and no attestation. Same blind spot applies to acceptBidAsTokensEnabled, which defaults to `true` (FWA.sol:484) and is also `internal` and never touched by any script — meaning token-denominated settlement is live from the moment rewards are bound, before ActivateNestMarket opens public buys.
findings.minimalFix: Add an explicit PROTOCOL_FEE_TO_TOKEN_BPS step with its intended value to the mainnet runbook and to a deploy script, and assert the resulting value in VerifyNestModules/ActivateHyperEVMMainnet (this requires exposing a public getter or an event-derived attestation, since the storage is internal). Decide and document ACCEPT_BID_AS_TOKENS_ENABLED explicitly relative to the ActivateNestMarket step rather than inheriting the `true` default. Until the value is set, remove or qualify the buyback claims in TokenScreen/RewardsScreen/docs.
findings.regressionTest: Add a mainnet-manifest assertion test that reads the ProtocolFeesToToken event (or a new getter) and fails if protocolFeeToTokenBps is 0 while the frontend advertises buybacks; add a script test asserting ActivateHyperEVMMainnet reverts if the value has not been configured.

refutationNotes.reason: THE FACT IS TRUE BUT IS THE REFERENCE'S DOCUMENTED DEFAULT, AND THE 'MISLEADING UI' HALF IS FACTUALLY WRONG. Repo-wide grep confirms PROTOCOL_FEE_TO_TOKEN_BPS / protocolFeeToTokenBps appear only in the reference and vendored FWA.sol — no script, runbook or frontend touches them. But FWA.sol:493-496 states the intent explicitly: '`0` = off (default) — flip on for Phase 2', and the live Ethereum deployment is in that same state (FWAToken/state-snapshot.json: balanceWei '0', lastBuybackBlock '0' — the reference has never routed a fee or run a buyback). Shipping with the Phase-2 sink off is exact parity with the audited deployment. The 'product asserts buybacks exist' claim does not survive: TokenScreen.tsx:64 sits inside `if (!market.moduleActive)` (lines 50-71) under 'The $FWA market is not live yet'; RewardsScreen.tsx:52 sits inside `if (!rewards.moduleActive)` (41-57) under 'FWA rewards are not activated yet'; docsContent.tsx:488-491 ends the same sentence with 'None of this is live; when it is, it appears under $FWA.' A repo-wide grep for 'buyback' in frontend/src returns only those three plus SwapPanel.tsx:101, an architectural note. No live-state UI claims buy pressure is flowing. The acceptBidAsTokensEnabled=true rider is also parity (FWA.sol:484) and the path it enables routes through rewards.buyFor with recipient = the rewards module, a registered protocol buyer by construction (FWATokenNest.sol:226) — the reference does the same via isPool[sender]. Residual info-level point: the variable is `internal` with no getter, so if Phase 2 is ever flipped no attestation script can read it.

REFUTED by the reference's own on-chain state. I reconstructed the full config history of the verified Ethereum deployment from FWA_ETHEREUM_REFERENCE/FWA/state-events.json: the 22 keys ever emitted via ConfigSet are VRF_COORDINATOR, VRF_SUB_ID, VRF_KEY_HASH, VRF_SERVICE, SURCHARGE_BPS, SETTLEMENT_DISCOUNT_BPS, OWNER_ACQUISITION_FEE_BPS, OWNER_SETTLEMENT_FEE_BPS, SETTLEMENT_WINDOW, FINALIZE_WINDOW, MIN_BACKING, MAX_ACTIVATIONS_PER_ACQUISITION, SELECTION_TIMEOUT_BLOCKS, REQUEST_CONFIRMATIONS, CALLBACK_GAS_LIMIT, TOP_LISTING_SHARE_BPS, TOP_THRESHOLD_BPS, PAYOUT_ADDRESS, WHITELIST_MANAGER, WHITELIST_ENABLED, RETAINED_TO_PROTOCOL, ACQUISITIONS_ENABLED. Key 23 (PROTOCOL_FEE_TO_TOKEN_BPS) and key 44 (ACCEPT_BID_AS_TOKENS_ENABLED) are ABSENT. Corroborated by FWA_ETHEREUM_REFERENCE/FWAToken/state-snapshot.json: balanceWei = 0 and lastBuybackBlock = 0 — the live Ethereum FWAToken has never received a wei of protocol fees and has never executed a buyback. HWA is therefore at EXACT PARITY, not diverging.

The factual observation (no script or runbook sets key 23) is correct but is not a defect: the value is a plain owner setUint, settable at any time post-launch, fully reversible, with zero irreversibility and zero fund impact. Nothing is broken at launch; the mechanic is simply dormant, exactly as on Ethereum.

The acceptBidAsTokensEnabled sub-claim is affirmatively wrong. Token-denominated settlement working before ActivateNestMarket is the DESIGNED behaviour, not a blind spot: acceptBidAsTokens routes through rewards.buyFor -> adapter -> router with recipient = the rewards module, which setRewardsPool marks isProtocolBuyer (FWATokenNest.sol:226). The reference does the identical thing via FWATokenHook.setPool registering FWARewards as a permitted pre-open buyer. That is the entire purpose of the protocol-buyer registry.

Residual: the TokenScreen/RewardsScreen/docs copy describes a mechanism that is unfunded at launch. Faithful to the reference product's own copy, no fund impact — info at most, and only if the team wants to be stricter than fwa.fun.

findings.title: FWATestnetNFT.closeMinting() does not freeze the snapshot: remint() bypasses it, so the 'minting closed' attestation recorded for the 998 Splitter snapshot collection does not mean the snapshot is immutable
findings.preconditions: The collection owner key. The contract is chain-guarded to 998/31337 (lines 48-50) so it cannot be deployed on 999, but it is the only snapshot-collection implementation in the repo and therefore the de-facto template for the mainnet one.
findings.scenario: `closeMinting()` sets `mintingClosed = true`, and `_mintNext` honours it (line 145). `remint(recipient, tokenId)` does not read `mintingClosed` at all: it only requires `isBurned[tokenId]`, then does `++currentSupply; --burnedTokenCount; _mint(recipient, tokenId)`. So after `closeMinting()`, the owner can still burn (anyone holding a token can) and then restore any id, changing which ids in [1, MAX_TOKEN_ID] answer `ownerOf`. The NatSpec on line 104 states this openly ('Burned IDs can still be reminted for tests'), but TESTNET_998_DEPLOYMENTS.md:19 records the Splitter snapshot fixture at 0x8D7b23482FF6c81248727AE50f64f4b337dC0aa4 with state 'minting closed' and no qualifier, and MAINNET_RELEASE_RUNBOOK step 4.1 does not distinguish the two. Concretely on 998 today: the owner can `burn` a snapshot token they hold, `remint` it to a second wallet, and that wallet claims a second full per-token share - which is the precondition of the high finding above. It is currently inert only because the 998 fixture has supply/cap 4/4 with zero burns.
findings.impact: No direct mainnet fund impact (chain guard). The impact is assurance: the recorded 'minting closed' state is not evidence that the Splitter snapshot is frozen, so the 998 smoke-test attestation in TESTNET_998_DEPLOYMENTS.md:138-140 ('zero residual HYPE', 'ids 1 through 4 were claimed') does not demonstrate that the accounting cannot be broken, and the same wording will be reused when the mainnet collection is chosen.
findings.minimalFix: Add `if (mintingClosed) revert MintingIsClosed();` to `remint()` (or delete `remint` and expose it only behind a separate, explicitly named flag), and change the wording in TESTNET_998_DEPLOYMENTS.md:19 from 'minting closed' to a statement of what is actually frozen. Whatever mainnet collection is chosen must have no equivalent path.
findings.regressionTest: In `test/FWATestnetNFT.t.sol` add `testRemintIsBlockedAfterCloseMinting()`: mint id 1, burn it, call `closeMinting()`, then assert `remint(bob, 1)` reverts with `MintingIsClosed`. Add a companion assertion that after `closeMinting()` the pair (`getCurrentSupply()`, `burnedTokenCount()`) can only move in the burn direction.

refutationNotes.reason:
The one true observation (remint() at src/hyperevm/testnet/FWATestnetNFT.sol:121-132 does not read mintingClosed) is already stated verbatim in the contract's own NatSpec at line 104: 'Burned IDs can still be reminted for tests.' Everything built on top of it is wrong.

The concrete scenario — 'the owner can burn a snapshot token they hold, remint it to a second wallet, and that wallet claims a second full per-token share' — is refuted by SplitterHyperEVM.sol:39 and 120-121: `claimed[tokenId]` is keyed by token id and is never reset by a burn or a remint. After burn+remint, the new holder receives `cumulativePerToken - claimed[id]`, i.e. exactly zero if the previous holder already claimed, and at most the single outstanding delta otherwise. There is no second share, so this is not 'the precondition of the high finding above'.

On the actual 998 fixture (supply/cap 4/4, TESTNET_998_DEPLOYMENTS.md:19) MAX_TOKEN_ID == SNAPSHOT_SUPPLY == 4, so no burn/remint sequence can ever place more than SNAPSHOT_SUPPLY live ids inside [1, MAX_TOKEN_ID]; aggregate NFT-side outflow stays bounded by nftAllocated under every ordering. The finding's own 'it is currently inert' concession understates this: it is structurally impossible, not incidentally inert.

The contract is chain-guarded to 998/31337 (lines 48-50) so it cannot touch mainnet, and the residual is a wording preference about one table cell in TESTNET_998_DEPLOYMENTS.md — a documentation opinion, not a defect. A one-word doc edit ('minting closed' -> 'new-id minting closed') is fine to make, but it does not belong in an audit findings list.

The mechanical observation is true (remint at FWATestnetNFT.sol:121-132 does not read `mintingClosed`) but the concrete scenario is arithmetically wrong and the residual is a wording preference. The scenario states: 'the owner can burn a snapshot token they hold, remint it to a second wallet, and that wallet claims a second full per-token share - which is the precondition of the high finding above.' It does not. `claimed[tokenId]` (SplitterHyperEVM.sol:39,120-122) is a per-token cumulative checkpoint that is untouched by burn or remint, so a reminted id pays only `cumulativePerToken - claimed[id]`, exactly like a transfer - proven by the existing testClaimRightsFollowCurrentNFTOwnerWithoutResettingCheckpoint (test/SplitterHyperEVM.t.sol:79-100). Over-claim requires deploy-time burned headroom (a live-in-range id whose `claimed` slot is still 0), not a remint capability; on the actual 998 fixture (supply 4 / max 4 / 0 burned, TESTNET_998_DEPLOYMENTS.md:19) MAX_TOKEN_ID == SNAPSHOT_SUPPLY so burn+remint yields exactly zero extra value. The finding calls it 'currently inert' but then asserts the second-full-share mechanism as fact. Beyond that: the behaviour is explicitly documented in NatSpec on the line immediately above the function (line 104, 'Burned IDs can still be reminted for tests'), `closeMinting` is accurately documented as preventing *new* token IDs and _mintNext honours it (line 145), the contract cannot be deployed on 999 (chain guard, lines 48-50), and the existing test testBurnAndOwnerRemintKeepSnapshotCountersConsistent pins the behaviour as intended. What remains is a request to change one word in a testnet attestation table - a documentation opinion about a chain-guarded test fixture, not a defect.

findings.title: receive() consumes up to 93,652 gas against solady's 100,000 GAS_STIPEND_NO_GRIEF; if it ever exceeds the stipend the payout silently bypasses all accounting and the HYPE is unrecoverable until the 365-day sweep
findings.lines: 94-104 (receive); caller at C:/Users/eliot/Documents/FWA FORK/vendor/fwa-reference-union/src/FWA.sol:1988-2003 (payoutFees, transfer at 1997); library at C:/Users/eliot/Documents/FWA FORK/vendor/fwa-reference-union/lib/solady/src/utils/SafeTransferLib.sol:52 and 149-164
findings.preconditions: Any future change that adds a storage write or an extra event to `receive()`, or any HyperEVM gas-schedule difference from mainnet Ethereum for SSTORE/LOG. No exploit is required and no party chooses the outcome.
findings.scenario: Measured with `./.tools/foundry/forge.exe test --match-contract SplitterHyperEVMTest --gas-report`: `receive` costs min 23,192 and max 93,652 gas over 266 calls. The max is the first deposit, where `totalReceived`, `nftAllocated` and `ownerAllocated` are all zero-to-nonzero SSTOREs. `FWA.payoutFees()` reaches the Splitter through `SafeTransferLib.forceSafeTransferETH`, which forwards a hard-coded `GAS_STIPEND_NO_GRIEF = 100_000` plus the 2,300 value-transfer stipend, i.e. about 102,300 gas - 8,648 gas of headroom, 8.5%. If `receive()` ever exceeds that, the inner `call` fails and solady falls through to `create(amount, <PUSH20 to; SELFDESTRUCT>)`, which deposits the HYPE into the Splitter's balance without executing `receive()` at all. `payoutFees()` still succeeds and still emits `FeesPaidOut`, so nothing anywhere signals failure; `totalReceived`, `nftAllocated` and `ownerAllocated` are unchanged, so NFT holders receive 0% of that payment, `claimOwner()` cannot see it either, and the only path to the funds is the owner-only `sweep()` after 365 days. The same silent-loss path already applies to any force-send (selfdestruct/coinbase) reaching the Splitter today.
findings.impact: Latent silent loss of a full protocol fee payout to the holder side, with no revert, no event and no on-chain reconciliation. Not currently triggerable at 93,652 gas, but the margin is thin, nothing in the test suite pins it (a grep for GAS_STIPEND / 100_000 across `test/` returns nothing), and the failure is only observable as a divergence between `address(splitter).balance` and the accounting totals.
findings.minimalFix: Add a compile-time-checked regression test that pins the worst-case `receive()` gas below `SafeTransferLib.GAS_STIPEND_NO_GRIEF`, and add a public reconciliation view such as `unaccountedBalance() = address(this).balance - (ownerAllocated - ownerClaimed) - (nftAllocated - totalNftClaimed)` so an operator or monitor can detect a bypassed deposit immediately. Do not change `receive()` itself - it is byte-for-byte parity with the verified Ethereum contract - but treat 100,000 gas as a hard budget any future edit must respect.
findings.regressionTest: `testReceiveFitsInForceTransferGasStipend()`: on a freshly deployed splitter, measure `gasleft()` around a raw `call{value: 1 ether}("")` and assert the consumed gas is strictly less than 100_000. findings.title: The Splitter has no read or claim surface anywhere in the HWA frontend or indexer, while an owner-only sweep at day 365 permanently confiscates every unclaimed holder allocation
findings.lines: 26 (splitter address in the manifest schema); C:/Users/eliot/Documents/FWA FORK/src/hyperevm/SplitterHyperEVM.sol:158-169 (sweep), 179-194 (pending views)
findings.preconditions: Mainnet launch as currently scripted: the Splitter is deployed (runbook 4.1) and bound as FWA's PAYOUT_ADDRESS (DeployHyperEVMMainnetCore.s.sol:98), so 30% of every protocol fee accrues to snapshot-NFT holders from the first payout onward.
findings.scenario: `splitter` is a required field of `DeploymentManifestSchema` (manifest.ts:26) but a grep across `frontend/src` finds it referenced only there and in `ViemProtocolClient.test.ts:15` - no component reads `claimablePerToken()`, `pending(tokenId)` or calls `claim()`. A grep across `indexer/` for 'splitter' returns nothing: no data source, no entity, no handler, so `ETHReceived` / `Claimed` / `Swept` are never indexed. Meanwhile `sweep()` (lines 158-169) is callable by the owner from `SWEEP_AVAILABLE_AT` onward with no notice period, takes `address(this).balance` in full - which includes every allocation holders had not yet claimed - and sets `claimsClosed = true` permanently, after which `claim()` reverts with `ClaimsClosed` and `pending()` returns 0 for every token. A snapshot holder therefore has no first-party way to learn a claim exists, and a holder who never manually interacts with the raw contract loses their entire accrued share on day 366.
findings.impact: No fund loss caused by a defect - this is exact behavioural parity with the Ethereum reference - but the deployed product silently accrues a liability to third parties that its own UI and indexer do not expose, and the wind-down that extinguishes it is unannounced. The runbook's decision table and FWA_PARITY_MANIFEST section 9 both describe the 70/30 split as a property of the release without noting that the holder side has no surface and a hard expiry.
findings.minimalFix: Either (a) add a minimal read path: index `ETHReceived`/`Claimed`/`Swept`, expose `claimablePerToken`, `pending(tokenId)` and `SWEEP_AVAILABLE_AT` in the frontend for connected snapshot holders, and surface a claim action; or (b) if the Splitter is deliberately out of the product surface for launch, state that explicitly in the runbook and in the public docs together with the day-365 sweep date, and stop requiring `splitter` in the manifest schema so the address is not implied to be a supported surface. Do not ship the current middle state.
findings.regressionTest: Frontend: a test asserting that if `manifest.contracts.splitter` is present the app renders a holder-facing claim surface (or, under option (b), a schema test asserting `splitter` is optional and unused). Contracts: `testSweepConfiscatesUnclaimedHolderAllocations()` - deposit, let a holder accrue but not claim, warp to `SWEEP_AVAILABLE_AT`, sweep, then assert the holder's `pending()` is 0 and `claim()` reverts with `ClaimsClosed`, pinning the confiscation as intended rather than accidental.

refutationNotes.reason:
The greps are accurate (splitter appears only at frontend/src/config/manifest.ts:26 and ViemProtocolClient.test.ts:15; zero hits across indexer/), but they do not establish a defect.

(1) Nothing is misleading. A grep of frontend/src for '70/30', 'revenue split' and 'snapshot holder' returns zero hits — the product makes no representation to snapshot holders at all. The rubric's 'low' requires misleading UI or fund impact; a silent UI is neither. The finding concedes the contract behaviour is exact parity and that no defect causes the loss.

(2) The premise 'silently accrues a liability to third parties' is unverified. FWA_SPLITTER_SNAPSHOT_NFT is still 0x0000...0000 (.env.mainnet.example:36) and MAINNET_RELEASE_RUNBOOK_2026-07-26.md:24 lists the collection as an undecided pre-launch parameter. If the 999 snapshot collection is team-held — the likeliest outcome, since it must implement the FWA-specific getCurrentSupply()/burnedTokenCount() pair that no third-party Hyperliquid collection exposes — there is no third party and no liability.

(3) `splitter` being required in DeploymentManifestSchema does not 'imply a supported surface'. The manifest is the deployment address record (it likewise requires randomnessCoordinator, which has no user-facing claim surface either), and manifest.ts's own docstring frames it as 'the single source of truth for contract addresses', not a UI contract. Making it optional, as the finding proposes, would weaken the deployment record for no safety gain.

This is a product-scope opinion ('should the splitter be in the launch surface?'), correctly a business decision, not an audit finding. If HWA ever publicly markets the 30% snapshot share, revisit it then — at info.

The greps are accurate but the inference is not, and the finding self-certifies 'No fund loss caused by a defect - this is exact behavioural parity with the Ethereum reference.' The core argument - that a required manifest field implies a supported product surface - is refuted by the schema itself: `randomnessCoordinator` (manifest.ts:25) and `whitelist` (line 23) are equally required and equally unread by any component; the only manifest addresses the frontend actually consumes are contracts.fwa, .rewards, .token and .nestPool (ViemProtocolClient.ts:237,906-907,961,1113-1114). manifest.ts:3-9 defines the file as 'the single source of truth for contract addresses' for fail-closed chain/address checks, not a UI contract, so removing `splitter` would break the registry's purpose without fixing anything. FWA_PARITY_MANIFEST.md:54 classifies the Splitter as `launch-only` + `infrastructure`, i.e. deliberately outside the product surface, so the 'current middle state' the finding refuses to ship is the documented intent. The premised liability to third parties is speculative: FWA_SPLITTER_SNAPSHOT_NFT is unset (.env.mainnet.example:36) and on 998 every snapshot fixture was minted to the deployer (TESTNET_998_DEPLOYMENTS.md). Finally, nothing in the UI claims to enumerate deployed contracts - TermsScreen.tsx:41-49 frames the interface as a convenience layer over public contracts that remain reachable independently - so this is absence of a feature, not misleading telemetry, which is what `low` requires. Worth recording as a launch-scope decision = info.
