findings.title: Depositor-timeout settlements are indistinguishable from purchaser-initiated ones in live mode, but the mock renders them separately
findings.preconditions: A purchaser lets the settlement window lapse and the depositor calls `depositorReclaimNFT` or `depositorReclaimBacking`.
findings.scenario: `depositorReclaimBacking` emits `NFTKept` and `depositorReclaimNFT` emits `DepositorBidAccepted` (FWA.sol:1810, 1823) — byte-identical to the purchaser's own `keepNFT`/`acceptDepositorBid`. The mapping therefore writes `settlement = "kept"` / `"bid_accepted"`, and `getListing`'s on-chain fallback inference (ViemProtocolClient.ts:486-501, based on `ownerOf`) collapses the same way. The economics displayed are correct, but `OUTCOME_LABEL` (PositionsScreen.tsx:26-34) declares `depositor_reclaim_nft` and `depositor_reclaim_backing` keys that live mode can never produce — while the mock engine does produce them (mock/engine.ts:900, 913). indexer/README.md:51-54 discloses the indexer half of this; the mock/live divergence is not covered.
findings.impact: A purchaser who lost the window sees "Bid accepted (HYPE)" — reading as a choice they made — with no signal that the depositor reclaimed after a timeout. Mock-mode QA and screenshots show a distinction production cannot render, so the gap is unlikely to be caught before launch. No fund impact.
findings.minimalFix: Either remove `depositor_reclaim_nft`/`depositor_reclaim_backing` from `Listing["settlement"]` and from the mock engine so mock and live agree, or reconstruct the initiator in the mapping — the information is derivable from `Listing.allocatedAt` plus the settling block timestamp and the live `settlementWindow`, so a handler could set `settlement = "depositor_reclaim_*"` when `block.timestamp >= allocatedAt + settlementWindow`. Add the resulting label to `OUTCOME_LABEL` in both cases.
findings.regressionTest: Type-level plus runtime test: assert `Object.keys(OUTCOME_LABEL)` is exactly the set of settlement strings the indexer and the mock can both produce. Matchstick case emitting `DepositorBidAccepted` for a listing whose `allocatedAt + settlementWindow` has elapsed, asserting the chosen settlement value.

refutationNotes.reason: This is the disclosed limitation, verbatim: indexer/README.md:51-54 states that FWA emits the same economic events for purchaser actions and equivalent depositor timeout actions (NFTKept / DepositorBidAccepted) and that the index 'does not invent an initiator that the event itself does not expose'. That is a deliberate, documented design decision, and the residual claim — that mock/engine.ts:900,913 can produce two settlement labels live cannot — is mock fidelity, not a production defect. More important, the proposed remedy is unsafe and would create a new bug: keepNFT, acceptDepositorBid, acceptDepositorBidAsTokens and relistNFT all go through _allocatedByPurchaser (FWA.sol:1733-1737), which has NO upper time bound — the NatSpec at 1749-1750 and 1762-1763 says 'Available the whole time the listing is allocated'. Inferring settlement = depositor_reclaim_* from `block.timestamp >= allocatedAt + settlementWindow` would therefore mislabel any purchaser who settles late as a depositor reclaim, converting a disclosed absence of information into an actively wrong label on the user's own position.

Refuted on three grounds. (1) It is an explicitly disclosed known limit: indexer/README.md:51-54 states in so many words that FWA emits the same economic events for purchaser actions and equivalent depositor timeout actions (NFTKept / DepositorBidAccepted) and that the index records the outcome faithfully rather than inventing an initiator. I confirmed the contract behaviour at FWA.sol:1810 (depositorReclaimBacking emits NFTKept) and 1823 (depositorReclaimNFT emits DepositorBidAccepted), which is unchanged parity-core code that the mandate says must ship untouched — so there is no HyperEVM divergence to report. (2) The proposed fix is provably wrong. _allocatedByPurchaser (FWA.sol:1733-1737) has no upper time bound — the NatSpec at 1749-1750 says keepNFT is "available the whole time the listing is allocated" — so a purchaser can settle at any point after the window lapses, right up until finalizeUnsettled. Inferring `settlement = depositor_reclaim_*` from `block.timestamp >= allocatedAt + settlementWindow`, as the finding recommends, would mislabel every late purchaser settlement as a depositor reclaim: it replaces a known unknown with confidently wrong data. (3) The only residual — that mock/engine.ts:900, 913 emit depositor_reclaim_nft / depositor_reclaim_backing and depositor_resolved that live mode cannot, leaving unreachable keys in OUTCOME_LABEL (PositionsScreen.tsx:26-34) — is a mock-parity tidy-up that already overlaps the unreachable-ActivityType point in the governance finding. Info at best, not a defect.

findings.lens: FWA core, parity and liability conservation (HyperEVM mainne
findings.title: minBacking ported as the numeric constant 0.01 rather than as an economic value, weakening the anti-sybil floor by ~75x
findings.preconditions: Mainnet 999 with the default `minBacking = 0.01 ether` (0.01 HYPE) left untouched by the deploy script, and whitelisted collections whose floor allows an adversary to accumulate many tokens.
findings.scenario: FWA's own comment (lines 326-331) states the floor exists because 'the acquisition-fee split is a flat share per active listing', so it 'raises the capital cost of sybil fee-farming with many tiny listings'. `FWA_PARITY_MANIFEST.md:62` records the decision as '0.01 HYPE, adaptation native explicite' — the numeral was carried over, not the value. A dust listing at 0.01 HYPE gets weight `1e36/1e16 = 1e20` versus `1e17` for a 10-HYPE listing, i.e. 1000x the selection probability, while earning an identical flat fee share; it also drags the harmonic-mean `acquisitionFee()` down toward the dust value for every purchaser.
findings.impact: No solvency or custody impact — the real gate is that a sybil must hold N allowlisted ERC-721s. But the parameter no longer performs the function the source documents: the capital cost of a dust listing and the price floor of the pool are both roughly two orders of magnitude lower than on Ethereum.
findings.minimalFix: Set `MIN_BACKING` explicitly in `DeployHyperEVMMainnetCore` from a reviewed env value chosen against the allowlisted collections' HYPE-denominated floors, and record the derivation in the parity manifest instead of the bare numeral.
findings.regressionTest: `testMinBackingIsExplicitlyConfiguredAtDeploy`: assert `pool.minBacking()` equals the env-provided value and is not the 0.01 ether default; plus a pricing test asserting the harmonic-mean fee stays above a configured floor when N dust listings are added.

refutationNotes.reason: REFUTED - economic-parameter opinion about a documented decision, not a defect. FWA_PARITY_MANIFEST.md section 4 records the value as '0.01 HYPE, adaptation native explicite' - i.e. this is a reviewed, deliberate parity decision that was written down, not a constant that was carried over unnoticed. The finding concedes both load-bearing points itself: 'No solvency or custody impact' and 'the real gate is that a sybil must hold N allowlisted ERC-721s'. The arithmetic it does present describes the protocol working as designed, not a bug: INVERSE_WEIGHT_NUMERATOR / value is the intended inverse weighting (FWA.sol:817-819, cheaper listings are deliberately more likely to be selected), and feeShare is a flat 1 by design (line 846). Nothing is locked in by not setting MIN_BACKING at deploy: setUint(FWAConfigKeys.MIN_BACKING, ...) (FWA.sol:2281-2282) is owner-callable at any time whenever unsettledAcquisitionCount == 0 and carries no bounds check, so the parameter is fully tunable post-launch with no migration. The cited 'evidence' is a comment in the unmodified Ethereum reference core, which the audit brief explicitly places out of scope for critique unless the HyperEVM port diverges - and here it does not diverge, it matches. There is no reachable state, no adversarial cost asymmetry beyond holding whitelisted NFTs, and no consequence to reproduce. At most an info-level note that the manifest could record the HYPE-denominated derivation next to the numeral.

REFUTED: this is an economic-parameter opinion, not a verified defect, and its central premise is contradicted by the very line it cites.

1. The premise 'the numeral was carried over, not the value' is false. FWA_PARITY_MANIFEST.md line 62 reads `| Backing minimum | 0.01 ETH | 0.01 HYPE, adaptation native explicite |` - the manifest records this as an EXPLICIT native adaptation decision, in the same table that marks other rows 'identique'. The finding quotes that line as evidence of thoughtlessness when it is evidence of a recorded decision.

2. The '~75x' figure rests entirely on an unstated HYPE/ETH price ratio that appears nowhere in the repository, in the manifest, or in the finding itself. An audit finding whose magnitude depends on an undisclosed external price assumption is not a verified defect.

3. 'The deploy script never sets MIN_BACKING' has no on-chain consequence. FWA.sol:2281-2282 accepts MIN_BACKING with no bound at all, subject only to the generic unsettledAcquisitionCount == 0 guard at 2235 - which is trivially satisfied before launch and in any idle window afterwards. The owner can set it at any time, so deferring it out of the deploy script changes nothing about what is achievable.

4. The mechanism is misstated. Inverse weighting (weight = 1e36/value, FWA.sol:819) makes a dust listing MORE likely to be selected and therefore removed from the pool - the pool self-corrects for dust rather than being permanently distorted by it. The real sybil gate is holding N allowlisted ERC-721s from a reviewed collection, which the finding itself acknowledges.

5. The finding concedes 'no solvency or custody impact'. Combined with the above, the correct disposition is info at most - a parameter to review before launch, not an audit finding. Reporting it as a defect in a production audit costs the team review time on a decision they already documented.

findings.title: Duplicate fulfilment reverts instead of no-op, diverging from GelatoVRFConsumerBase and risking a Gas-Tank-draining retry loop
findings.preconditions: Gelato's Web3 Function double-executes for the same RequestedRandomness event, or an operator retries after a successful delivery — both ordinary occurrences in Gelato operations.
findings.scenario: Gelato's reference `GelatoVRFConsumerBase.fulfillRandomness` guards with `if (requestPending[requestId]) { requestPending[requestId] = false; _fulfillRandomness(...); }` — a second delivery is a silent no-op. Here line 148 is `if (request.status != RequestStatus.Pending) revert UnknownRequest();`, so a repeat delivery reverts. A W3F that classifies a reverting execution as 'not yet fulfilled' will re-attempt, each attempt billing the Gas Tank for a transaction that can never succeed. `testTamperedPayloadAndReplayAreRejected` (test/GelatoVRFCoordinator.t.sol:113-114) encodes the reverting behaviour as intended.
findings.impact: No fund or randomness-integrity impact — replay is correctly prevented either way. Operational cost and noisy failed-execution telemetry; in the worst case a retry loop that quietly drains the Gas Tank and thereby triggers the coverage/liveness failure above.
findings.minimalFix: Distinguish the two cases: revert `UnknownRequest` only when `status == RequestStatus.None`; when `status == RequestStatus.Fulfilled`, emit a `DuplicateFulfillmentIgnored(requestId, round)` event and `return` without state change. Keeps replay impossible while matching the base contract's idempotence contract.
findings.regressionTest: `testDuplicateFulfillmentIsIdempotentNotReverting`: fulfil once, capture `fulfilledWord`, fulfil again with the same payload and a DIFFERENT `randomness`, assert no revert, assert `fulfilledWord` unchanged, assert the consumer's callback counter did not increase, and assert `DuplicateFulfillmentIgnored` was emitted.

refutationNotes.reason: REFUTED as a style preference with no defect behind it. The finding itself concedes 'No fund or randomness-integrity impact — replay is correctly prevented either way'. The parity oracle for this contract is the Chainlink VRF v2.5 coordinator surface it emulates for the unmodified core (GelatoVRFCoordinator.sol:14-18, 99, 179, 185, 197), not GelatoVRFConsumerBase, which this contract neither inherits nor claims to implement; reverting on a terminal request is the coordinator-side convention. The reverting behaviour at line 148 is also deliberate and load-bearing for the retry story documented at line 139 and exercised by testCallbackFailureRollsBackAndCanBeRetried (which I ran, passing): a reverting fulfilment is precisely the signal that leaves the request retryable. The only claimed harm — 'a W3F that classifies a reverting execution as not yet fulfilled will re-attempt, each attempt billing the Gas Tank' — is an assumption about Gelato's off-chain executor that cannot be verified anywhere in this repo and runs against how Gelato Web3 Functions work (executions are simulated before submission and only on-chain executions are billed). Reporting an unverifiable external-infrastructure hypothesis as a contract finding is exactly the kind of item that costs an audit credibility.

REFUTED. The code fact is right (line 148 reverts `UnknownRequest` for a non-Pending request), but no defect is demonstrated. The finding itself concedes there is no fund and no randomness-integrity impact — replay is correctly prevented either way. The only claimed consequence, a Gelato Web3 Function retry loop draining the Gas Tank, is pure speculation about off-chain Gelato behaviour with zero supporting evidence in the repository; Gelato Automate simulates before submitting and does not bill executions it never broadcasts. Worse, the proposed change collides with a deliberate and load-bearing design decision here: this coordinator reverts the WHOLE fulfilment when the consumer callback fails so the request stays retryable (line 139 comment; `testCallbackFailureRollsBackAndCanBeRetried`, which I ran and which passes). Converting a non-Pending fulfilment into a silent success would need careful separation from that path for no security gain. This is a style/parity preference against a reference implementation FWA does not inherit from, not a finding.

findings.title: Legacy HyperSwap token/factory/adapter stack ships in the audit manifest as mainnet-unreachable dead code with a materially weaker launch model
findings.preconditions: None — this is a release-hygiene finding.
findings.scenario: release/audit-manifest.json includes src/hyperevm/FWATokenHyperEVM.sol, src/hyperevm/FWATokenHyperEVMFactory.sol, src/hyperevm/FWAHyperSwapAdapter.sol, src/hyperevm/interfaces/IHyperSwapV3.sol and their scripts/tests, but every HyperSwap script is hard-gated to chain 998 (DeployHyperSwapToken.s.sol:45, DeployHyperSwapModules.s.sol:54-55, ActivateHyperSwapMarket.s.sol:30, VerifyHyperSwapModules.s.sol:32) and the mainnet runbook references only the Nest stack. The contracts themselves carry no chain gate, so the weaker variant is deployable on 999 by hand: FWATokenHyperEVM.launch (line 212) mints the whole 500M LP position to an arbitrary `lpRecipient` with no locker — its own NatSpec at line 211 says "The LP NFT remains recoverable on testnet; mainnet locking is a separate explicit gate" — and FWATokenHyperEVMFactory.deployAndLaunch (line 62-66) hands that recipient and the entire non-LP allocation to caller-supplied addresses with only a zero-address check. It also lacks the pool-config assertions, the plugin and the liquidity locker that the Nest variant relies on. Additionally, the only test that exercises FWARewardsHyperEVM's swap path (test/FWARewardsHyperEVM.t.sol:46-48) binds it to FWAHyperSwapAdapter, i.e. the dead adapter — the mainnet FWANestSwapAdapter is never paired with FWARewardsHyperEVM in any test.
findings.impact: A production release ships two token implementations with different security models; a reviewer or an operator reading src/hyperevm/ cannot tell from the contracts which one is canonical, and the weaker one is one manual `forge create` away from being deployed on 999. It also inflates the audited surface with code that cannot be exercised by the mainnet sequence.
findings.minimalFix: Move the HyperSwap variant (contracts, interfaces, scripts, tests, mocks) under an explicitly named archive/ or testnet-only directory excluded from the mainnet release manifest, or delete it. If it is kept, add an in-contract chain guard (`if (block.chainid == 999) revert`) to FWATokenHyperEVM's constructor and to FWATokenHyperEVMFactory.deployAndLaunch so the script-level gate is backed by an on-chain invariant.
findings.regressionTest: Add a manifest test asserting release/audit-manifest.json contains no path matching HyperSwap when the target chain is 999; add a unit test asserting FWATokenHyperEVM's constructor reverts on chainid 999 if the guard is adopted.

refutationNotes.reason: RELEASE-HYGIENE OPINION BUILT ON A MISREAD ARTIFACT, PLUS A DUPLICATE. The facts check out (files present in the manifest; all four HyperSwap scripts hard-gate to chain 998 at DeployHyperSwapToken.s.sol:45, DeployHyperSwapModules.s.sol:54-55, ActivateHyperSwapMarket.s.sol:30, VerifyHyperSwapModules.s.sol:32; FWATokenHyperEVM.launch mints to an arbitrary lpRecipient with NatSpec conceding testnet-only recoverability). But release/audit-manifest.json is the AUDIT INTEGRITY ANCHOR — {schemaVersion, generatedAtUtc, containsSecrets, fileCount 239, files:[{path,bytes,sha256}]} — a hash snapshot of the working tree so the reviewer can prove what was reviewed. It is not a deployment allowlist: it also lists .env.mainnet.example and every markdown doc. Testnet-only contracts belonging to the repo SHOULD be in it; excluding them would be the defect, and the proposed regression test ('assert the manifest contains no path matching HyperSwap when the target chain is 999') would defeat the anchor's purpose. 'One manual forge create away from being deployed on 999' is not an attack — anyone can deploy any bytecode anywhere; the weaker token cannot be wired into the shipped stack because FWA.setRewards is one-shot and requires r.fwa() == address(this) (FWA.sol:2347-2354), and no mainnet script or manifest references it. The one substantive point inside — that FWARewardsHyperEVM + FWANestSwapAdapter are never tested together — is a duplicate of finding 12, where it belongs.

REFUTED on its central premise. release/audit-manifest.json is the AUDIT SCOPE for the whole workspace, not a mainnet bill of materials: of its 239 entries it also lists src/hyperevm/DrandRelayCoordinator.sol, src/hyperevm/testnet/FWATestnetNFT.sol and src/hyperevm/testnet/NestTestnetHarness.sol — all 998-only artifacts that the mandate itself names as a deliberate, disclosed part of this release. Finding HyperSwap files in that manifest is therefore expected, not an anomaly, and the proposed regression test ('assert the manifest contains no path matching HyperSwap when the target chain is 999') would equally have to delete the drand stack the mandate says is in scope.

The safety argument is also thin. All four HyperSwap scripts are hard chain-gated (DeployHyperSwapToken.s.sol:45, DeployHyperSwapModules.s.sol:54-55, ActivateHyperSwapMarket.s.sol:30, VerifyHyperSwapModules.s.sol:32 all `if (block.chainid != 998) revert WrongChain`). 'One manual forge create away from being deployed on 999' is true of every contract in every repository; it is not a property of this stack. And a hand-deployed FWATokenHyperEVM on 999 would be wired to nothing — FWA.setRewards is one-shot and the core is bound to the Nest module — so it is not reachable by the product.

The one substantive sub-claim — that test/FWARewardsHyperEVM.t.sol:46-48 binds FWARewardsHyperEVM to FWAHyperSwapAdapter and that FWANestSwapAdapter is never paired with the rewards module in any test — is TRUE (I confirmed the setUp constructs FWAHyperSwapAdapter over MockHyperSwapV3), but it is finding 11's, where it is already reported. Reduce to info release hygiene.

findings.title: 200M legacy allocation is sent to an unconstrained env address that is neither owner nor distributor, so it can only be dumped into the pool until the owner whitelists a destination
findings.preconditions: FWA_LEGACY_ALLOCATION_RECIPIENT set to an address other than the deployer.
findings.scenario: DeployNestModules transfers LEGACY_ALLOCATION = 200_000_000 ether to `legacyRecipient` (line 99) while the deployer is still the token owner, so the transfer itself passes FWATokenNest's guard via the `from == currentOwner` exemption (line 417-418). Ownership then moves to finalOwner (line 106). From that point the legacy recipient is neither the owner nor a distributor, so _afterTokenTransfer (lines 415-428) permits only: transfers to the pool (a sell), or transfers to/from an address the owner has whitelisted with setDistributor. Nothing in script/, scripts/ or any runbook calls setDistributor for the legacy recipient or for any claim contract — a repo-wide grep returns zero hits. FWA_PARITY_MANIFEST.md:152 and :252 record the 20% v1 allocation and the fate of FWAClaim as an open gate, and the Ethereum reference distributes it through FWAClaim, which is registered as a distributor. The recipient is validated only as non-zero (line 71).
findings.impact: 20% of supply lands in an address whose only unblocked action is selling into the single locked LP position. Distributing it to individual holders is impossible without a per-destination setDistributor call; the intended FWAClaim-style path has no HyperEVM equivalent and no deployment step. If ownership is ever renounced before a claim contract is whitelisted, the allocation is permanently confined to the pool.
findings.minimalFix: Decide the legacy allocation's destination before launch: either deploy a HyperEVM FWAClaim and have DeployNestModules whitelist it with setDistributor and send the 200M there, or require FWA_LEGACY_ALLOCATION_RECIPIENT to be a contract and assert `token.isDistributor(legacyRecipient)` after the transfer. Add an explicit runbook step either way, and gate it behind FWA_TOKENOMICS_CONFIRMED (which the script already requires).
findings.regressionTest: Script/unit test: run the DeployNestModules wiring against mocks with legacyRecipient != deployer, transfer ownership, then assert legacyRecipient.transfer(thirdParty, 1) reverts InvalidTransfer today, and succeeds after the intended setDistributor step is added.

refutationNotes.reason:
REFUTED as a disclosed known limit. This is verbatim open gate #3 in FWA_PARITY_MANIFEST.md:252 — 'Tokenomics de saison : destination des 20 % v1 et maintien ou non de FWAClaim' — and is recorded again at line 152 as 'Gate tokenomics : allocation des 20 % et nécessité de FWAClaim' with the divergence stated as '20 % v1 n'a pas d'équivalent naturel'. MAINNET_RELEASE_RUNBOOK_2026-07-26.md:27 lists 'Tokenomics | allocation 500 M LP / 300 M rewards / 200 M legacy et recipients' among the decisions that must be frozen before any broadcast. The finding cites both lines and then reports the gate as a finding anyway.

The technical detail is accurate and I confirmed it (post-transferOwnership, a transfer from legacyRecipient to a third party falls through FWATokenNest._afterTokenTransfer :415-428 to revert InvalidTransfer; only sells into the pool and owner-side transfers pass) — but it is EXACT PARITY with the verified reference, whose _afterTokenTransfer (FWA_ETHEREUM_REFERENCE/FWAToken/sources/src/FWAToken.sol:434-455) applies the same lock: 'Allow: mints, burns, owner<->anyone, distributor<->anyone, and PoolManager<->anyone ... Everything else reverts — the lock.' On Ethereum the allocation flows through FWAClaim precisely because FWAClaim is registered as a distributor. So this is not a defect discovered in the port; it is the exact reason the gate exists and is already logged.

Fold the transfer-lock detail into the existing tokenomics gate; do not raise it as a separate finding. Info.

findings.title: buyback() passes minOut = 0; its only slippage bound is a static absolute sqrt-price limit fixed at launch
findings.lines: 357-365 (limit derived once in finalizeLaunch), 369-405 (line 383 passes minOut = 0); src/hyperevm/FWANestSwapAdapter.sol:111-121
findings.preconditions: Market launched. For the sandwich variant, external buys open and the owner has widened buybackSqrtPriceLimitX96 to keep buybacks alive after price appreciation.
findings.scenario: finalizeLaunch derives buybackSqrtPriceLimitX96 once from the launch price (sqrtP * 10000/9535 when FWA is token0, sqrtP * 9535/10000 otherwise ≈ a 10% price band) and never updates it. Two consequences. (a) Once the market price moves past that band, Algebra rejects an already-crossed limitSqrtPrice and the pool swap reverts, so buyback() reverts entirely and the HYPE reserve stops being spent until the owner calls setBuybackSqrtPriceLimitX96 — and per the recipient-gate finding an outsider can force this while the market is nominally closed, by buying with recipient = address(token). (b) Once the owner widens the limit far enough to avoid constant re-tuning, the effective slippage tolerance relative to the *current* price becomes as wide as that gap, and because minOut is hardcoded to 0 a searcher can sandwich the permissionless 1-HYPE-per-block buyback across the full width.
findings.impact: Slow bleed of protocol HYPE bounded at ~1 HYPE per block minus two crossings of the 1% pool fee, plus operational stalls of the buyback engine. The shape is inherited from the Ethereum reference (FWA_ETHEREUM_REFERENCE/FWAToken/sources/src/FWAToken.sol:57, 257-259, 386-390), so it is not a port regression — but on HyperEVM the stall is externally triggerable, which the reference's design does not permit.
findings.minimalFix: Derive the limit from the live pool price at call time inside buyback() (read globalState().price and apply the 9535 bps factor in the correct direction for the token orientation), keeping the owner-set absolute value as an outer bound rather than the sole bound. Optionally back minOut with a short TWAP maintained by the plugin.
findings.regressionTest: Fork test: launch, appreciate the price 15% with a legitimate buy, then assert buyback() still executes and that the realised price is within the intended band of the pre-swap pool price.

refutationNotes.reason: REFUTED. Three independent reasons. (1) Out of mandate: the finding concedes the shape is inherited byte-for-byte from the parity oracle (FWA_ETHEREUM_REFERENCE/FWAToken/sources/src/FWAToken.sol:56-57 DEFAULT_BUYBACK_SQRT_LIMIT_BPS = 9_535, launch() derives the limit once, unlockCallback swaps with sqrtPriceLimitX96 only and no minOut). I verified the port's orientation handling is actually CORRECT in both directions — FWATokenNest.sol:357-359 uses 10000/9535 when FWA is token0 (price rises on a buy, so the limit must be above) and 9535/10000 when FWA is token1 (matching the reference, where FWA is currency1) — both yielding the same intended ~10% appreciation band. That is a faithful port, not a divergence. (2) The stall behaviour is the reference's stated design intent, not a defect: the reference comment says the limit bounds appreciation 'until the owner deliberately updates it'. It fails closed and is cleared by one owner tx (setBuybackSqrtPriceLimitX96, :240-244, which additionally cannot be set to an out-of-range value). (3) The sandwich claim does not survive arithmetic. Buyback is capped at BUYBACK_INCREMENT = 1 ether per block (:34, :376) and the pool fee is 1% (POOL_FEE = 10_000 in Algebra 1e-6 units), so a sandwicher pays ~2% round-trip on their own size A to extract roughly V*(A/L) from a victim of size V; that is profitable only when V/L > ~2%, i.e. when a sub-1-HYPE buyback is more than 2% of a pool seeded with 500M FWA. It is not, by orders of magnitude. The only genuinely port-specific element — 'on HyperEVM the stall is externally triggerable' — is not a separate defect but a restatement of the recipient-gate finding, and is already counted there.

REFUTED - this is faithful parity with the oracle, and the behaviour it describes is the reference's explicitly documented intent, not a defect. The finding itself concedes 'it is not a port regression', which under the audit mandate ('findings in the reference only matter if the HyperEVM port DIVERGES') ends the matter. I verified the parity claim rather than taking it: FWA_ETHEREUM_REFERENCE/FWAToken/sources/src/FWAToken.sol:57 carries the identical DEFAULT_BUYBACK_SQRT_LIMIT_BPS = 9_535 with the natspec 'bounding token-price appreciation during a buyback to roughly 10% until the owner deliberately updates it' - the owner re-tune the finding calls an 'operational stall' is the stated design, and the reference's buyback likewise passes no minOut (it swaps straight against poolManager with sqrtPriceLimitX96 alone). The port is if anything stricter: FWATokenNest.sol:357-361 handles both token orientations correctly (10000/9535 up when FWA is token0, 9535/10000 down otherwise, matching the reference's ETH-token0 case) and clamps BOTH rails, where the reference clamps only the floor; and FWANestSwapAdapter.sol:124-134 adds PartialFill, NoTokenOut, SlippageBuy and OutputMismatch checks on top. The only claim of divergence - 'on HyperEVM the stall is externally triggerable' - is not an independent defect but a restatement of the recipient-gate finding, and is weak on its own terms because the protocol's own permissionless 1-HYPE-per-block buybacks walk the price into the same ceiling with no outsider involved. Nothing here should be filed separately; fold the one real observation into the recipient-gate finding.

findings.title: VerifyNestModules does not attest the closed state, the fee recipient, or the buyback price limit
findings.preconditions: Phase 7 attestation run before NEST_E2E_CONFIRMED is set.
findings.scenario: The script asserts thirty-plus wiring invariants but never reads token.externalBuysEnabled() — the single property phase 7 exists to prove — never reads FWANestLiquidityLocker.feeRecipient(), and never checks token.buybackSqrtPriceLimitX96() != 0. Those are precisely the fields implicated by the fee-collection brick and by the buyback-limit stall, so the attestation can pass while both are misconfigured.
findings.impact: The launch-gate attestation gives false assurance on the exact parameters most likely to be wrong. No direct fund impact.
findings.minimalFix: Add three reads to the InvalidWiring condition: token.externalBuysEnabled() must be false, locker.feeRecipient() must be non-zero and must be a registered distributor (or the owner), and token.buybackSqrtPriceLimitX96() must be non-zero.
findings.regressionTest: Run VerifyNestModules against a fixture where externalBuysEnabled has been flipped true and assert it reverts InvalidWiring.

refutationNotes.reason: REFUTED — two of its three recommendations target states that are unreachable by construction, and the third is already covered by the runbook. (a) 'locker.feeRecipient() must be non-zero': FWANestLiquidityLocker.sol:32-36 reverts InvalidAddress on a zero feeRecipient in the constructor and :55 reverts again in setFeeRecipient, so feeRecipient can never be zero. The check would always pass. (b) 'token.buybackSqrtPriceLimitX96() must be non-zero': finalizeLaunch clamps rawLimit to at least MIN_SQRT_RATIO + 1 (FWATokenNest.sol:360-363) and setBuybackSqrtPriceLimitX96 reverts InvalidRange for anything <= MIN_SQRT_RATIO (:241), while VerifyNestModules.s.sol:56 already requires token.launched(). A zero value is therefore unreachable and the check is a provable no-op. (c) 'never reads token.externalBuysEnabled()' is factually true but is not an attestation gap in practice: NEST_DEPLOYMENT_RUNBOOK.md:63 already lists externalBuysEnabled() == false as an explicit phase-5 acceptance check, and the only way the flag can be true is a deliberate owner tx (setExternalBuysEnabled is onlyOwner and reverts MarketNotLaunched before launch). Reading it back in VerifyNestModules would be mildly nice defence in depth, but a finding whose stated premises are two-thirds unreachable should not appear in the report; at most this is an info-level suggestion folded into the fee-recipient finding, where attesting that feeRecipient is a registered distributor does carry real content.

REFUTED - two of the three proposed checks are provably always-true, and the third would break the script. (1) `token.buybackSqrtPriceLimitX96() != 0` is vacuous: it is written unconditionally inside finalizeLaunch (FWATokenNest.sol:355 sets launched = true, :360-363 sets the limit with a floor clamp to MIN_SQRT_RATIO+1, same transaction, no early return between them), and setBuybackSqrtPriceLimitX96:241 rejects anything <= MIN_SQRT_RATIO - so `launched`, which VerifyNestModules ALREADY asserts at line 56, mathematically implies a non-zero limit. (2) `locker.feeRecipient() != 0` is equally vacuous: the constructor (FWANestLiquidityLocker.sol:34-36) rejects address(0) and setFeeRecipient:55 rejects both address(0) and address(this). Neither is a gap; adding them attests nothing. (3) `externalBuysEnabled() == false` is genuinely absent, but hard-coding it into the InvalidWiring condition would make the wiring verifier permanently unrunnable the moment trading legitimately opens, and it duplicates a check the runbook already performs at phase 5 (NEST_DEPLOYMENT_RUNBOOK.md:63, 'externalBuysEnabled() == false' in the post-launch control list). The only defensible residue - attesting that feeRecipient is a distributor or the owner - belongs to the fee-collection finding, not here. No code defect, no fund impact, and the 'false assurance' framing does not hold once two of the three attestations are shown to be tautologies.

findings.title: The 365-day claim window starts at Splitter deployment, which the runbook places before the core, Nest, verification and the canary - there is no on-chain link between the sweep clock and the start of revenue
findings.lines: 80 (SWEEP_AVAILABLE_AT = block.timestamp + SWEEP_DELAY); C:/Users/eliot/Documents/FWA FORK/MAINNET_RELEASE_RUNBOOK_2026-07-26.md:53-55 (step 4.1) versus sections 4.2-4.4, 5.1-5.5 and 6
findings.preconditions: Any elapsed time between the Splitter deployment broadcast and the moment acquisitions are enabled.
findings.scenario: `SWEEP_AVAILABLE_AT` is fixed in the constructor from `block.timestamp`, and the Splitter is the very first mainnet broadcast (runbook 4.1). Everything that must happen before the first HYPE can reach it comes after: core + Gelato coordinator (4.2), the whole Nest market lifecycle (4.3), rewards binding and three verification scripts (4.4), Gelato task creation and Gas Tank funding (5.1), manifest, indexer publication, metadata allowlisting and block-explorer source verification (5.2-5.5), then the read-only canary phase and only then public promotion (6). Source verification and the canary alone are realistically multi-day. Every day of that sequence is subtracted from the holder claim window, and nothing on-chain notices: `SWEEP_AVAILABLE_AT` is immutable and unrelated to `totalReceived`.
findings.impact: Holders' effective claim window is 365 days minus the full launch sequence, not 365 days of revenue. No loss beyond that shortening, and it is parity with the Ethereum reference (which sets the same immutable at construction). Recorded so the launch team can decide deliberately.
findings.minimalFix: No contract change required for parity. Either deploy the Splitter as late in the sequence as the dependency graph allows (DeployHyperEVMMainnetCore only needs the address and `splitter.owner() == finalOwner`, so it can immediately precede 4.2 rather than lead the launch), or record the resulting `SWEEP_AVAILABLE_AT` timestamp in the release notes and treat it as the published claim deadline. If a deliberate change is acceptable, gate `sweep()` on 365 days since the first accounted deposit instead of since deployment.
findings.regressionTest: `testSweepAvailableAtIsAnchoredToDeployment()` already implied by `testConstructorCapturesSameSnapshotInvariantsAsFWA` (line 37); add a release-gate assertion in `scripts/` that reads `SWEEP_AVAILABLE_AT` from the deployed splitter and fails the mainnet manifest write if more than N days have already elapsed since deployment when `acquisitionsEnabled` is first set true.

refutationNotes.reason:
Factually correct (SplitterHyperEVM.sol:80 fixes SWEEP_AVAILABLE_AT from block.timestamp, and runbook 4.1 is the first broadcast) but non-actionable, and its headline remedy is already implemented.

The finding proposes 'deploy the Splitter as late in the sequence as the dependency graph allows... so it can immediately precede 4.2 rather than lead the launch'. In MAINNET_RELEASE_RUNBOOK_2026-07-26.md, 4.1 *is* immediately followed by 4.2, and DeployHyperEVMMainnetCore.s.sol:98 consumes the splitter address inside the core deployment sequence (`fwa.setAddr(FWAConfigKeys.PAYOUT_ADDRESS, splitter)`), so the splitter cannot be moved any later without switching to the BindSplitter path. Everything the finding lists as 'coming after' (4.3 Nest, 4.4 rewards, 5.x, 6 canary) is downstream of the core and is therefore unavoidably downstream of the splitter. The recommended reordering is a no-op.

Magnitude: the residual shortening is the launch duration — days out of 365, under 1% of the window — and it is exact parity with the reference, which sets the same immutable at construction.

The one useful line ('publish the resulting SWEEP_AVAILABLE_AT as the claim deadline in the release notes') is a release-note item, not an audit finding, and the alternative ('gate sweep() on the first accounted deposit') is a deliberate divergence from a verified contract that the finding itself does not recommend.

The observation is factually correct but has no consequence and its own remedy is already in place. The proposed fix says the Splitter 'can immediately precede 4.2 rather than lead the launch' - runbook step 4.1 *is* immediately followed by 4.2, and DeployHyperEVMMainnetCore.s.sol:97 (`fwa.setAddr(FWAConfigKeys.PAYOUT_ADDRESS, splitter)`) binds the payout at core construction, so the Splitter must precede the core; the only way to defer it is BindSplitterHyperEVM, which `grep -rn BindSplitterHyperEVM` over all .md/.ps1/.sol shows is referenced nowhere outside its own definition. So no reordering is available and none is needed. Substantively: sweep() is a discretionary owner right gated by onlyOwner (SplitterHyperEVM.sol:158-159), not an automatic expiry - nothing forces a day-365 sweep, and claims accrue and remain claimable throughout; the magnitude is de minimis (even a two-week launch sequence is under 4% of 365 days); and SWEEP_AVAILABLE_AT is construction-anchored in the verified reference too (reference Splitter.sol:114), so it is exact parity. This is an operational preference with no verifiable consequence, not an observation that changes any launch decision.

findings.title: On-chain BLS verification is possible for the evmnet beacon the repo already pins, and is not implemented anywhere
findings.preconditions: None — design observation.
findings.scenario: DrandRelayCoordinator pins drand evmnet (chain hash 0x04f1e9062b8a81f848fded9c12306733282b2727ecced50032187751166ec8c3, genesis 1727521075, 3 s period) and accepts a 64-byte signature, but its header states it 'intentionally does NOT verify the drand BLS signature onchain'. evmnet is the bls-bn254-unchained-on-g1 beacon, designed specifically so that signatures verify with the EVM's BN254 pairing precompile; the 64-byte signature length is exactly a G1 point. The runbook's justification for the mainnet design (line 38, 'la preuve BLS est vérifiable hors chaîne et non directement dans l'EVM') is true for Gelato's quicknet (BLS12-381, GelatoVRFCoordinator.sol:22 genesis 1692803367) but false for the beacon this codebase already uses.
findings.impact: No live impact, but it is the root of the critical trust finding: the project holds a verifiable beacon in one hand and ships an unverifiable one to mainnet, on the strength of a general claim that is not true of the verifiable one.
findings.minimalFix: Implement `_verifyBeacon(uint64 round, bytes calldata signature)` in DrandRelayCoordinator using the ecPairing precompile against the pinned evmnet group public key and `H(abi.encodePacked(round))` hashed to G1, then use the same construction as the mainnet source (Gelato retained only as delivery transport, or replaced).
findings.regressionTest: Reuse the real fixture already present at test/FWADrandRelayIntegration.t.sol:212-214 (evmnet round 19,159,982): assert `fulfillRandomness` succeeds with the genuine signature and reverts `InvalidSignature` for that signature with any single byte flipped.

refutationNotes.reason: REFUTED as a disclosed known limit restated as a finding. The audit brief explicitly discloses 'Gelato does not support HyperEVM testnet so 998 uses a supervised drand relayer without on-chain BLS' — this finding is that limit, targeting the testnet-only contract, whose own header at DrandRelayCoordinator.sol:13-18 states the choice openly ('it intentionally does NOT verify the drand BLS signature onchain. Anyone can audit every fulfillment against evmnet…') and whose runbook repeats it at DRAND_GELATO_RANDOMNESS_RUNBOOK.md:16. The finding's own preconditions field reads 'None — design observation', and its impact field concedes 'No live impact'. There is no defect: no state is reachable that the code fails to handle, nothing is mis-implemented, and the contract is scoped out of mainnet by the three script guards verified under finding 6. The one substantive assertion it adds — that mainnet randomness is not verified on-chain — is already fully carried by finding 1 at critical, where the fix belongs; duplicating it here as a separate item against the testnet contract adds no launch-actionable content and would pad the report.

REFUTED on three grounds. First, it re-reports a disclosed known limit: the audit brief states outright that 'Gelato does not support HyperEVM testnet so 998 uses a supervised drand relayer without on-chain BLS', and the contract header (DrandRelayCoordinator.sol:13-18) says the same thing explicitly and deliberately. Second, its central rhetorical claim is a misreading. DRAND_GELATO_RANDOMNESS_RUNBOOK.md:38 reads 'Gelato précise aussi que la preuve BLS est vérifiable hors chaîne et non directement dans l'EVM' — an attributed statement by Gelato about Gelato's own quicknet beacon, not a project claim about evmnet. Calling it 'false' and building 'the project ships an unverifiable beacon on the strength of a claim that is not true' on top of it does not survive reading the sentence. Third, the substance is a redesign proposal — implement BN254 pairing verification — for a contract that the scripts confine to chain 998 and that the disclosed limits already place out of scope, with the finding itself stating 'no live impact'. The underlying trust concern for MAINNET is already captured, correctly, by finding #1; restating it here as a separate item against the testnet contract adds no verified defect. Design opinion, not a finding.

findings.title: The launch latch uses persistent storage where the Ethereum reference deliberately uses transient storage
findings.preconditions: None — this is a structural observation about the latch, not a reachable exploit today.
findings.scenario: The reference stores launching() in transient slot 1 with the explicit rationale "Transient (slot 1) so it is only ever true within this call — pool init can't be front-run and the window can't be left open." The port uses a plain storage bool set true/false around the external calls in initializeMarket and finalizeLaunch. While _launching is true, FWANestPlugin.beforeInitialize and beforeModifyPosition(liquidityDelta > 0) both open. I traced every external call inside both windows — Nest's position manager, the pool, the plugin, and the locker's view-only onERC721Received — and none hands control to attacker-supplied code with trusted tokens (FWA itself and wHYPE), so the window is not reachable today. But the guarantee has degraded from an EVM property to an argument about the current Nest call graph, which changes if Nest ever upgrades the position manager or if a non-view receiver is introduced.
findings.impact: No exploitable path found. Loss of a structural safety property relative to the parity oracle.
findings.minimalFix: Use transient storage for the latch (tstore/tload), matching the reference. evm_version is already cancun in foundry.toml, so TSTORE is available.
findings.regressionTest: Assert token.launching() == false in the same transaction immediately after a reentrancy-probing mock position manager calls back into the token during finalizeLaunch.

refutationNotes.reason: REFUTED as a defect; the specific safety property it claims was lost is in fact preserved. The reference's own rationale (FWAToken.sol:270-312) is that transient storage means 'pool init can't be front-run and the window can't be left open'. In the port, the window equally cannot be left open: _launching is set at FWATokenNest.sol:272 and cleared at :274 inside initializeMarket, and set at :328 and cleared at :347 inside finalizeLaunch, with no early return, no low-level call that swallows a revert, and no branch between; any revert after the set unwinds the storage write, so _launching is false in every observable post-transaction state. Within a transaction, tload and sload behave identically for this read, so there is no reachable difference in the gate FWANestPlugin.beforeInitialize (:76) and beforeModifyPosition (:92) evaluate. The finding itself confirms no exploitable path after tracing every external call in both windows. What actually remains is a gas difference and an aesthetic parity preference, which the mandate places out of scope ('findings there only matter if the HyperEVM port DIVERGES ... or if a divergence is required by HyperEVM and was done wrong'). Labelling it category contract-bug is also wrong — nothing behaves incorrectly. If the team wants the tstore form for cheapness that is fine, but it does not belong in an audit report even at info, because it invites a code change to a correct launch path days before mainnet.

REFUTED - transient and persistent storage are behaviourally identical here, so there is no property to lose. The reference's two stated rationales both already hold in the port. (a) 'The window can't be left open': _launching is set and cleared unconditionally with no early return or conditional branch between the pair in either window (FWATokenNest.sol:272 set / 274 clear around one external call; :328 set / :347 clear around _approve, POSITION_MANAGER.mint, _approve), and any revert inside those calls rolls the storage write back with the whole transaction. There is no execution path that returns successfully with _launching == true, and no path that persists it across transactions. (b) 'Pool init can't be front-run': the port gets this from FWANestPlugin.beforeInitialize:76, which reverts NotLaunching for any third-party initialize once the plugin is installed - the same protection by a different mechanism. The one residual risk the finding actually describes - a callback re-entering while the latch is open and adding liquidity via beforeModifyPosition:92 - is COMPLETELY UNAFFECTED by the storage class, because tload(1) returns 1 inside that same transaction exactly as sload does; the reference has identical intra-transaction exposure. The finding also concedes it traced every external call and found no reachable path. This is a stylistic parity preference with zero behavioural delta, not an observation worth a line in the report.
